terms.name: accuracy
terms.abstract: Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions made by a hypothesis on a dataset with a finite label space, equal to one minus the average 0/1 loss. It is widely used as a single-number metric for classification methods. Accuracy is not suitable as an objective function for training, since the 0/1 loss is non-smooth and non-convex. empirical risk minimization uses a surrogate loss instead, a convex or smooth approximation of the 0/1 loss, and accuracy is reported on a validation set or a test set. On imbalanced data, accuracy alone cannot tell a classifier from a baseline that ignores the features, which calls for other means of evaluation such as the confusion matrix.
terms.description: Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions made by a hypothesis h: X → Y on a dataset D = (x(r), y(r) ) r=1m with a finite label space Y. With the 0/1 loss zh, which is 1 for a wrong prediction on the data point z and 0 otherwise, accuracy is \begin{align*} \operatorname{acc}(\hypothesis|\dataset) & \defeq 1 - \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunczo{\big(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}, \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)}\big)}{\hypothesis} & = \frac{1}{\samplesize} \Big| \Big\{ \sampleidx \in \{1, \,\ldots, \,\samplesize\} : \hypothesis\big(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big) = \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} \Big\} \Big| \text{.} \end{align*} Accuracy ranges from 0 (no prediction is correct) to 1 (every prediction is correct). Equivalently, accuracy equals one minus the average 0/1 loss on the dataset. For example, in image classification with the label space Y = cat, dog, bird, the hypothesis assigns each image, represented by its feature vector x, a category h(x). Accuracy is then the fraction of images whose assigned category equals the true label y: 94 correct assignments among 100 images give an accuracy of 0.94. Fig. 1 compares two classifiers on the same training set D(train) of 60 data points, the dataset from which both were learned. The linear classifier h misclassifies three data points near its decision boundary. The nonlinear classifier h' curves around each of these data points and classifies them correctly. % Data generated by pythondemos/accuracy.py The classifier h' in Fig. 1 achieves the optimal accuracy of 1 on D(train): its decision boundary closely follows the positions of the individual data points that the linear classifier misclassifies. As a result, h' is sensitive to small perturbations of the feature vectors, such as measurement noise. A slight shift in the feature vector of a data point near the decision boundary can flip the prediction. Optimizing accuracy on the training set therefore does not by itself ensure good generalization. Good generalization means a small loss on data points outside the training set, such as new measurements of the same kind. Accuracy is often used as a single-number metric to compare learned classifiers: on a validation set, to select among candidate hypotheses during validation, and on a test set, whose data points entered neither training nor selection, to assess the selected hypothesis. It is not suitable as an objective function for training. Accuracy is defined via the 0/1 loss, which is non-smooth and non-convex. The 0/1 loss is constant except where a prediction flips, so its gradient with respect to the model parameters is zero wherever it exists and indicates no direction of improvement. gradient-based optimization methods therefore cannot maximize accuracy directly. Instead, training methods for classifiers, e.g., via empirical risk minimization, use a surrogate loss that approximates the 0/1 loss and is chosen convex or smooth, so that those methods have a gradient to follow . Two widely used examples for such a surrogate loss are the logistic loss, which is convex and smooth, and the hinge loss, which is convex but not differentiable. Fig. 2 shows the three loss functions as functions of the margin, for binary classification with Y = -1, 1, where a real-valued hypothesis h predicts via the sign of h(x). Each loss function depends on the data point only through the margin y · h(x). The hinge loss lies above the 0/1 loss everywhere; the logistic loss equals ln 2 at margin 0, so it is the logistic loss scaled by 1 / ln 2 that lies above the 0/1 loss. Accuracy can also be misleading for imbalanced data. Consider a frost warning for Krems an der Donau (Austria): the features of a data point are the minimum and the maximum air temperature of one day, and its label indicates whether the minimum temperature of the following day falls below 0 ∘C. Frost days are the minority class: only 6 of 40 recorded days are followed by frost. The constant prediction ``above zero'' (a baseline that ignores the features) is therefore correct on 34 of the 40 days, an accuracy of 0.85, and a classifier learned by logistic regression from the 40 data points reaches the same accuracy of 0.85. Both make 6 errors and 34 correct predictions on the 40 days, so accuracy cannot tell the two apart; they differ in where they are right, which calls for other means of evaluation such as the confusion matrix. The confusion matrices in Fig. 3 show that the learned classifier detects one of the six frost days and raises one false alarm, while the baseline detects none and raises none.

terms.name: artificial neural network (ANN)
terms.abstract: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a hypothesis space whose hypothesis maps are all built on one directed graph. Each hypothesis in this space is a map from the features of a data point to a prediction for the label, obtained for a particular choice of the learnable model parameters carried by the graph's edges (edge weights) and nodes (offset terms). Each node is an artificial neuron that applies an activation function to the weighted sum of its inputs plus its offset. The connectivity pattern, the architecture, is an important design choice: a feedforward network uses a directed acyclic graph, whereas a recurrent neural network allows a cycle. Depending on the connectivity, ANNs include deep nets, CNNs, RNNs, and transformer-based architectures.
terms.description: The face recognition of a smartphone camera and the speech transcription of a voice assistant are computed by ANNs whose connection strengths were learned from data . An ANN is a hypothesis space whose hypothesis maps are all built on one directed graph: the graph fixes which artificial neurons feed which. A choice of the edge weights and offset terms then selects one hypothesis map, from the features of a data point at the input to an output used as the prediction for the label. The nodes of the graph represent elementary computational units, the artificial neurons; these are connected via weighted links (or edges), and the nodes are often assigned offset terms. Together with the edge weights, these offset terms form the learnable model parameters w of an ANN, and each map in the space is obtained for a particular choice of w: the learned hypothesis h = h(w) is one such choice. Each artificial neuron applies an activation function σ(·) to the weighted sum of its inputs plus an offset term (Fig.~1). The activation function can itself carry model parameters (parametric activation functions, ), but it is customarily prescribed in advance, for example the rectified linear unit , so that only the node-wise offset and the edge weights are learned. The output of a neuron can be used either as the final output of the ANN or as an input to other neurons. The directed graph of the ANN records these uses: its nodes are the artificial neurons together with the input features, and each directed edge carries the output of one node to the input of another (Fig.~2). Which outputs are connected to which downstream neuron's inputs, the connectivity structure (or architecture) of the ANN, is therefore an important design aspect . Whether the graph is acyclic or contains a cycle separates the two broad families of ANN. The graph of Fig.~2 is acyclic, so this ANN is feedforward : the signal passes from the inputs to the output without returning to any node. One widely used type of ANN is deep nets where neurons form consecutive layers (Fig.~3). In a deep net, the outputs of neurons in a given layer are typically only connected to the inputs of the neurons in a consecutive layer. By contrast, in the general directed acyclic graph of Fig.~2 an output may feed any downstream neuron, and there x1 connects straight to the prediction. Each layer l then applies a feature transformation Φ(l) whose components are computed by the neurons of that layer (each as in Fig.~1), and the deep net computes the concatenation of these layer-wise maps. A shortcut or skip connection directly connects the outputs of neurons in one layer to the inputs of neurons in a nonconsecutive layer; Fig.~3 shows one as a dashed edge. With that edge removed, the network of Fig.~3 delivers the prediction \hypothesis^{(\weights)}(\featurevec) = \featuretrafovec^{(3)}\Big(\featuretrafovec^{(2)} \big(\featuretrafovec^{(1)}(\featurevec)\big)\Big) \text{.} Here, the input is the feature vector x = (x1, x2, x3)ᵀ. The two hidden layers compute Φ(1), Φ(2): R3 → R3, and the output layer computes Φ(3): R3 → R. The graphs seen so far are acyclic. A recurrent neural network instead includes a feedback edge , so its graph contains a cycle and is not a directed acyclic graph (Fig.~4): a self-loop feeds a neuron's output back to its own input. This feedback lets the network carry information across the steps of a sequence; unrolling the recurrence over the sequence, one copy of each neuron per step, recovers a directed acyclic graph. The networks of Figs.~2, 3, and 4 differ only in which nodes their directed edges join. This connectivity pattern names the common architectures. Feedforward networks have an acyclic graph, a directed acyclic graph (deep nets are the layered case), while CNNs are also feedforward but share weights across spatial positions. RNNs add feedback connections for sequence processing, and transformer-based architectures, which underlie modern LLMs, are likewise feedforward and use attention to connect every token to every other. skip connections recur across these architectures as the residual connections of deep CNNs and transformers . The architecture need not be chosen by hand: neural architecture search learns a useful connectivity automatically . Each architecture fixes a different hypothesis space, within which empirical risk minimization learns a single hypothesis h = h(w) by choosing the model parameters w that minimize the average loss on a training set. The architecture also governs the generalization of the learned hypothesis to data points outside the training set, which is what the choice of an architecture is judged by.

terms.name: attention
terms.abstract: Attention is a mechanism that models the dependencies between the tokens that make up a data point, such as the words in a sentence or the pixel patches of an image. The idea is to represent the relationship between two tokens by a parameterized weight function whose model parameters are learned from a training set. An attention head then computes a new vector representation for each token as a weighted combination of the value vectors of all tokens. Like the weight function, the value vectors are learned. An attention head acts as a differentiable associative memory: a token uses its query vector to retrieve, through the key vectors of the other tokens, the values most relevant to it. Attention heads capture long-range dependencies between tokens regardless of their positions within a data point, and they are a core component of modern LLMs.

terms.name: autoencoder
terms.abstract: An autoencoder is a machine learning method that learns an encoder and a decoder together. The encoder maps the feature vector of a data point to a new feature vector, referred to as code. The decoder reconstructs the original feature vector from the code. The code delivered by the encoder is typically much shorter than the original feature vector, so the encoder has to decide what to keep. Different autoencoders use different choices for the hypothesis spaces from which the encoder and the decoder are chosen. principal component analysis is obtained as the special case where both are linear maps, and a deep autoencoder uses a deep net on each side.
terms.description: An autoencoder learns an encoder h from a hypothesis space H along with a decoder h* from a second hypothesis space H* . The encoder maps the feature vector x ∈ Rd of a data point to a code z = h(x) ∈ Rd'. The decoder maps the code back to a reconstruction x = h*(z) of the original feature vector (see Fig.~1). The encoder and the decoder can be learnt via empirical risk minimization with a loss that measures the reconstruction error x - h*(h(x)), such as the squared error loss , \begin{equation} \min_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace,\; \hypothesis^{*} \in \hypospace^{*}} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \loss\Big( \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)},\, \hypothesis^{*}\big( \hypothesis\big( \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} \big) \big) \Big) \text{,} \end{equation} The training set needs no labels: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself, so an autoencoder is a form of self-supervised learning, as it does not require manual labelling. The length d' of the code is typically much smaller than the length d of the original feature vector, in which case the autoencoder is called undercomplete . The encoder then implements a form of compression that still allows the decoder to reconstruct the original feature vector with a small reconstruction error . The encoder map can afterwards be used as a feature transformation for learning tasks based on the same data points, which makes the autoencoder a feature learning and a dimensionality reduction method . Different autoencoder methods are obtained by different choices for the hypothesis spaces H, H* and the loss function in \eqref{eq:autoencoder_erm}. The special case of linear maps for the encoder and the decoder, paired with the squared error loss, coincides with principal component analysis . For some applications, nonlinear encoder and decoder maps represented by ANNs are more useful, and a deep autoencoder uses a deep net on each side (Fig.~3). On the curve of Fig.~2, a code of one number and one hidden layer on each side leave an average squared error loss of 0.003, against 0.457 for the best linear map with the same code, a factor of 150. The gain is not the ANNs as such but the shape of the reconstruction: linear maps with a code of one number can only place the reconstructions on a straight line, and these data points do not lie on one. An autoencoder is rarely used for the reconstruction itself: the decoder is dropped and the code kept, so that a later learning task learns a hypothesis with few model parameters on the code rather than on the raw features (see transfer learning).

terms.name: backpropagation
terms.abstract: Backpropagation is an algorithm that computes the gradient of an objective function with respect to the model parameters of an artificial neural network. It runs in two passes. The forward pass sends a batch of data points through the artificial neural network and evaluates the loss of the resulting predictions. The backward pass then applies the chain rule from the output back to the input, computing on the way the partial derivative with respect to every weight. Obtaining all of them this way costs a small multiple of one forward pass, where perturbing each weight separately would cost one pass per weight. Backpropagation is not itself an iteration: it yields one gradient, which a gradient step then consumes. Every training step of a deep net uses it.
terms.description: An image classifier reads the features of a photograph, passes them through layers of neurons, and delivers at its output a prediction of the label. Training it requires the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each of its millions of weights. Obtaining those one at a time, by perturbing a single weight and evaluating the loss again, would cost one pass through the network per weight. Backpropagation delivers all of them in two passes. It is an algorithm that computes the gradient ∇w f(w) of an objective function f(w) with respect to the model parameters w of an artificial neural network, which are the weights of its layers collected into one vector. It applies the chain rule of calculus to evaluate the partial derivatives of f one layer at a time (see Fig.~1). In the forward pass, a batch of data points travels through the artificial neural network: each layer applies its weights and its activation function, producing predictions at the output, and the loss function compares those predictions to the true labels. In the backward pass, the partial derivatives of the loss with respect to the weights of each layer are computed recursively from the output back to the input, which yields the whole gradient ∇w f(w). Obtaining every partial derivative this way costs a small multiple of one forward pass, instead of one pass per weight. Backpropagation is not itself an iteration: one forward and one backward pass yield one gradient. The iteration is gradient descent, which consumes that gradient in a gradient step \[ \weights^{(\iteridx+1)} = \weights^{(\iteridx)} - \lrate \nabla f(\weights^{(\iteridx)}) \text{,} \] with step size η, and calls backpropagation again at the new model parameters. The objective function f(w) is the average loss on a training set, while the goal of training is a small loss on data points outside that training set. Backpropagation makes the search over w affordable; it does not close that gap. Every training step of a deep net uses backpropagation, once per batch. In image classification, for example, it computes the partial derivatives needed to update millions of weights spread over dozens of layers.

terms.name: bagging
terms.abstract: Bagging is an ensemble method that uses randomly sampled subsets of a dataset as training sets for its base learners. Aggregating the predictions delivered by the base learners, by a majority vote in classification or by averaging in regression, yields the prediction of the ensemble method. A random forest is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees.
terms.description: On twenty-four days of 2020, twelve from winter and twelve from summer, the weather station Krems an der Donau recorded a minimum and a maximum temperature. Predicting the maximum temperature y of a day from its minimum temperature x is a regression problem, and a decision tree solves it by splitting the feature axis at a threshold and predicting the mean label on each side. Fig.~1 shows what happens when two decision trees are each learned from five of those days chosen at random: they place their threshold at 5.4 and 9.2 degrees Celsius, and their predictions differ by up to 22 degrees Celsius. This spread hints at a lack of stability of the base learner: it is too sensitive to the specific choice of training set, which in turn implies poor generalization. Bagging is an ensemble technique that suppresses this instability. Bagging executes its base learners in parallel, in contrast to boosting, which runs its base learners sequentially. The name is short for bootstrap aggregating. Bagging uses randomly sampled subsets of a dataset as training sets for its base learners. Given the original training set D, it generates perturbed copies D(1), …, D(M) (typically via bootstrap sampling) and trains one base learner on each, producing hypotheses 1, …, M. The final hypothesis aggregates these by majority vote for classification (i.e., the class predicted by the most base learners) or averaging for regression, a task whose label space is R (see Fig.~2). Bagging methods differ in their choice of base learner. A random forest, for example, is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees; it randomizes the features as well as the data points. Bagging reduces the variance of the machine learning method used for the base learners : each base learner sees a different resample, so their prediction errors are only partly correlated. In an idealized setting of bagging with M base learners that deliver uncorrelated predictions, each with variance σ2, the averaged prediction has variance σ2/M. In general the predictions are correlated. For M identically distributed predictions, each with variance σ2 and with pairwise correlation ρ, the averaged prediction has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{\numlearners}\, \sigma^{2} \text{.} The second term vanishes as M grows, while the first does not: the correlation between the base learners sets a lower bound ρ σ2 that no number of base learners brings down . Fig.~3 shows, in a small numerical experiment, the estimated variance of the average of M bagged decision trees against the value this identity predicts from an estimated σ2 and ρ. The predictions of the base learners are independent only if the overall training set is assumed fixed and given. If the training set itself is also modeled as a random variable, the predictions of the base learners are no longer independent. Every base learner is grown from a resample of the same m data points: a resample holds any one of them with probability about 1 - 1/e ≈ 63.2% , two resamples therefore share about (1-1/e)2 ≈ 40%, and all of them share the same empirical distribution. Bagging reduces only the variance of an machine learning method, not its bias. Indeed, for the regression setting, the average and each of its members have the same expectation, so averaging leaves the bias of a member unchanged. Averaging also yields stability: the learned hypothesis depends only weakly on any single data point of the training set. Consider any machine learning method with predictions in [0,1] whose base learners are each trained on a share p of the m data points, drawn without replacement, and whose predictions are averaged over all such subsamples. Then, removing a single data point from the training set changes the prediction at a test point by more than ε for at most a δ-fraction of the removed data points, for every pair (ε, δ) with δ ε2 ≥ (1)/(4(m-1)) · (p)/(1-p) . This guarantee holds for every training set and requires nothing of the base learner beyond the bounded predictions — the stability is created by the averaging itself. A random forest applies bagging to decision trees and, in addition, lets each split choose only among a small random subset of the features. The random choice reduces the correlation between the learned decision trees, and a lower correlation means a smaller variance of their average.

terms.name: baseline
terms.abstract: A baseline is a reference level against which the performance of a trained model is compared. The cheapest baseline uses no features at all and predicts the same value for every data point, e.g., the sample mean of numeric label values, or the most frequent label in classification. Any useful method must beat that level. Baselines can be obtained from human performance, from an existing machine learning method, or from a probabilistic model. Given an accurate probabilistic model of the data generation, the smallest achievable risk is the Bayes risk, incurred by the Bayes estimator of the label given the features. In practice, however, the Bayes estimator is infeasible for at least two reasons. First, the probability distribution of the data generation process might be impossible to determine. Second, computing the Bayes risk might be computationally too expensive.
terms.description: Consider some machine learning method that produces a learned hypothesis (or trained model) h ∈ H. Its quality is typically evaluated by computing the average loss on a test set. But how can it be verified that the measured performance is satisfactory? The question is whether the learned hypothesis is already so close to optimal that little is gained by investing more resources, for data collection or for computation, to improve it. Answering it needs a baseline, a reference level for the smallest loss achievable by any method. Sometimes a baseline is computed directly from a scatterplot such as Fig.~1. That figure shows weather records of the station Krems an der Donau. Each of the 366 days of 2024 is a data point whose feature x is the minimum air temperature of the day and whose label y is its maximum air temperature. On the 15 days with x between 11.5 and 12.5 degrees Celsius, the label ranged from 13.2 to 33.4 degrees Celsius. Two of these days even share the same feature value x = 11.8, with labels 13.2 and 29.9. A hypothesis is a map, so it assigns both days the same prediction and incurs, on these two days, an average squared error loss of at least (16.7/2)2 ≈ 69.7. The gray strips of Fig.~1 repeat this measurement across the whole feature axis. Each strip holds at least four days and is drawn over the range of labels those days carry. A strip is therefore wide where the days are sparse and narrow where they are dense. Averaging the variance of the label within the strips yields 18.75 (in squared degrees Celsius) as an estimate for the smallest achievable average squared error loss. A hypothesis learned by linear regression incurs an average squared error loss of 19.17 on the 366 days. That is above the estimate, as it must be, and within three percent of it: this hypothesis is already close to optimal. Baselines can provide lower bounds or upper bounds on the achievable average loss. The strip-wise estimate of Fig.~1 is a lower bound: no method can do better. An upper bound, i.e., a baseline that any useful method should beat, comes from a trivial hypothesis map that does not depend on the features at all. For numeric labels, such a trivial prediction could be the sample mean of the labels in the training set. In classification, the constant prediction could be the label value of the majority class in the training set, which on imbalanced data already attains a high accuracy. For the temperature dataset of Fig.~1, the sample mean is 17.91 degrees Celsius and incurs an average squared error loss of 84.64, more than four times the 18.75 that the strips leave achievable. A baseline might be obtained from human performance, e.g., the misclassification rate of dermatologists who diagnose cancer from visual inspection of skin . For LLMs, baselines are often obtained from a benchmark, i.e., a fixed collection of test problems together with an evaluation protocol. As an example, the benchmark GSM8K measures the ability of an large language model to solve grade-school mathematics word problems . Another source for a baseline is an existing, but for some reason unsuitable, machine learning method: it might be computationally too expensive for the intended machine learning application, yet its test set error can still serve as a baseline. A more principled source of a baseline is a probabilistic model. Given an accurate probabilistic model p(x,y) of the data generation, the minimum achievable risk among any hypotheses (not even required to belong to the hypothesis space H) can often be determined precisely . This minimum achievable risk (referred to as the Bayes risk) is the risk of the Bayes estimator of the label y of a data point, given its features x. For the squared error loss, the Bayes risk equals the expectation of the conditional variance of the label, given the features ; the strip-wise estimate in Fig.~1 approximates exactly this quantity. The constant prediction of the majority class is itself a Bayes estimator. If the features carry no information about the label, the Bayes estimator under the 0/1 loss is the most probable label, and the Bayes risk is the probability of the other one. The trivial baseline is thus the Bayes risk of the probabilistic model in which the label does not depend on the features. It measures what is already known before any feature is read. For a given choice of loss function, the Bayes estimator (if it exists) is fully determined by the probability distribution P . However, computing the Bayes estimator %need to recheck if indeed chap.4 - and if possible to cite sth more specific e.g. Sect. or Example and Bayes risk presents two main challenges. First, the probability distribution P is unknown and must be estimated from observed data. Second, even if P were known, computing the Bayes risk exactly may be computationally infeasible . One probabilistic model makes both quantities explicit: the multivariate normal distribution xy ~ μC, for data points xy generated by independent and identically distributed RVs with numeric features and labels. Here, for the squared error loss, the Bayes estimator is given by the posterior mean μy|x of the label y, given the features x. The corresponding Bayes risk is given by the posterior variance σ2y|x (see Fig. 2). For the multivariate normal distribution this posterior variance does not depend on x, and it is the reciprocal of the diagonal entry of the inverse C-1 of the covariance matrix that corresponds to the label y . In practice, the mean vector μ and the covariance matrix C can be estimated from a dataset by the sample mean and the sample covariance matrix .

terms.name: binary classification
terms.abstract: Binary classification is the machine learning problem of predicting which of two labels a data point carries, from its features. The label space holds two elements, written either -1, +1 or 0, 1; the margin-based loss functions assume the first convention. A classifier partitions the feature space into two decision regions separated by a decision boundary, which is a hyperplane for a linear classifier. The natural loss function is the 0/1 loss, whose average over a dataset is 1 minus the accuracy. That loss is not convex in the model parameters, so practical methods minimize a convex surrogate that upper bounds it: the logistic loss for logistic regression, the hinge loss for the support vector machine. Because the two kinds of mistake usually carry different costs, the confusion matrix is reported beside the accuracy.
terms.description: A weather service that answers whether the maximum temperature of the coming day will reach 25 degrees Celsius returns one of two answers, yes or no, and nothing in between. The same shape of question is asked of an email (spam or not), of a credit application (default or not) and of a biopsy image (malignant or benign). Binary classification is the machine learning problem behind all of them: predict which of two labels a data point carries, from its features. Binary classification is classification with a label space Y that holds two elements. The two elements are usually written Y = -1, +1 or Y = 0, 1. The choice is a convention and not a modelling decision, but it must be fixed before a loss function is written down: the logistic loss and the hinge loss are defined through the margin y · h(x) and therefore assume -1, +1. A classifier is a hypothesis h: X → Y, and it partitions the feature space into two decision regions, one per label, separated by a decision boundary. For a linear classifier the decision boundary is a hyperplane wᵀ x + w0 = 0, and the label predicted for x is the side of that hyperplane on which x lies . A data point that lands on the side of the other label is misclassified and incurs a 0/1 loss of 1 (Fig.~1). The natural loss function for binary classification is the 0/1 loss, which charges 1 for a wrong label and 0 for a right one, so that its average over a dataset is the fraction of data points misclassified, i.e., 1 minus the accuracy. The 0/1 loss is not convex in the model parameters and empirical risk minimization with it is computationally hard, so practical methods minimize a convex surrogate that upper bounds it : the logistic loss, which gives logistic regression, or the hinge loss, which gives the support vector machine. A single number is a thin summary of a binary classifier. The two kinds of mistake, a wrong yes and a wrong no, generally carry different costs, and on imbalanced data the accuracy of the constant answer is already high (baseline). Both are reasons to report the confusion matrix, and the precision, recall and F1 score computed from it, beside the accuracy. For example, a spam filter reads the features of an email and returns y = +1 for spam and y = -1 for legitimate mail. A wrong +1 hides a legitimate email from the user while a wrong -1 only delivers one more piece of spam, so the two mistakes are not interchangeable and the classifier is tuned to keep the first rare.

terms.name: boosting
terms.abstract: Boosting is an iterative optimization method that sequentially combines base learners, referred to as weak learners. Starting from an initial hypothesis, each iteration adds the hypothesis of a base learner, scaled by a learning rate, to the current hypothesis. This update generalizes the gradient step of gradient-based methods for empirical risk minimization: each new base learner corrects what the previous ones got wrong. gradient boosting is the special case of this scheme with decision trees as base learners.
terms.description: A weather station records, for each day, the minimum and the maximum temperature. Predicting the maximum from the minimum is a regression task, and a single decision tree of depth one answers it with two numbers: one prediction below a threshold on the minimum temperature and one above it. Such a tree is too coarse to follow five days recorded at Krems an der Donau (Fig.~1). Boosting adds a second tree that corrects the predictions of the first, a third that corrects what the first two leave over, and so on. Boosting combines a sequence of base learners, each trained to correct what the previous ones got wrong, into one accurate hypothesis (referred to as a strong learner). Boosting is an instance of an ensemble method, since it combines base learners that may use different models. Other ensemble methods such as bagging average their base learners. Boosting instead accumulates them in a sequential fashion, each one correcting the predictions of those before it. Boosting methods start from an initial hypothesis h(0), which is iteratively improved by the update \widetilde{\hypothesis}^{(\iteridx)} = \widetilde{\hypothesis}^{(\iteridx-1)}+ \lrate^{(\iteridx)} \learntlocalhypothesis{\iteridx}\text{.} Here, η(t) denotes a learning rate and t is provided by the t-th base learner (see Fig.~2). The boosting update is structurally similar to a gradient step for the model parameters. The boosting update, however, is carried out directly on the hypothesis space, while a gradient step is carried out on a parameter space. The t-th base learner is trained to compensate the prediction errors incurred by the current hypothesis on the training set, y(r) - h(t-1)(x(r)) for r = 1, …, m. For the squared error loss these errors are the negative gradient of the training error with respect to the current predictions . Its output t therefore plays the role of a negative gradient. The update is a fixed-point iteration on the hypothesis space, h(t) = T(h(t-1)) with the operator T(h) := h + η B(h), where B(h) is the base learner fitted to the prediction errors of h on the training set. A hypothesis is a fixed point of T when the base learner fitted to its prediction errors no longer points downhill, so that a step in its direction would not decrease the training error; boosting halts there . If the training error is convex in the predictions and each iteration picks the base learner that decreases it most, every accumulation point of the sequence h(t) attains the smallest training error the base learners can reach . Boosting methods differ in their choice of base learners for computing the generalized gradients t. For instance, gradient boosting most commonly uses decision trees as base learners .

terms.name: bootstrap
terms.abstract: The bootstrap estimates how much the output of a machine learning method moves when its dataset is drawn again, using only the one dataset at hand. It reads the data points as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs and replaces their unknown probability distribution by the empirical distribution of the dataset, so that drawing a new dataset becomes drawing with replacement from the old one. Each of the B datasets so drawn has the same size as the original, repeats some data points and omits others, and holds about 0.63 m distinct ones. model training on each gives B learned hypotheses whose spread estimates the variance of the method. Resampling a test set with replacement, with the learned hypothesis held fixed, gives a confidence interval for a reported accuracy. The overlap with the original dataset is what distinguishes the bootstrap from k-fold cross-validation, whose blocks do not overlap, and it makes a naive bootstrap estimate of prediction error optimistic. bagging puts the same resampling to a different use, averaging the hypotheses instead of measuring their spread.
terms.description: Forty days of weather recordings fix one straight line through them. Had forty other days been recorded, the line would have come out slightly different, and how much it would move is what decides whether its slope means anything. Only one set of forty days was ever recorded, so the repetitions that would answer the question do not exist. The bootstrap manufactures them from the forty days in hand. To manufacture them, the forty days are read as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. A dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) is then a draw of m such RVs with a common probability distribution P. That P is unknown and must be estimated from D itself. The bootstrap estimates it by the empirical distribution P(D) of D. For every event A, the fraction of the data points z(r) that fall into it approximates its probability, \[ \frac{1}{\samplesize} \big| \sampleidx: \datapoint^{(\sampleidx)} \in \mathcal{A} \big| \approx \prob{\mathcal{A}} \text{.} \] Once P has been replaced by P(D), the shortage of data is gone. The empirical distribution P(D) is a fully specified probability distribution and can be sampled as often as wanted. As many data points and as many datasets as needed can therefore be generated from the one dataset that was collected. The gain is replicates, not information. Each replicate keeps the size m of D, because the quantity being imitated is the spread of a dataset of that size drawn from P. Nor does a replicate reach new data points: P(D) places all its mass on the m data points observed, so no draw can produce one that D does not already contain. Sampling m data points from P(D) is the same as drawing m times from D with replacement: every draw is made from the whole of D, so a data point can be drawn twice and another not at all (Fig.~1). Let B be the number of such draws, a number limited only by the computation they cost. Repeating the draw B times yields datasets D(1), …, D(B), each of m data points. Running model training on each, e.g., via empirical risk minimization, gives learned hypotheses h(1), …, h(B). Their spread estimates how much the output of the machine learning method moves when the dataset is drawn again, which is what the variance of the method means ; the same hypotheses also yield an estimate of the error of the method on new data points . For the forty weather days, the forty-day slope is reported together with the range that the B bootstrap slopes cover, which is a confidence interval for it. Fig.~2 draws that picture with measured data: not forty days but m = 1096, the daily minimum and maximum temperature at Krems an der Donau from 2022 to 2024. In the left panel each dot is one data point, its feature the minimum temperature and its label the maximum temperature, and the thick line is the hypothesis learned from all of them by empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss. The thin lines are learned by the same empirical risk minimization problem from bootstrap datasets. Their spread is narrow here, and the 95% confidence interval for the slope runs from 1.07 to 1.13. The dots are also all the mass that P(D) has, which is what the right panel makes visible. Smearing each dot into a small bump and adding the bumps gives a density. Its contours show two crowded regions, the winter days and the summer days. Drawing from that smoothed density rather than from the dots is a variant called the smoothed bootstrap; it produces temperatures that no day of D recorded, which the bootstrap itself never does. The same resampling turns a single test set into a confidence interval for a reported accuracy. A hypothesis h is learned once from the training set D(train), and the held-out test set D(test) is resampled B times with replacement, each draw holding as many data points as D(test). Evaluating the same h on each of them gives B values of the accuracy, and the interval between the 2.5th and the 97.5th percentile of those values is a 95% confidence interval for the accuracy . Only the test set is redrawn here, while h is held fixed, so the interval reports how much the measured accuracy depends on which data points happened to be collected for testing. A single number such as 94% accuracy on 200 test data points says nothing about that dependence; the interval it comes with does. A data point is left out of a bootstrap dataset with probability (1 - 1/m)m, so it appears in one with probability 1 - (1 - 1/m)m, which approaches 1 - 1/e ≈ 0.63 as m grows, since (1 - 1/m)m converges to 1/e. A bootstrap dataset therefore holds about 0.63 m distinct data points and overlaps D heavily. That overlap is what separates the bootstrap from k-fold cross-validation, which partitions D into blocks that do not overlap at all. Used naively to estimate prediction error, the bootstrap therefore evaluates the learned hypotheses on data points that entered their own training, and the estimate comes out optimistic . The repair is to imitate k-fold cross-validation: keep, for each data point, only the predictions of those bootstrap datasets that do not contain it. That leave-one-out bootstrap then trains on about 0.63 m distinct data points. Its bias therefore behaves like that of k-fold CV with k = 2, as Hastie et al.\ note. The 0.632 estimator, a weighted average of the leave-one-out bootstrap estimate and the training error, corrects it . bagging is the bootstrap put to a different use: instead of measuring the spread of h(1), …, h(B), it averages them into one hypothesis, which is how a random forest is built from decision trees.

terms.name: concept activation vector (CAV)
terms.abstract: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction in the activations of one hidden layer of a deep net that stands for a concept named by a user. The user supplies data points that carry the concept and data points that do not, and a linear classifier is trained to tell the two apart from their activations. The CAV is the direction perpendicular to the hyperplane that separates them, pointing to the concept side. Moving the activations of a data point a little along the CAV changes the score the deep net assigns to a label; the rate of that change is the sensitivity of the prediction to the concept. The fraction of data points with a positive sensitivity is the TCAV score. That score belongs to one layer and one label; it aggregates the per-data point sensitivities and thereby describes a whole class of data points rather than a single prediction.
terms.description: A deep net predicts from five consecutive days of weather at a station whether it rains on the sixth day. Whether it uses the notion of a heat wave, five hot days in a row, to arrive at that prediction cannot be decided by inspecting a single neuron. A heat wave is not a feature the network was built with, since its features are the daily temperatures and rain amounts. Nor need it be represented by any one neuron . A concept is a property that a user can name and exemplify but that the network was not built to compute, such as a heat wave. The concept is specified by examples instead: five-day windows that form a heat wave, the positive examples, and windows that do not, the negative examples . A CAV turns such a concept into a direction in the activations of one hidden layer, the direction along which the positive examples lie apart from the negative ones. Consider such a deep net, with several hidden layers, trained to predict the label of a data point from its feature vector; the trained network is the learned hypothesis h. Fix one hidden layer and write z = f(x) for its activations, with f the function computed by the layers up to that point. The deep net is applied to the positive and to the negative examples of a concept C. A binary linear classifier g(z), whose features are those activations, is trained to tell the two apart. Its decision boundary is a hyperplane; the CAV for C is the normal vector w of that hyperplane . A hyperplane has two normal vectors, one pointing to each side. The CAV is the one pointing towards the side that g(z) assigns to the concept class. Training g(z) with the positive examples as the positive class delivers this orientation, and when the two sets of activations are linearly separable, it is the side of the positive examples. In the terminology of mechanistic interpretability, this direction defines a feature of the trained deep net, the projection of the activations onto it: a human-interpretable concept represented by a direction in the space of activations. Fig.~1 draws the CAV of the heat-wave concept for a deep net with two hidden layers of 16 neurons, trained on the daily weather at Krems an der Donau of the training years 2000--2018 and tested on 2019--2024. A data point is a window of five days, its feature vector holds the daily maximum and minimum temperature and the rain amount of each day, and its label says whether at least 1\,mm of rain fell on the sixth day. The concept is specified by 40 heat waves, windows with a daily maximum of at least 30 ∘C on all five days, and 40 windows that are not, drawn from the 9127 windows of the record. The plane drawn passes through the mean activation of the first hidden layer and is spanned by the CAV and the direction orthogonal to it along which the activations vary most. The concept hyperplane therefore meets the plane in a vertical line, and the CAV is its horizontal axis. Two classification problems appear in the figure. The first is the concept classification that g(z) solves on the activations. The second is the task the deep net is trained for, whose decision boundary on the plane is the solid line: rain is predicted to its right, where every heat wave lies. Training g(z) on all 9127 windows instead turns the CAV by 26 degrees. Like any good explanation, a CAV must be understandable and faithful (see explanation). It is understandable by construction: the user supplies the examples that define the concept. Faithfulness is a separate question, because the concept is a direction in the activations whether or not the deep net responds to it. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) decides it. Write the trained deep net as a concatenation of two functions, the activations z = f(x) of the chosen hidden layer and a score s(z) that the remaining layers assign to one label. The conceptual sensitivity of a data point is the directional derivative of that score along the unit CAV v := w / w, which for differentiable s equals the inner product of the gradient of s with v , \begin{equation} S(\featurevec) \defeq \innerprod{\nabla s\big(f(\featurevec)\big)}{\vv} \text{.} \end{equation} It measures how much the score for that label moves when the activations move a little towards the concept . The orientation convention gives the sign its meaning: S(x) > 0 says the score rises towards the concept, and the opposite normal vector would flip every sensitivity. The sensitivity \eqref{equ_cav_sensitivity} delivers one number per data point. TCAV collects these numbers over one label: the TCAV score is the fraction of the data points carrying that label for which S(x) > 0 . A random set of non-concept data points also yields a CAV, so a single such fraction is not evidence alone. A random concept is a set of data points drawn at random and labelled as if they carried a concept. It is as likely to raise the score as to lower it, so its TCAV score, the fraction of positive sensitivities, is one half on average. The CAV is therefore refitted against many fresh draws of non-concept data points, and the resulting TCAV scores are compared with those of random concepts: a concept the deep net responds to scores consistently away from one half, a random one does not . The explanation delivered is a single number attached to a concept, a label and a layer. Unlike the sensitivity S(x), which is defined for a single data point, it describes a whole class of data points rather than a single prediction . For the deep net of Fig.~1, moving along the heat-wave CAV raises the rain score at every test window followed by rain. A cold wave is five days with a minimum of at most -5 ∘C, and moving along its CAV lowers that score at every one of those windows. The record agrees: rain follows 30\% of the heat waves and 16\% of the cold waves, against 23\% of all windows. Random concepts score one half on average. Training the linear classifier g(z) and evaluating the sensitivity S(x) both read quantities inside the deep net: the activations f(x) of the chosen layer, and the gradient ∇ s(z) of the score with respect to them. A CAV is therefore unavailable for a system that returns predictions for submitted feature vectors and nothing else, such as a deep net served behind an interface or supplied by a vendor. An explanation produced by local interpretable model-agnostic explanations, by contrast, needs predictions and nothing else: its local approximation is fitted to predictions obtained by querying the learned hypothesis h . A second consequence of reading the internals is that a CAV is not a property of h alone: the split into f and s is a choice of layer, and two deep nets that deliver the same h through different layers have different CAVs. Both functions a CAV involves are defined on the space of activations: g(z) approximates concept membership there, and the sensitivity S(x) is a directional derivative of the score s on that same space. A CAV therefore concerns the interpretability of the deep net rather than its explainability; mechanistic interpretability studies such directions.

terms.name: classification
terms.abstract: Classification is the task of predicting a discrete-valued label for a given data point, based solely on its features. The label belongs to a finite label space: binary classification uses two label values, and multi-class classification more than two. A hypothesis whose predictions take values in the finite label space is a classifier; it partitions the feature space into decision regions separated by the decision boundary. A widely used construction compares a real-valued hypothesis against a threshold to obtain the predicted label. A natural quality measure is the 0/1 loss; since it is neither convex nor differentiable, training methods minimize surrogates such as the logistic loss or the hinge loss, and the learned classifier is judged by the accuracy and the confusion matrix on a test set. When the label space is continuous, the task is regression.
terms.description: A weather station records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. From these two numbers, it must be decided whether the following day brings frost, that is, whether its minimum temperature falls below 0 ∘C. A library must file each incoming text into one of the categories math, novel, or engineering. Both are classification problems: the task of predicting a discrete-valued label y of a given data point, based solely on its feature vector x, the vector of its features. Classification assigns each feature vector a label from a finite set. The label takes values in a finite label space Y and names the category of the data point. binary classification uses a label space with two label values, such as Y = -1, 1 with y = 1 marking a frost day; multi-class classification uses more than two label values, such as Y = math, novel, engineering for the texts. When the label space is continuous instead, the task is regression: predicting tomorrow's minimum temperature is regression, predicting whether tomorrow brings frost is classification. Classification is also distinct from clustering: as a form of supervised learning, classification learns from data points whose labels are known, while clustering groups data points without any given labels. A hypothesis whose predictions take values in a finite label space is referred to as a classifier. A classifier partitions the feature space into decision regions, one region per label value, separated by the decision boundary (Fig.~1). Each classifier is fully determined by its decision regions: all feature vectors within the same decision region obtain the same predicted label. A widely used construction of a classifier proceeds in two steps. First, a real-valued hypothesis h: X → R quantifies the confidence in one particular label value. Second, the confidence h(x) is compared against a threshold to obtain the prediction y ∈ Y. logistic regression, for the label space Y = -1, 1, uses a linear map h(x) = wᵀ x as the confidence in the label value 1. This confidence is compared against the threshold 0, \predictedlabel \defeq \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \hypothesis(\featurevec) \geq 0\text{,} -1 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} The real-valued hypothesis h is not itself the classifier: the classifier is the thresholded map x ↦ y, and calling h the classifier is a slight abuse of language. The two decision regions are then the halfspaces on either side of the hyperplane wᵀ x = 0. A natural quality measure for a classifier is the 0/1 loss: its average over a dataset is the fraction of misclassified data points, and one minus that fraction is the accuracy. Even the best classifier cannot always achieve zero error: when data points with the same feature vector carry different labels, some misclassifications are unavoidable, and the smallest achievable risk is the Bayes risk. The 0/1 loss is rarely used as the objective function for training: it is neither convex nor differentiable as a function of the model parameters, so its minimization is computationally hard. Practical methods therefore minimize the average of a surrogate loss over the training set: a loss function that approximates the 0/1 loss while having more convenient properties, such as convexity or differentiability. logistic regression uses the logistic loss, which is convex and differentiable ; the support vector machine uses the hinge loss, which is convex but not differentiable. Fig.~2 compares the three as functions of the margin y · h(x). The learned classifier is then judged by the accuracy and the confusion matrix on a test set.

terms.name: clustering
terms.abstract: Clustering decomposes a dataset into subsets, called clusters, such that data points within the same cluster are more similar to each other than to data points in other clusters. Clustering methods differ in the measure of similarity between data points, in the representation of a cluster, and in whether each data point is assigned to exactly one cluster (hard clustering) or to several with varying degrees of belonging (soft clustering). k-means represents a cluster by a cluster centroid and a Gaussian mixture model by a multivariate normal distribution, so their clusters are convex regions and ellipsoids. graph clustering represents the data points as the nodes of a similarity graph and uses its weighted edges to determine the clusters.
terms.description: A photograph taken in the Wachau shows sky, clouds, forested slopes, sunlit vineyards and rock (Fig.~1(a)). Cutting it into 96 × 128 patches of 5 × 5 pixels gives 12288 data points, each characterized by a feature vector x ∈ R3 that holds the mean red, green and blue values of the patch. Clustering is the task of decomposing such a dataset into clusters, such that data points within the same cluster are more similar to each other than to data points in other clusters. Fig.~1(b)--(f) shows the segmentations delivered by five clustering methods, k-means, a Gaussian mixture model, density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise, spectral clustering and convex clustering. The number k of clusters is either an input, as in k-means, or determined by the method from its other hyperparameters, as in density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise. Clustering methods differ in three design choices : \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)] \item the measure of similarity between data points , e.g., the Euclidean distance between their feature vectors, which makes the feature space a metric space, or the edge weights of a graph whose nodes are the data points; \item the representation of a cluster, e.g., a cluster centroid, a multivariate normal distribution, a set of data points connected by short hops, or a well-connected subset of the nodes of a graph; and \item whether each data point is assigned to exactly one cluster (hard clustering) or to several with varying degrees of belonging (soft clustering). \end{enumerate} Fig.~2 illustrates three families of clustering methods: hard clustering, such as k-means; soft clustering, such as a Gaussian mixture model; and graph clustering, where the data points are the nodes of a graph and a cluster is a densely connected subset of nodes. k-means represents a cluster by a point of the feature space, referred to as cluster centroid. Each data point is assigned to the cluster whose cluster centroid is nearest in Euclidean distance. The cluster centroids are chosen to minimize the average squared Euclidean distance between a data point and its nearest cluster centroid, which Lloyd's algorithm does by alternating assignment and averaging . For a large dataset, k-means is run on a coreset: a small weighted subset of the data points whose weighted average squared Euclidean distance to the nearest cluster centroid approximates that of the full dataset for every choice of the cluster centroids . On the photograph, the five cluster centroids of k-means with k = 5 are five representative colors, and each cluster consists of the patches whose color is nearest to one of them: sky, cloud, shaded forest, sunlit slopes and rock (Fig.~1(b)). Painting each patch in the color of its cluster centroid also compresses the photograph to five colors. A clustering learned from one photograph is judged by how it assigns new patches: in k-means, a new data point joins the cluster of the nearest cluster centroid, so the cluster centroids are the learned hypothesis. A Gaussian mixture model represents each cluster by a multivariate normal distribution: a cluster index is drawn first, then the feature vector from that cluster's multivariate normal distribution. The degree of belonging of a data point to a cluster is the posterior distribution of its cluster index, and the expectation–maximization algorithm learns the model parameters by maximum likelihood . The result is a soft clustering whose clusters are ellipsoids; hard clustering is the extreme case in which every degree of belonging is 0 or 1. On the photograph, each surface type becomes a multivariate normal distribution over colors, and the degree of belonging of a patch to the sky cluster is the probability that its color was drawn from the multivariate normal distribution of the sky. Painting each patch by the cluster with the largest degree of belonging gives Fig.~1(c); one in eight patches, mostly along the horizon and the cloud edges, has no degree of belonging above 0.8. density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise defines a cluster through two hyperparameters, a distance ε and a minimum size m* of a cluster . A data point is a core point if at least m* data points lie within Euclidean distance ε of it. A cluster is a maximal set of data points that are connected through a chain of core points at most ε apart, and data points that are neither core points nor within ε of one are noise. A cluster can therefore have any shape that a chain of nearby data points can trace, and the number of clusters is an output, not an input. On the photograph, ε is a distance between colors. With ε = 0.03 and m* = 32, the blue of the sky and the white of the clouds are joined by a chain of intermediate colors, so sky and cloud form one cluster and the land another. The patches along the horizon, whose mixed colors are rare, are noise (Fig.~1(d)). graph clustering methods represent the dataset as the nodes r = 1, …, m of a graph whose edge weights express the similarity between data points, e.g., the k-nearest-neighbor graph that connects each data point to its nearest neighbors . The clusters are determined by the connectivity of the nodes: a cluster is a subset of nodes whose total edge weight to the rest of the graph, divided by the number of nodes in the subset, is small. The sum of this ratio over the clusters is the ratio cut that spectral clustering minimizes approximately . spectral clustering computes the clusters from eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of the graph and flow-based clustering from network flows between selected nodes . There are also graph clustering methods that incorporate node-wise feature vectors x(r), r = 1, …, m: convex clustering combines the connectivity of the nodes with the node-wise feature vectors. graph clustering methods are appealing for data points without an obvious choice for numeric feature vectors: scientific papers connected by citations, users of a social network connected by friendships, or web pages connected by links. On the photograph in Fig.~1(a), the nodes are the patches and each patch is connected to the ten patches of most similar color; spectral clustering then separates the five surface types (Fig.~1(e)), since the patches of one surface type are neighbors in color. Fig.~3 arranges the methods by the representation of the data points and of a cluster. convex clustering draws on both branches of Fig.~3. It gives every data point x(r) its own cluster centroid r, which avoids the non-convexity of the clustering error. The method minimizes the convex objective function \[ \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \normgeneric{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} - \clustercentroid{\sampleidx}}{2}^{2} + \regparam \sum_{1 \le \sampleidx < \sampleidx' \le \samplesize} \edgeweight_{\sampleidx,\sampleidx'} \normgeneric{\clustercentroid{\sampleidx} - \clustercentroid{\sampleidx'}}{2} \text{.} \] The penalty term fuses cluster centroids with weights Ar,r' ≥ 0. The data points that share a cluster centroid at the unique minimizer form a cluster, and their number falls from m to 1 as α grows, so the number of clusters is set indirectly through α. With the edge weights of a similarity graph as weights, the penalty term fuses only neighboring data points and the clusters follow the graph . On the photograph, with the edge weights of the color graph of the patches and α ≈ 18, the fused cluster centroids leave 65 clusters, four of them with at least 80 patches; like density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise, the method fuses sky with cloud along the gradual color transition (Fig.~1(f)). Beyond image segmentation, clustering is used for customer segmentation , for grouping documents by topic in natural language processing , for community detection in social networks , and for anomaly detection, where a data point that falls into no cluster or into a tiny one is an outlier . As a preprocessing step for supervised learning, clustering reduces a dataset to its cluster centroids as prototypes , or adds the distances of a data point to the cluster centroids as new features . It can also split the dataset so that a separate hypothesis is learned per cluster, e.g., one linear regression per cluster .

terms.name: confusion matrix
terms.abstract: The confusion matrix of a hypothesis on a finite dataset with k label values is the k × k matrix whose entry (c, c') counts the data points with true label c and prediction c'. Its diagonal counts the correct predictions, and each off-diagonal entry counts one kind of misclassification. The accuracy, the precision, and the recall are obtained from the matrix by normalizing the diagonal, a column, or a row. On a dataset with label skewness, the confusion matrix exposes failure on the rare class that the accuracy alone hides.
terms.description: The weather station in Krems an der Donau (Austria) records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. A linear classifier is learned by logistic regression from 40 such data points from February and April 2024 (Fig.~1). The features of a data point are the two temperatures of one day; its label indicates whether the minimum temperature of the following day stays above 0 ∘C or falls below it — a frost warning. Most days pose no risk: only 6 of the 40 following days bring frost. The constant prediction ``above zero'', a baseline that ignores the features, is therefore correct on 34 of the 40 days, an accuracy of 0.85, and the learned classifier reaches the same accuracy of 0.85. Both numbers are accuracies on the 40 days the classifier was learned from; a frost warning is judged on days it has not seen, so the same comparison must be repeated on a validation set. The single number cannot tell the two apart, nor reveal which mistakes either makes. Does the classifier miss the frost days, or does it raise false alarms? The confusion matrix breaks the count of predictions down by what was true and what was predicted (Fig.~2). The learned classifier detects one of the six frost days at the cost of one false alarm, while the baseline detects none. Consider a finite dataset with m data points, each characterized by a feature vector x and a label y from a finite label space Y = 1, …, k. For a given hypothesis h, the confusion matrix is a k × k matrix whose row c collects the data points with true label y = c and whose column c' collects those with prediction h(x) = c' . The entry at position (c, c') is the number of data points with y = c and h(x) = c'. The diagonal therefore counts the correctly classified data points, and the off-diagonal entries count each kind of misclassification separately. The standard classification metrics are ratios of entries of the confusion matrix. The accuracy is the sum of the diagonal divided by m. Normalizing a row by its sum yields the fraction of data points of that class that are detected (for the positive class, the recall), while normalizing a column yields the fraction of predictions of that class that are right, the precision. On a dataset with label skewness, the confusion matrix exposes what a large accuracy can hide. A classifier that never predicts the rare class fills the row of that class with misclassifications while keeping most predictions correct. The always-above-zero baseline in Fig.~2 does exactly that (see baseline).

terms.name: convex
terms.abstract: A subset of the Euclidean space is convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points. A function is convex if its epigraph is a convex set. A convex optimization problem is the minimization of a convex function over a convex set. empirical risk minimization is a convex optimization problem whenever the hypothesis space is parameterized by a convex set of model parameters and the loss function is convex in those model parameters. Any local minimizer of a convex objective function is necessarily also a global minimizer, so a method that reaches a local minimum has solved the optimization problem.
terms.description: Many machine learning methods learn model parameters by an iterative optimization method: each iteration updates the current model parameters to reduce an objective function within a neighborhood of these model parameters. Widely used examples are gradient descent and its variants. These optimization methods work particularly well when the objective function is a convex function of the model parameters. Indeed, for a convex function every local minimum is necessarily a global minimum: any choice of model parameters at which no small change reduces the objective function already attains the smallest value that the objective function takes anywhere. The average squared error loss of linear regression is a convex function of the model parameters, and so is the objective function of the support vector machine. empirical risk minimization over a hypothesis space parameterized by a convex set of model parameters, with a loss function that is convex in them, is a convex optimization problem: the minimization of a convex function over a convex set. For differentiable convex objective functions and suitable step size choices, gradient descent converges to such a minimum . Convexity is defined both for sets and for functions. For sets, the definition is geometric. A subset C ⊆ Rd of the Euclidean space Rd is referred to as convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points . For w, w' ∈ C, that is \expcoeff \weights + (1-\expcoeff) \weights' \in \mathcal{C} \quad \text{for all } \expcoeff \in [0,1] \text{.} Similarly, a function f: Rd → R is convex if its epigraph ( wᵀ,t )ᵀ ∈ Rd+1 : t ≥ f(w) is a convex set . Examples of a convex set and of a convex function are illustrated in Fig. 1. Two families of convex sets appear throughout machine learning. The first is the halfspace w ∈ Rd : aᵀ w ≤ b. It is determined by a nonzero normal vector a ∈ Rd 0, which fixes the direction of the bounding hyperplane, and an offset b ∈ R, which fixes its position. If two points satisfy the inequality, so does every point of the segment between them. The second is the convex hull of finitely many vectors x(1), …, x(m). It is defined as the set of all their convex combinations, \[ \operatorname{conv}\big\{ \featurevec^{(1)}, \ldots, \featurevec^{(\samplesize)} \big\} \defeq \Big\{ \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \expcoeff_{\sampleidx} \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} \; : \; \expcoeff_{\sampleidx} \geq 0 \text{ for } \sampleidx = 1, \ldots, \samplesize, \; \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \expcoeff_{\sampleidx} = 1 \Big\} \text{.} \] It is the smallest convex set that contains these vectors. halfspaces are not merely one example among others. Every closed convex set is given by the intersection of all halfspaces that contain it \begin{equation} \mathcal{C} = \bigcap \big\{ \mathcal{H} \subseteq \reals^{\featuredim} \;:\; \mathcal{H} \text{ is a halfspace}, \; \mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{H} \big\} \text{.} \end{equation} In general, intersecting a subset of the halfspaces containing a convex set yields a convex set that contains the original one, i.e., an outer approximation (see Fig.~2). Approximate inference in probabilistic models defined over a graph uses this construction. The set of achievable marginal distributions is a convex set described by a large number of linear inequalities. Message-passing methods optimize over an outer approximation of it obtained from a subset of those inequalities. Returning to the halfspace intersection \eqref{equ_halfspace_intersection_dict}, that intersection can be narrowed: it needs to consider only those halfspaces that are bounded by a supporting hyperplane. Every boundary point of a non-empty convex set carries such a hyperplane, and each point outside the set is already excluded by one of the halfspaces that these supporting hyperplanes bound: for a point x ∉ C and C closed, there is a unique nearest point p ∈ C to x . That nearest point is a boundary point of C, and therefore one of the points that carry a supporting hyperplane: a point of the interior could be moved a little toward x and would still lie in C, so it would not be the nearest one. The hyperplane through p with normal vector x - p supports C at p, and the halfspace it bounds contains C but not x (see Fig.~3). Fig.~4 shows eight supporting hyperplanes of an ellipse. For the epigraph of a differentiable convex function f, the supporting hyperplane is determined by the gradient. At the boundary point (wᵀ, f(w))ᵀ, its normal vector is (∇ f(w)ᵀ, -1)ᵀ, since \[ \big(\nabla f(\weights)^{\top}, -1\big) \left[ \begin{pmatrix} \weights' t \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} \weights f(\weights) \end{pmatrix} \right] \leq 0 \quad \text{for every } \big(\weights'^{\top}, t\big)^{\top} \in \operatorname{epi} f \text{.} \] This is the first-order condition f(w') ≥ f(w) + ∇ f(w)ᵀ (w' - w) written as a statement about the epigraph . Of the two families of convex sets introduced above, the convex hull is the one that characterizes the linear separability of data points with binary label values. Consider m data points with feature vectors x(r) ∈ Rd and labels y(r) ∈ -1,+1, for r = 1, …, m. These data points are linearly separable if some linear classifier predicts every label correctly, i.e., there are w ∈ Rd 0 and b ∈ R with y(r) ( wᵀ x(r) + b ) > 0 for r = 1, …, m. This holds precisely when the convex hull of the feature vectors labeled +1 and the convex hull of those labeled -1 do not intersect. Separability is therefore a property of two convex sets built from the data points. Convexity also appears in the study of probabilistic models, where it singles out a widely used family. In particular, an exponential family is constituted by the probability distributions whose probability density function has the form \[ p(\featurevec; \weights) = h(\featurevec) \exp\big(\weights^{\top} \suffstat(\featurevec) - A(\weights)\big) \text{.} \] This probability density function is parameterized by the vector w and the sufficient statistics t(·). The log-partition function A is fully determined by requiring p(x; w) to integrate to one. Its Hessian is the covariance matrix of the sufficient statistics t(x) under p(x; w), \[ \nabla^{2} A(\weights) = \E \big\{ \suffstat(\featurevec) \suffstat(\featurevec)^{\top} \big\} - \E \big\{ \suffstat(\featurevec) \big\} \E \big\{ \suffstat(\featurevec) \big\}^{\top} \text{,} \] which is positive semi-definite. A twice-differentiable function whose Hessian is positive semi-definite is convex , so A is a convex function on its domain. The convexity of A implies that the negative log-likelihood function of a training set, up to an additive constant that does not depend on w, \[ - \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \weights^{\top} \suffstat\big(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big) + \samplesize A(\weights) \text{,} \] is a convex function of w. Thus, for an exponential family, maximum likelihood estimation is a convex optimization problem.

terms.name: covariance matrix
terms.abstract: The covariance matrix of a random vector consists of the covariances between its entries. In particular, the diagonal entries are the variances of the individual entries. Together with the mean vector, the covariance matrix collects the second-order statistics of a random vector. For a Gaussian random vector, the mean vector and the covariance matrix provide full information about the optimal method for linear regression: the model parameters of the optimal linear hypothesis map, along with the incurred risk, are computed from the entries of the covariance matrix.
terms.description: The covariance matrix of a random vector x ∈ Rd is defined as the expectation (if it exists): \covmtx{\featurevec} \defeq \expect \bigg \{ \big( \featurevec - \expect \big\{ \featurevec \big\} \big) \big(\featurevec - \expect \big\{ \featurevec \big\} \big)^{\top} \bigg\} \text{.} The entry in row j and column j' is the covariance of the entries xj and xj', with the diagonal entries being the variances of the individual entries. A covariance matrix is always positive semi-definite, i.e., vᵀ x v ≥ 0 for every v ∈ Rd. It is invertible, and then positive definite, exactly when no entry of x is, with probability one, an affine function of the other entries. Invertibility is assumed wherever the inverse ( x )-1 appears below. The empirical counterpart computed from a dataset is the sample covariance matrix. Fig.~1 shows how the entries of the matrix are visible in a cloud of realizations: the variances set the spread of the cloud along the two axes, and the covariance sets its tilt. Fig.~2 illustrates the role of the covariance matrix for a simple regression task. The data points of a training set, a validation set and a test set are modeled as realizations of i.i.d. Gaussian random vectors z(r) = ( x(r), y(r) )ᵀ ~ μC (see multivariate normal distribution). The ellipse in Fig.~2 is the constant-density contour z : (z - μ)ᵀ C-1 (z - μ) = 4 of this probability distribution. Its principal axes point along the eigenvectors v(1), v(2) of the covariance matrix C, with lengths proportional to the square roots 1, 2 of the corresponding eigenvalues (see eigenvalue decomposition). The long axis of the ellipse is the direction in which feature and label vary together. The hypothesis map with the smallest risk under the squared error loss is linear for this probabilistic model, with slope given by the ratio of the covariance between x and y to the variance of x (see linear regression). Predicting one feature of a data point from its other features is a common task in health records . Each data point is a patient, and the entries x1, …, xd of x are biomarker measurements. The biomarker xj of a new patient, being expensive to measure, is to be predicted from the remaining ones. The smallest risk achievable by such a prediction is the reciprocal of one diagonal entry of the inverse ( x )-1 of an invertible covariance matrix, as shown below. This inverse is referred to as the precision matrix . Collect the remaining features in the vector x-j := ( x1, …, xj-1, xj+1, …, xd )ᵀ ∈ Rd-1. For a Gaussian random vector x ~ μx (see multivariate normal distribution), the conditional probability distribution of xj, given x-j, is Gaussian with a variance that does not depend on the value of x-j. This conditional variance is 1 / ( ( x )-1 )j,j . Consider data points modeled as realizations of i.i.d. random vectors x(r) ~ μx. This conditional variance is then also the smallest risk that any hypothesis can achieve under the squared error loss, \[ \min_{\hypothesis: \reals^{\featuredim-1} \to \reals} \expect \Big\{ \big( \feature_{\featureidx} - \hypothesis\big(\featurevec_{-\featureidx}\big) \big)^{2} \Big\} = 1 \big/ \big( \big( \covmtx{\featurevec} \big)^{-1} \big)_{\featureidx,\featureidx} \text{.} \] This smallest risk is the Bayes risk of this regression problem. It is attained by the Bayes estimator E xj | x-j, which depends linearly on x-j in the Gaussian case. The diagonal of ( x )-1 therefore yields a baseline, one entry per feature. A large diagonal entry marks a biomarker that the remaining biomarkers predict accurately, and no machine learning method can push the risk of predicting that biomarker below the reciprocal of the entry.

terms.name: data
terms.abstract: Data are representations of information, recorded in a form suitable for storage, communication and processing, and the word carries three technical senses in machine learning. In its general sense, it denotes recorded information in a form suitable for processing by machine learning methods. As a data point, it is an elementary information-carrying unit; as a dataset, it is an indexed collection of data points.
