A related regulatory term, personal data, is defined in the general data protection regulation and adopted by the EU AI Act.
terms.description: A weather station measures the temperature at its location and stores the value 23.4 ∘C together with a timestamp (see Fig.~1(a)). Such recorded values are data: representations of information, recorded in a form suitable for storage, communication, and processing by ML systems . Every machine learning method trains a model on data, and the usefulness of the hypothesis the method learns is limited by the quality and quantity of the available data. The word \emph{data} is used in three technical senses, summarized in Fig.~1, and additionally in a legal sense. In its broadest use, data refer to recorded information. This sense applies when the distinction between unit and collection is irrelevant. Examples are raw sensor measurements such as the temperature reading in Fig.~1(a) and compound terms such as data parallelism, networked data, and data augmentation. As a formal unit, a data point is the fundamental information-carrying unit (Fig.~1(b)). Its information is contained in two types of properties: features, which are easy to measure or compute, and labels, which are difficult to measure or compute or need human annotation. The formal model of a domain set, a label set and a labeling function that assigns each domain point its label is given by . As a formal collection, a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) is the indexed collection of data points on which model training and validation are performed (Fig.~1(c)) . The word \emph{data} also carries a regulatory meaning. The general data protection regulation defines personal data as any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person . The EU AI Act adopts that definition and defines biometric data as personal data resulting from specific technical processing . Several regulatory obligations on ML systems, including the data minimization principle, the right to erasure, and the right to explanation, refer to data in this legal sense.

terms.name: data augmentation
terms.abstract: Data augmentation enlarges a training set with synthetic data points obtained by perturbing or transforming the measured ones. It is one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes, beside shrinking the hypothesis space and adding a penalty term. A perturbation is admissible when it is known to leave the label alone, either because the feature space carries a symmetry, such as the rotation of an image, or because the measurement is only accurate to within a stated tolerance. Enlarging the training set this way removes hypothesis maps that the training error alone cannot rule out, since a copy displaced along the feature axis misses its label whenever the hypothesis is steep there. For the squared error loss, perturbing the features with noise is equivalent to adding a penalty term that grows with the noise variance, which is why the three routes often coincide.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau measured a maximum temperature of 3.5 ∘C on 21 January 2024, 20.7 ∘C on 15 April and 30.2 ∘C on 19 July. On the day after each of them it measured 0.0, 13.6 and 27.0 ∘C. Take these three days as a training set for predicting tomorrow's maximum temperature from today's, and let the hypothesis space be the polynomials of degree five (see polynomial regression). A polynomial of degree five carries six model parameters and the training set holds three data points, so empirical risk minimization has infinitely many solutions. Three independent directions change the polynomial without moving it at the three measured temperatures, so every solution has a training error of zero and the training error cannot choose among them. Between the measured days the solutions take every value: at a today-maximum of 12 ∘C the smoothest of them predicts 6.8 ∘C for tomorrow, while the solution drawn in Fig.~1 predicts 21.0 ∘C. The two differ by up to 15 ∘C between the measured days. This is overfitting: the hypothesis space is too large for three data points. What rules the wild solutions out is something the thermometer already says. It reports the air temperature only to within its accuracy, taken here to be 0.5 ∘C. Both the feature and the label of one of these data points are readings of that instrument, so a day whose two numbers are moved anywhere inside that tolerance is just as consistent with what was measured. Replacing each measured day by copies drawn that way gives an augmented training set (the open squares in Fig.~1). The perturbation is justified by the instrument, not invented: it asserts only that the labels of two days whose readings agree to within the sensor accuracy should agree too, which is the smoothness assumption read at the scale of the measurement error. The copies carry many distinct features, so the feature matrix of the augmented training set has full column rank and empirical risk minimization on it has a unique solution. A polynomial that is steep where the copies lie pays for that steepness, because a copy displaced along the feature axis then misses its label. On the 309 days of 2024 that were held out and whose today-maximum lies between 3.5 and 30.2 ∘C, the solution drawn in Fig.~1 incurs an average squared error loss of 71.8 squared degrees. The solution on the augmented training set incurs 32.6, against 30.9 for the straight line through the three measured days. In general, data augmentation methods add synthetic data points to an existing set of data points. These synthetic data points are obtained by perturbations (e.g., adding noise to physical measurements) or transformations (e.g., rotations of images) of the original data points. Enlarging the training set with perturbed copies is one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes, beside shrinking the hypothesis space and adding a penalty term. The three are often equivalent: for the squared error loss, perturbing the features with noise of variance σ2 is equivalent to adding a penalty term proportional to σ2 , and replacing every data point by a probability distribution centered at it is the vicinal form of empirical risk minimization . When the features are perturbed, the operation is chosen so that the synthetic data points keep the same label. An operator that maps the feature space X into itself and is known to leave the label alone is called a symmetry of the learning task. For example, a rotated cat image still shows a cat, while its feature vector (obtained by stacking pixel color intensities) differs from that of the original image (see Fig.~2). Augmentation can instead perturb the label of a data point. Replacing the labels of training data points with randomly softened or flipped values (label smoothing) is also a form of regularization: it discourages the machine learning method from fitting individual labels too closely and improves robustness to label noise. For example, logistic regression on a linearly separable training set drives the model parameter vector w to grow without bound under hard labels: the logistic loss keeps decreasing as the predictions are pushed toward 0 and 1. Smoothing the labels caps the optimal predictions away from 0 and 1, so w stays finite.

terms.name: data imputation
terms.abstract: Data imputation replaces the missing feature or label values of data points by estimates computed from the values that were recorded. It is one response to missing data, alongside discarding the incomplete data points. The filling becomes a machine learning problem once it is read as a prediction task: the quantity to estimate is treated as a label and the values that survive around it as a feature vector, so the intact data points form a training set on which a hypothesis is learned. For a photograph with lost pixels, each pixel is a data point whose feature vector holds the colors of its neighbors and whose label is its own color. Where a lost value sits among other lost values, the hypothesis is applied repeatedly until the estimates stop changing, which is a fixed point of one sweep. An imputed value is an estimate and not a measurement, so a method trained on imputed data points reports a training error that flatters it.
terms.description: An aerial photograph of the vineyards at Rossatz on the Danube comes back from the survey with a rectangular patch of its pixels lost, because the sensor dropped them. The photograph is still wanted, so those pixels need values. Data imputation is that filling in: it replaces the missing feature or label values of data points by estimates computed from the values that were recorded . It is one response to missing data, alongside discarding the incomplete data points or using a method that tolerates the gaps. The filling becomes a machine learning problem once it is read as a prediction task . For the photograph, each pixel is a data point. Its feature vector holds the red, green and blue values of the eight pixels surrounding it, which is 24 numbers, and its label is its own triple of red, green and blue values (Fig.~1). The intact pixels then form a training set: each one supplies both a feature vector and the label that belongs with it, so a hypothesis can be learned from them by empirical risk minimization. Applying that hypothesis to a lost pixel yields the estimate that fills it. A lost pixel usually has lost pixels among its neighbors, so its feature vector is not available and the hypothesis cannot be applied once and be done. The lost pixels instead start at the average color of the training set and are re-predicted from their current neighbors, sweep after sweep. Writing u for the values currently held by the lost pixels, one sweep applies an operator T to them, \[ \vu^{(\iteridx+1)} = T\big(\vu^{(\iteridx)}\big) \text{,} \] and the filling stops at a fixed point of T, where another sweep leaves the values unchanged. The experiment \texttt{pythondemos/dataimputation.py} reaches one after 413 sweeps on a view of 64 × 96 pixels with 6% of them lost. What imputation can and cannot recover is visible in the numbers of that experiment (Fig.~2). A linear regression hypothesis learned from the intact pixels halves the average squared error loss on the lost ones against the baseline that fills them all with the average color. The gain is not spread evenly: inside a region of nearly constant color the error is a quarter of that baseline, while on the pixels where the river meets the meadow it is as large. The filled river runs through the gap, but its banks come out blurred. An imputed value is an estimate and not a measurement, and a method trained on imputed data points cannot tell the two apart. The training error it reports therefore flatters it, since part of the training set was produced by a hypothesis rather than observed. Recording which values were imputed, and keeping them out of the test set, is what preserves an honest estimate of the risk.

terms.name: data leakage
terms.abstract: Data leakage arises when a machine learning method uses features that are available during training but not at prediction time. For example, in weather forecasting each data point covers a time interval, and one feature is the temperature one hour ahead of the forecast time. On historic data this later measurement is available, but when a forecast is actually computed it is not, so the feature leaks information. A leaked feature makes the loss on the training set and test set look near zero, yet the learned hypothesis fails after deployment, because the feature cannot be reproduced at prediction time. The term is also used, in a security sense, for the unintentional release of sensitive information.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method trained on an hourly temperature sequence, where each data point is a sliding window of three consecutive hours (Fig.~1). The label is the temperature of the middle hour, and one of the features is the measurement one hour later. On historic data this later measurement is available, so the loss on the training set and test set looks near zero; but in real time the middle hour must be predicted before the next hour is measured, so the learned hypothesis is useless. This is data leakage: a feature used during training or evaluation is unavailable when a prediction must be delivered. More generally, a leaked feature is one whose value cannot be reproduced at prediction time, whether it is measured only later (as above) or computed from the label. Data leakage is formalized by , who also give methods to detect and avoid it. survey it as a cause of the reproducibility crisis in machine learning-based science. test set contamination, the presence of test set data points in the training set, is a related form of data leakage. The term \emph{data leakage} is also used, in an unrelated security sense, for the unintentional release of sensitive information (data exfiltration from a trained system), a meaning distinct from the methodological one defined above.

terms.name: data point
terms.abstract: A data point is the elementary information-carrying unit on which machine learning methods operate. The properties of a data point fall into two categories: features, which are easily measurable or computable, and labels, which are higher-level facts that typically can only be determined using human expertise. Whether a given property is treated as a feature or a label is a design choice that depends on the machine learning application.
terms.description: A data point is an object that conveys information~; such objects are the elementary units on which machine learning methods operate. Examples include students, radio signals, trees, images, RVs, real numbers, or proteins. data points of the same type are described by two categories of properties. The first category includes features that are measurable or computable properties of a data point. They can be automatically extracted or computed using sensors, computers, or other data collection systems. The second category includes labels that are higher-level facts, or quantities of interest, that typically require human expertise or domain knowledge to determine rather than being directly measurable. Whether a given property serves as a feature or a label is ultimately a design choice that depends on the resources available in a given machine learning application. Fig. 1 shows an image as an example of a data point. Several properties of the image can serve as features: the color intensities x1, …, xd of all image pixels, the timestamp xd+1 of the image capture, and the spatial location xd+2 of the image capture. Higher-level facts can serve as labels: the number of cows y1, the number of wolves y2, and the condition of the pasture y3 (e.g., healthy or overgrazed). For a data point that represents a patient, a feature could be the body weight, while the label could be the presence of cancer, the ground-truth fact of interest. Determining this label requires a medical expert (or even a committee of experts) to examine the patient. A property treated as a label in one setting (e.g., a cancer diagnosis) may serve as a feature in another, where reliable automation (e.g., image analysis) allows the property to be computed without human intervention. machine learning aims to predict the label of a data point from its features. Both kinds of properties are error-prone. For many machine learning applications, it is rarely possible to access the true labels. For example, a medical expert's diagnosis can be wrong, rendering it a noisy proxy for the patient's true condition. Errors of this kind, called label noise, arise whenever a label is only a proxy for the true quantity of interest, whether that proxy is produced by human judgment or by an automated system. features are also a source of error within an machine learning method. A feature is obtained by measuring or computing a property of a data point. Physical and chemical sensing devices have a finite measurement uncertainty, and computing a feature on a finite computer introduces rounding errors. These imperfections make the recorded value deviate from the true feature value. This discrepancy is feature noise. machine learning methods should be robust to both feature and label noise. Their predictions on new data points should not degrade sharply when some features or labels in the training set are corrupted. The EU AI Act reflects this concern: training data must, to the best extent possible, be ``free of errors'', and high-risk AI systems must attain an appropriate level of robustness. Robustness to feature and label noise can be improved by data augmentation, which deliberately perturbs the features or the label of a training data point (see Fig.~2). Training on such perturbed data points acts as regularization and reduces the influence of corrupted feature or label values on the learned hypothesis.

terms.name: dataset
terms.abstract: A dataset is a finite collection of data points on which model training and validation are performed. Strictly speaking, a dataset is a set of distinct data points. With slight abuse of terminology, the term is also used interchangeably with sample, a finite sequence that may contain repetitions. In practice, machine learning methods do not access the data points themselves but a representation of them, such as a table of the relational model, which records their attributes and nothing about the dataset's fitness for a purpose.
terms.description: A dataset is a collection D = z(1), …, z(m) of data points. machine learning methods use a dataset for model training and validation. Strictly speaking, a dataset is an unordered collection of distinct data points, i.e., a set with no repetitions. In machine learning literature, however, the term is often used for a sample: a sequence of m data points, indexed by r = 1, …, m, that may contain repetitions (see Fig.~1). The notion of a dataset is broad: data points may represent concrete physical entities (such as humans or animals) or abstract objects (such as numbers). For illustration, Fig.~2 depicts a dataset whose data points are cows. In machine learning applications, it is often not possible to directly access the underlying dataset. For instance, accessing the dataset in Fig.~2 would require visiting the cow herd. What an machine learning method processes instead is a representation of the dataset within some data model, a rigorous formalism for representing and processing data. For example, the relational model organizes data as a collection of tables, or relations. A single table consists of rows and columns, where each row corresponds to a single data point and each column represents a specific attribute of a data point. The order of rows is immaterial, and each attribute is associated with a domain that specifies its set of admissible values. machine learning methods use these attributes as the features or the label of a data point, so the attribute domains correspond to the feature space and the label space. Table~1 shows an example obtained from the dataset in Fig.~2. \begin{table}[H] \refstepcounter{table} \caption*{ \centering \scshape TABLE \thetable [0.5ex] \scshape Relation (or Table) Representing a Dataset of Cows } \centering \begin{tabular}{lcccc} \hline \textbf{Name} & \textbf{Weight} & \textbf{Age} & \textbf{Height} & \textbf{Stomach temperature} \hline Zenzi & 100 & 4 & 100 & 25 Berta & 140 & 3 & 130 & 23 Resi & 120 & 4 & 120 & 31 \hline \end{tabular} \end{table} A table captures the content of a dataset, but not whether that content is appropriate for a given purpose. A dataset used in ethical and lawful ML systems is required to satisfy further properties. For example, the EU AI Act requires that datasets on which high-risk ML systems are trained be ``sufficiently representative'' of the intended use cases. trustworthy artificial intelligence also requires documenting how a dataset was assembled, for example through a datasheet that records the dataset's motivation, composition, and collection process . When the data points are personal data, this becomes a legal duty: under the purpose limitation principle, the general data protection regulation requires that such data be collected for ``specified, explicit and legitimate purposes'' that are fixed at the time of collection.

terms.name: decision tree
terms.abstract: A decision tree is a flowchart-like representation of a hypothesis map: a root node reads in the feature vector of a data point and evaluates a basic test on it. Depending on the test result, the feature vector is forwarded to one of the child nodes. The child nodes apply further tests and forward the feature vector accordingly. This forwarding continues until the feature vector reaches a leaf node. A leaf node has no children and represents one specific function value, i.e., a prediction. The tree partitions the feature space into decision regions, one per leaf node, on which the represented hypothesis is constant. Decision trees serve as base models of the random forest and of gradient-boosted decision tree methods. Small decision trees yield interpretable machine learning if the user can comprehend the tests executed at their nodes.
terms.description: A bank's loan approval can be written as a chain of simple tests on the applicant's features that ends in an ``approve'' or ``reject'' prediction. For example, is the income above a threshold? Is the credit score large enough? A decision tree is such a chain in general form: a flowchart-like representation of a hypothesis map h. More formally, a decision tree is a directed acyclic graph containing a root node that reads in the feature vector x of a data point. The root node then forwards the data point to one of its child nodes based on some elementary test on the features x. If the receiving child node is not a leaf node, i.e., it has child nodes itself, it represents another test. Based on the test result, the data point is forwarded to one of its descendants. This testing and forwarding of the data point is continued until the data point ends up in a leaf node without any children, which carries the prediction y = h(x) returned by the tree for this data point (Fig.~1). The leaf nodes partition the feature space into decision regions; in Fig.~1, each test compares an entry of x with a threshold, so the decision regions are rectangles. Next to each node, Fig.~1 highlights the part of the feature space that contains the feature vectors reaching that node. training a decision tree amounts to extending a leaf node by attaching another decision tree. In the simplest case, a leaf node is replaced with a test node whose children are new leaf nodes (Fig.~2). Widely used training methods for decision trees include classification and regression trees (CART) , iterative dichotomiser 3 (ID3) , and C4.5 . Starting from a single leaf node, CART repeatedly replaces a leaf node with a test node. An impurity measure assigns a nonnegative number to a set of labels: it is zero when the labels agree, and it grows as they spread out. Among candidate tests that compare a single feature with a threshold, CART scores each test by the impurity of the two children, weighted by the fraction of data points routed to each of them, and greedily selects the test with the smallest score, i.e., with the largest reduction against the impurity of the parent node. Common impurity measures are the Gini index and the entropy for classification, and the squared error around the mean label for regression . This selection is a combinatorial search over candidate tests rather than a gradient-based update of continuous model parameters. The growth stops only when a leaf node contains too few data points, not when no candidate test reduces the impurity much, since a test that reduces the impurity little can enable a strong test below it . The large tree is then pruned back by cost-complexity pruning, which removes the subtrees whose impurity reduction does not pay for the leaf nodes they add . The depth of a decision tree is the number of tests on the longest path from the root node to a leaf node; the tree in Fig.~1 has depth two. Fig.~3 shows, as a scatterplot, the result of this training on real data. Each day of 2024 at the Finnish Meteorological Institute weather station Helsinki Kaisaniemi is a data point, with the minimum temperature of the day as its feature and the maximum temperature as its label. The learned depth-2 tree is a piecewise constant hypothesis with four pieces, one per leaf node, each equal to the mean label of the days routed there. The tree was grown to depth two rather than until the stopping rule above fired, so that each of its four pieces is visible in the picture. Decision trees serve as base models of the random forest and of gradient-boosted decision tree methods . A decision tree with a small number of nodes is often considered interpretable: its computation can be traced by following the data point from the root node to a leaf node . This makes small decision trees a common choice in interpretable machine learning.

terms.name: dimensionality reduction
terms.abstract: Dimensionality reduction uses a map h: Rd → Rd' to replace a raw feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ by a shorter feature vector z = (z1, …, zd')ᵀ, with d' < d. Using fewer features lowers the effective dimension of a model, which reduces the chance of overfitting. Moreover, it lowers the amount of computation needed for model training and for inference. It also enables visualization: two features can be used as the coordinates in a scatterplot. principal component analysis learns a linear map by minimizing the reconstruction error, while a random projection uses a linear map drawn at random, without any training. An autoencoder learns a nonlinear map represented by an artificial neural network.
terms.description: Dimensionality reduction uses a map (or transformation) h: Rd → Rd' to replace the raw feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ of a data point by a shorter feature vector z = (z1, …, zd')ᵀ, with d' < d (Fig.~1). Using a shorter feature vector is beneficial in several ways: \begin{itemize} \item \emph{Statistical benefit:} It typically reduces the chance of overfitting, as reducing the number of features often reduces the effective dimension of a model. \item \emph{Computational benefit:} Using fewer features lowers the amount of computation needed for model training and for inference. As a case in point, linear regression methods need to invert a matrix whose size is determined by the number of features. \item \emph{Visualization:} A map can be learned that delivers two features z1,z2, which can then be used as the coordinates in a scatterplot. Fig.~2 places each square patch of a photograph at the two features that principal component analysis learns for it, which keep most of the variance of the raw feature vectors. Each patch is naturally represented by one color value for each of its pixels, so its raw feature vector is long. \end{itemize} Dimensionality reduction methods differ in the hypothesis space used for the map, in the criterion they learn it by, and in whether the map is learned from data at all. principal component analysis learns a linear map: the map is a matrix chosen so that the reconstruction error, the squared distance between x and the feature vector reconstructed from z by a second linear map, is minimal on average over the training set . An autoencoder learns a nonlinear map represented by an artificial neural network, under the same criterion . A random projection uses a random matrix without any training: by the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma, the distances between the feature vectors of the data points are approximately preserved . Nonlinear methods beyond the autoencoder include the manifold-learning family, among them t-SNE and UMAP, which are used mainly for visualization.

terms.name: distribution shift
terms.abstract: Distribution shift is a mismatch between the probability distribution underlying the training set and test set of a machine learning method and the probability distribution of the data points that the learned hypothesis faces after deployment. The average loss on the test set estimates the risk under the training probability distribution only, so a small test error is no evidence for a small loss on data points outside the test set. Factoring the joint probability distribution of features and labels separates the named special cases of covariate shift and label shift.
terms.description: The Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI) station Helsinki Kaisaniemi records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. Every summer day is a data point: its feature is the day's minimum temperature, its label the day's maximum. A linear hypothesis h(x) = 0.481 x + 14.5, learned from 62 days of June--August 2026 by minimizing the average squared error loss, reaches a training error of 5.0 and a test error of 6.5 on a test set of the 30 remaining summer days. Deployed at the northernmost FMI station, Utsjoki Nuorgam (70.1∘\,N), on the 90 days of December 2025--February 2026, the same hypothesis incurs an average error of 242.1, which is 37 times its test error (Fig.~1). Every winter morning at Nuorgam is colder than each summer morning in the training set, and the extrapolation overshoots: the mean winter day at Nuorgam has a minimum of -19.8 ∘C and a maximum of -9.6 ∘C, while h assigns such a morning a maximum of +5.0 ∘C. Distribution shift is a mismatch between the probability distribution p underlying the training set and test set of a machine learning method and the probability distribution p' of the data points the learned hypothesis faces after deployment . The average loss on the test set estimates the risk under p, since the independent and identically distributed assumption covers draws from p, not from p'. A small test error is therefore no evidence for a small loss under p' ≠ p: the densities in Fig.~2 show how a threshold placed for p fails under p', and the two stations of Fig.~1 realize the failure with measured temperatures. The named special cases of distribution shift correspond to the two factorizations of the joint probability distribution of a data point (x, y) . Under the factorization p(x, y) = p(y | x) p(x), covariate shift changes only the marginal p(x) of the covariates (the features) and leaves the conditional p(y | x) untouched. An example is a second weather station in a colder climate at which cold mornings precede rain in the same way. Concept drift changes that conditional itself over time, as when a warming climate alters which morning temperatures precede rain. Under the reverse factorization p(x, y) = p(x | y) p(y), label shift changes only the frequency p(y) of the label values and leaves the class-conditional p(x | y) untouched. The two-station example is a pure case of none of the three: the marginal of the feature moves, since winter mornings are colder, and the conditional moves as well, since a line fitted to the winter days has slope 0.77 against the summer slope 0.48. Distribution shift is detected by comparing summary statistics of the features between the training set and the data points arriving after deployment, or by monitoring the incurred loss whenever labels become available . One response is sample weighting: each data point of the training set is weighted by the ratio p'(x)/p(x). This weighting corrects covariate shift under two conditions: the conditional p(y | x) is unchanged, and every feature vector occurring under p' also occurs under p, so that the ratio is defined . Both conditions fail in the two-station example: no reweighting of summer days produces a winter morning at -20 ∘C. Responses that remain applicable are transfer learning and fine-tuning on data points from p', domain adaptation, which uses unlabeled data points from p' while the hypothesis is still being learned, and online learning, which updates the hypothesis as data points from the drifting probability distribution arrive .

terms.name: eigenvalue
terms.abstract: An eigenvalue of a square matrix A is a number λ for which some nonzero vector x satisfies Ax = λx. Such a vector is an eigenvector of A. Multiplying an eigenvector by the matrix rescales it without moving it off the line it spans. The eigenvalues of a diagonalizable matrix form the diagonal factor of its eigenvalue decomposition. An iterative method that applies an affine update, such as gradient descent for linear regression, converges to the unique fixed point of the update, for every initialization, exactly when each eigenvalue of the update matrix has magnitude less than one. The second-smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph measures how well the graph is connected and underlies spectral clustering.
terms.description: A square matrix A represents a linear map from Rd to Rd; the image of a vector x under this map is the product Ax. Multiplying a vector by a square matrix normally moves it off the line it spans. Some nonzero vectors are exceptions: each stays on the line it spans and is only rescaled. The factor by which such a vector is rescaled is an eigenvalue. Formally, a number λ ∈ R is an eigenvalue of a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d, one with d rows and d columns, if A x = λ x for some nonzero vector x ∈ Rd; such a vector is an eigenvector of A . For an eigenvector, the image Ax stays on the line x spans, pointing the same way when λ > 0 and the opposite way when λ < 0 (see Fig.~1). Arranging d linearly independent eigenvectors of a diagonalizable matrix as the columns of V, and the corresponding eigenvalues in a diagonal matrix Λ, yields the eigenvalue decomposition A = V Λ V-1. Eigenvalues can be used to study iterative machine learning methods with an update of the form \[ \weights^{(\iteridx+1)} = \mM \weights^{(\iteridx)} + \vb \text{.} \] An example is gradient descent for linear regression, whose update operator η : w ↦ M w + b is affine with iteration matrix M = I - (2η/m) XᵀX. Here, I is the identity matrix, η the learning rate, m the number of data points, and X the feature matrix of the training set (see linear regression). Such an iteration converges to the unique fixed point w of η, for every initialization, if and only if the spectral radius ρ of M, the largest magnitude of an eigenvalue of M, satisfies ρ < 1 . Beyond the convergence of iterative methods, eigenvalues are also used to measure the connectivity of an undirected graph G with n nodes. The Laplacian matrix G of G is positive semi-definite, with eigenvalues 0 = 1 ≤ 2 ≤ … ≤ n. The second-smallest eigenvalue 2, the algebraic connectivity of G, quantifies connectivity: 2 > 0 if and only if G is connected, and 2 close to zero indicates two clusters of nodes with few edges between them. Fig.~2 shows three edge sets on the same six nodes: adding edges increases 2 from 0, for two clusters without a connecting edge, to 6, for the complete graph. The eigenvector corresponding to 2, referred to as the Fiedler vector, can be used to partition G into two clusters: each node is assigned according to the sign of its own component of the Fiedler vector.

terms.name: expectation–maximization (EM)
terms.abstract: The expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative optimization method for a particular class of maximum likelihood problems. In particular, EM is useful for probabilistic models that involve observed and unobserved (or latent) attributes of a data point. Each iteration of the EM algorithm alternates an E-step with an M-step. The E-step computes the posterior distribution of the unobserved attributes under the current model parameters. The M-step minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the complete data points averaged under this posterior distribution, which for many probabilistic models has a closed form. Mathematically, the EM algorithm is an instance of a majorize–minimize method. A canonical soft clustering method uses the EM algorithm to learn the model parameters of a Gaussian mixture model.
terms.description: The nightly minimum temperatures recorded over one year at the weather station of Krems an der Donau (Austria) scatter around two regimes, cold-season and warm-season nights. A probabilistic model for such data points has, besides the observed temperature, an unobserved attribute: the regime a night belongs to. Fig.~1 shows the histogram of the temperatures together with a Gaussian mixture model consisting of a separate normal distribution for each regime. The EM algorithm is an iterative optimization method for approximately solving maximum likelihood optimization problems for probabilistic models with an unobserved attribute. Consider a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) whose data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. The underlying probability distribution is a probabilistic model x',y'x,y;w for the observed feature vector x and an unobserved attribute y with values in a finite set Y. This probabilistic model is a family of probability distributions parameterized by model parameters w in a parameter space W. maximum likelihood is an instance of empirical risk minimization: it minimizes the empirical risk \begin{equation} \emprisk{\weights}{\dataset} \defeq - \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \log \sum_{\truelabel \in \labelspace} \pmf{\featurevec',\truelabel'}{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)},\truelabel;\weights}\text{,} \end{equation} the average negative log-likelihood of the observed feature vectors. The sum inside the logarithm is what makes \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} hard to minimize directly: if the attributes y(r) were observed, the empirical risk would be an average of -log x',y'x(r),y(r);w, which for many probabilistic models has a closed-form minimizer. The EM algorithm solves the maximum likelihood problem \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} by alternating two steps. The E-step computes, for every data point, the posterior distribution of the unobserved attribute under the current model parameters w, \begin{equation} \pmf{\truelabel'|\featurevec'}{\truelabel;\widehat{\weights}} = \frac{\pmf{\featurevec',\truelabel'}{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)},\truelabel;\widehat{\weights}}} {\sum_{\truelabel'' \in \labelspace} \pmf{\featurevec',\truelabel'}{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)},\truelabel'';\widehat{\weights}}} \quad \text{for } \truelabel \in \labelspace \text{ and } \sampleidx = 1, \ldots, \samplesize\text{.} \end{equation} The M-step minimizes over w ∈ W the empirical risk of the complete data points, averaged under these posterior distributions, \begin{equation} Q(\weights \mid \widehat{\weights}) \defeq - \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \sum_{\truelabel \in \labelspace} \pmf{\truelabel'|\featurevec'}{\truelabel;\widehat{\weights}} \log \frac{\pmf{\featurevec',\truelabel'}{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)},\truelabel;\weights}} {\pmf{\truelabel'|\featurevec'}{\truelabel;\widehat{\weights}}}\text{.} \end{equation} Algorithm~1 states the method in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Expectation-maximization } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Require dataset D, probabilistic model with parameters w ∈ W, initialization w(0), iteration count T \For{t = 0, 1, …, T-1} \State \textbf{E-step:} form Q(w | w(t)), the expectation of the complete-data empirical risk under the current parameters \State \textbf{M-step:} w(t+1) argminw ∈ W Q(w | w(t)) \EndFor \Ensure w(T) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} One E-step followed by one M-step constitutes one iteration of the EM algorithm. The EM algorithm is a majorize–minimize method: each iteration minimizes a surrogate Q(w | w) of the empirical risk \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict}. The surrogate \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} has three properties (whose lower bound on the log-likelihood is this surrogate written for the negative log-likelihood; ). First, it majorizes the empirical risk, Q(w | w) ≥ wD for all w ∈ W, by Jensen's inequality applied to the concave logarithm. Second, it is tight at the current iterate, Q(w | w) = wD. Third, it is minimized exactly by the M-step. Any model parameters w(t+1) that minimize the surrogate built at w(t) therefore satisfy w(t+1)D ≤ Q(w(t+1) | w(t)) ≤ Q(w(t) | w(t)) = w(t)D: no iteration increases the empirical risk . The monotone decrease of the empirical risk \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} along the EM iterates yields a stopping criterion: the iteration stops as soon as the decrease of the empirical risk achieved by the last iteration falls below a given threshold . The empirical risk \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} is in general a non-convex function of the model parameters, and EM might converge to a local minimum . It is therefore typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest empirical risk . The EM algorithm is a fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)). The operator F maps the current model parameters w to the result of one E-step followed by one M-step. The E-step \eqref{equ_em_estep_dict} at w builds the surrogate Q(· | w), and the M-step \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} minimizes it, \fixedpointop(\widehat{\weights}) \defeq \argmin_{\weights \in \paramspace} Q(\weights \mid \widehat{\weights})\text{.} The fixed points of F are model parameters that minimize their own surrogate: there, the surrogate touches the empirical risk from above, so no further descent step is available, and the gradient of the empirical risk vanishes . EM is used to learn the model parameters of a Gaussian mixture model, where the unobserved attribute of a data point is its cluster index I(r) ∈ 1, …, k and the model parameters are the cluster probabilities pc, means c, and covariance matrices c . The E-step \eqref{equ_em_estep_dict} becomes the degree of belonging \begin{equation} \dob{\clusteridx}{\sampleidx} \defeq \prob{I^{(\sampleidx)} = \clusteridx \mid \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}} = \frac{p_{\clusteridx}\, \mvnormal{\meanvec{\clusteridx}}{\covmtx{\clusteridx}}(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)})} {\sum_{\clusteridx'=1}^{\nrcluster} p_{\clusteridx'}\, \mvnormal{\meanvec{\clusteridx'}}{\covmtx{\clusteridx'}}(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)})}\text{,} \end{equation} and minimizing the surrogate \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} yields the M-step in closed form. The cluster probability pc is the average of cr over the data points, while c and c are the mean and covariance matrix of the feature vectors weighted by cr. The learned degrees of belonging \eqref{equ_em_gmm_estep_dict} constitute a soft clustering. Fixing every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix I with a common σ2 that shrinks towards 0 turns the degrees of belonging into 0 or 1, and EM reduces to Lloyd's algorithm for k-means . Consider next, as an illustration of the EM algorithm, the Gaussian mixture model of Fig.~1 for the temperature dataset. The feature of a data point is the nightly minimum temperature x ∈ R, and its unobserved attribute is the regime y ∈ cold, warm. The model parameters are the probabilities pcold, pwarm = 1 - pcold of the two regimes, the means μcold, μwarm and the variances σ2cold, σ2warm of the two normal distributions, so w = (pcold, pwarm, μcold, μwarm, σ2cold, σ2warm)ᵀ ∈ R6. The E-step \eqref{equ_em_estep_dict} computes for every night the probability of the cold regime, and the M-step \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} re-fits w as averages weighted by these probabilities. On the 366 nights of 2024, EM learns pcold = 0.83, μcold = 5.1, μwarm = 17.2, σ2cold = 39.7, and σ2warm = 3.3. Fig.~2 shows the majorize–minimize view for this Gaussian mixture model as the cold-season mean μcold varies, while pcold, μwarm and σ2warm are fixed at their learned values and σ2cold is fixed at 16. The empirical risk is then a function of μcold alone, and so is each surrogate. Each surrogate lies above the empirical risk, touches it at its iterate, and its minimizer is the next iterate. Fig.~3 shows how the empirical risk decreases monotonically as the EM iterations proceed.

terms.name: ensemble
terms.abstract: An ensemble method combines several machine learning methods, each referred to as a base learner. Ensemble methods differ in how they construct the base learners and in how they combine their results. bagging trains each base learner on a resampled copy of the training set. boosting runs them sequentially, each one fitted to the errors of the previous ones. stacking uses base learners to train different models on the same training set and learns an aggregation rule. For the squared error loss the gain is exact: the error of the average prediction is the average error of the base learners minus their average disagreement, so base learners that disagree are what makes an ensemble worth forming.
terms.description: Predicting the maximum temperature of a day at the weather station Krems an der Donau from the minimum temperature of the same day can be done with a linear model, with a decision tree, or with an artificial neural network. Fig.~1 shows all three fitted to the 366 days of 2020. None of them is the best everywhere: the straight line is too stiff at the cold end, the decision tree answers with a staircase, and the artificial neural network bends where the other two cannot. model selection would keep one of them and discard the rest. Is there a better way to combine these base learners instead of choosing one of them? Combining several machine learning methods into one predictor is an ensemble method: each combined method is a base learner . The base learners can be empirical risk minimization-based, using different choices for the loss, model, and training set. Of M base learners, base learner ℓ learns a hypothesis ℓ from its hypothesis space ℓ and its, possibly perturbed, training set D(ℓ), and an aggregation rule φagg combines the outputs of these hypotheses into the final prediction. The aggregation can amount to averaging (in regression), as in Fig.~1, or to a majority vote (in classification); Fig.~2 shows the general shape. What the combination buys is exactly the disagreement among the base learners. For the squared error loss, the error of the average prediction is the average error of the base learners minus their average disagreement, where the disagreement of a base learner is the squared difference between its own prediction and the average one . This is an identity, not an approximation: on the held-back days of Fig.~1 the average member error 26.47 minus the average disagreement 0.52 is the 25.95 that the average prediction actually incurs. Two consequences follow. The average is never worse than its base learners are on average, since a disagreement cannot be negative. And base learners that agree everywhere buy nothing, which is why they are trained on different models or on different data points. Beating the \emph{best} single base learner is a different and weaker claim: over 50 repetitions on random halves of the training set, the average did so 22 times. The same point in terms of variance: consider M base learners whose predictions are identically distributed, each with variance σ2 and pairwise correlation ρ. The average of these predictions has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{\numlearners}\,\sigma^{2}\text{.} The second of these two summands vanishes as M grows, while the first, set by the correlation between the base learners, limits what averaging can achieve. Ensemble methods differ in how they construct the base learners and in how they combine their results. bagging trains each base learner on a random resample of the training set and averages them; it reduces the variance of an unstable base learner such as a deep decision tree, while the systematic part of its error, the bias, is left unchanged . A random forest is bagging of decision trees with, in addition, a random choice of the features considered at each split, which lowers the correlation between the trees . boosting runs the base learners sequentially, each one fitted to the errors of the previous ones. The number of rounds is a hyperparameter: the training error keeps decreasing while the validation error eventually rises, so boosting overfits when run for too long . stacking trains the base learners on the same training set with different models and learns the aggregation rule itself by a second machine learning method. The second method is trained on predictions for data points the base learners did not see. Otherwise the base learners that fit the training set best are favored regardless of how they generalize .

terms.name: empirical risk minimization (ERM)
terms.abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) selects a hypothesis by minimizing the average loss on a given training set D(train), the empirical risk. machine learning methods aim at a hypothesis that incurs a small loss on any data point, and ERM replaces this unknown quantity by its average over the training set. Different machine learning methods arise from different choices of the model H and the loss function L, both of which depend on the feature space X and the label space Y of a given method.
terms.description: A weather forecaster predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature is useful only if its predictions are accurate on the large majority of days, not only on the days it was tuned on. This forecaster is a hypothesis: it maps a day's features to a prediction of tomorrow's temperature, and its loss quantifies how far that prediction lies from the measured value. More generally, machine learning methods aim to find a hypothesis that incurs a small loss for any data point. The phrase \emph{any data point} is made precise by a probabilistic model for the generation of data points, as follows. If data points are assumed to be drawn from a probability distribution, then the risk of a hypothesis is defined as the expectation of its loss under that probability distribution. The ideal choice is then the hypothesis with minimal risk. However, in most machine learning applications, the underlying probability distribution is not known. Instead, only a finite training set D(train) of data points is available. ERM replaces the intractable risk with its sample-average surrogate, the empirical risk on D(train), and picks the hypothesis that minimizes this surrogate. For a fixed choice of loss function and hypothesis space, ERM is a map A that reads in a training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m of data points z(r) = x(r)y(r). The map returns a learned hypothesis h = A(D(train)) ∈ H that minimizes the empirical risk on D(train), \[ \learnthypothesis \in \argmin_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\datapoint^{(\sampleidx)}}{\hypothesis} \text{.} \] The hypothesis h is chosen from the underlying hypothesis space (or model) H. For an ERM-based method, model training is to compute A. In practice, the map A is computed by an iterative optimization method. Many of these optimization methods can be represented as a fixed-point iteration that starts with an initial hypothesis h(0) and then repeatedly applies an update operator F, \hypothesis^{(\iteridx+1)} = \fixedpointop\big( \hypothesis^{(\iteridx)} \big) \text{, for } \iteridx=0,1,\ldots \text{.} The update operator F depends on the training set, the loss function, and the hypothesis space. It is chosen such that its fixed points are minimizers of the empirical risk. For ERM using a parametric model H, the fixed-point iteration can be formulated directly in terms of the model parameters w instead of the hypothesis h. In particular, starting with initial model parameters w(0), the update operator F is applied repeatedly to the model parameters, \weights^{(\iteridx+1)} = \fixedpointop\big( \weights^{(\iteridx)} \big) \text{, for } \iteridx=0,1,\ldots \text{.} One important example of such a fixed-point iteration is gradient descent, which updates the model parameters in the direction of the negative gradient of the empirical risk (which needs to be differentiable). ERM presupposes that the loss z(r)h can be evaluated for every hypothesis h ∈ H and every training data point z(r). This full-feedback requirement is what distinguishes ERM from reinforcement learning algorithms, which use partial feedback. In particular, at each time instant t = 1, 2, …, an reinforcement learning algorithm chooses an action, the prediction of its current hypothesis h(t), and observes only the loss incurred by that action. It has no information about the loss that would have been incurred by any other hypothesis h ∈ H h(t). ERM can also be implemented as an online algorithm, which is useful when the data points in D(train) can only be accessed sequentially. Such sequential access arises, for instance, when memory limits prevent loading the entire training set at once. The canonical online form of ERM is the Follow-The-Leader algorithm, which, at every round, solves a partial ERM problem on all data points seen so far. Assuming that the data point z(t) arrives at time instant t=1,2,…, Follow-The-Leader updates the learned hypothesis h(t) by \learnthypothesis^{(\timeidx)} \in \argmin_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace} \frac{1}{\timeidx} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\timeidx} \lossfunc{\datapoint^{(\sampleidx)}}{\hypothesis} \text{.} Implementing this partial ERM separately for each time instant can become computationally expensive (and wasteful), as it does not exploit the similarity between consecutive partial ERM problems. This similarity can be exploited by online gradient descent, which performs a single gradient descent step on the new data point z(t) at every time instant t . Different machine learning methods arise from different design choices for the two ingredients of the map A: the model H and the loss function L. Both depend on the nature of the data points, i.e., on the feature space X and the label space Y. For example, image data points with a high-dimensional feature space and a finite label space typically call for an artificial neural network together with the logistic loss . Conversely, data points with few real-valued features and a real-valued label often allow for a linear model together with the squared error loss . Fig.~1 illustrates ERM for a linear model on data points with a single feature x and label y. Each hypothesis is a linear map h(x) = w1 x + w0 with model parameters w0, w1. ERM picks the model parameters that minimize the empirical risk on D(train).

terms.name: eigenvalue decomposition (EVD)
terms.abstract: An eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) of a square matrix breaks the linear map it represents into elementary operations: expanding a vector in the eigenvectors of the matrix, multiplying each expansion coefficient by the corresponding eigenvalue, and summing the scaled terms up again. A matrix that has an EVD is called diagonalizable; symmetric matrices and matrices with distinct eigenvalues are diagonalizable. A dataset with numeric feature vectors can be characterized by the EVD of its sample covariance matrix. The EVD can be used to speed up computations such as the gradient step of gradient descent methods. For linear regression, each gradient descent iteration then reduces to element-wise operations. The EVD of the Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph is instrumental for spectral clustering.
terms.description: Each day of 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) is recorded with its lowest and its highest temperature, stacked into a feature vector x = ( x1, x2 )ᵀ ∈ R2. Fig.~1 shows the m = 366 days x(1), …, x(m) as a scatterplot together with an ellipse that is computed from their sample mean and sample covariance matrix. The sample mean of the days is \[ \samplemeanvecgeneric = \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} \text{,} \] and their sample covariance matrix is \[ \samplecovmtxgeneric = \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \big( \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} - \samplemeanvecgeneric \big) \big( \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} - \samplemeanvecgeneric \big)^{\top} \in \reals^{2 \times 2} \text{.} \] The shape of the ellipse, which outlines the dataset, is determined by an EVD of the sample covariance matrix C. An EVD for a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d is a factorization of the form \[ \mA = \mV {\bm \Lambda} \mV^{-1} \text{.} \] The columns of the matrix V = ( v(1), …, v(d) ) are eigenvectors of the matrix A. The diagonal matrix Λ = diag 1, …, d contains the eigenvalues j corresponding to the eigenvectors v(j). Multiplying the factorization by v(j) gives A v(j) = j v(j): each eigenvector is a direction that A only scales, by the factor j; a single such pair satisfies A x = λ x, and the EVD collects d of them, indexed by j. Unlike the singular value decomposition, which exists for every matrix, square or not, the EVD is defined for square matrices only, and it need not exist. Moreover, the same matrix might allow for different EVDs: any nonzero linear combination of eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue is again an eigenvector with this eigenvalue. The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue is the maximum number of linearly independent eigenvectors with this eigenvalue . The EVD breaks the linear map u ↦ A u into three elementary operations. A vector u is expanded in the eigenvectors, u = Σj=1d βj v(j) with the expansion coefficients β = V-1 u; each coefficient is multiplied by its eigenvalue; and the scaled terms are summed up again, A u = Σj=1d j βj v(j). matrices that allow for an EVD are called diagonalizable. One example of a diagonalizable matrix is \[ \mA = \begin{pmatrix} 1.3 & 0.8 \ 0.4 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \text{.} \] Fig.~2 illustrates its EVD. Two sufficient conditions for a real-valued square matrix to be diagonalizable are that it is a symmetric matrix or that its d eigenvalues are distinct. For a real-valued symmetric matrix, the EVD has additional structure: the eigenvectors can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis, i.e., the matrix V in the factorization can be chosen to be orthogonal . For a complex-valued matrix, the first condition is that it is Hermitian; a complex symmetric matrix need not be diagonalizable . The condition that is both necessary and sufficient is that every root of the minimal polynomial of the matrix is simple. The matrix A of Fig.~2 is not symmetric, since its off-diagonal entries 0.8 and 0.4 differ, but its two eigenvalues 1.7 and 0.5 are distinct, so it has an EVD. When neither condition holds, an EVD may not exist: the matrix \[ \mN = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] is not symmetric and has the eigenvalue 0 twice, since the eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries . The eigenvectors of N are all located on the line (a, 0)ᵀ : a ∈ R, so there is no invertible matrix V whose columns are eigenvectors of N. The ellipse in Fig.~1 is the set of feature vectors x for which the quadratic form (x - μ)ᵀ C-1 (x - μ) equals 4. This set can be characterized more conveniently using an EVD of the sample covariance matrix C. The matrix C is symmetric, so it has an EVD C = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V that contains the eigenvectors in its columns. Transforming the feature vector x of a day according to x := Vᵀ (x - μ) turns the quadratic form into \[ (\featurevec - \samplemeanvecgeneric)^{\top} \samplecovmtxgeneric^{-1} (\featurevec - \samplemeanvecgeneric) = \widetilde{\featurevec}^{\top} {\bm \Lambda}^{-1} \widetilde{\featurevec} = \frac{\widetilde{x}_{1}^{2}}{\eigval{1}} + \frac{\widetilde{x}_{2}^{2}}{\eigval{2}} \text{,} \] since C-1 = V Λ-1 Vᵀ. The ellipse is therefore the set where x12/1 + x22/2 = 4, with half-axes 21 and 22 along the coordinate axes of x, that is, along the eigenvectors. The transformed days have the sample covariance matrix Vᵀ C V = Λ: the two new coordinates have sample covariance zero, and the eigenvalues are their sample variances. Replacing each day by its first coordinate x1 alone keeps the direction of largest variance, which is the idea of principal component analysis . Besides describing the shape of a dataset, the EVD can be used to speed up the implementation of a machine learning method. Consider gradient descent for linear regression, with the update w(t+1) = w(t) - (2η/m) Xᵀ ( X w(t) - y ) for the feature matrix X and label vector y of the training set (see linear regression). The matrix XᵀX is symmetric, so it has an EVD XᵀX = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V. In the transformed coordinates w(t) := Vᵀ w(t), the update decouples into \[ \widetilde{w}_{\featureidx}^{(\iteridx+1)} = \big( 1 - (2\lrate/\samplesize) \eigval{\featureidx} \big) \widetilde{w}_{\featureidx}^{(\iteridx)} + (2\lrate/\samplesize) \big( \mV^{\top} \featuremtx^{\top} \labelvec \big)_{\featureidx} \text{.} \] After the one-time computation of the EVD, each iteration is an element-wise multiplication and addition of vectors of length d (\texttt{pythondemos/evd.py}). Another application of the EVD in machine learning is the clustering of graph-structured data . Consider data points represented as the nodes i = 1, …, n of an undirected graph G, e.g., the users of a social network with edges given by friendships. The Laplacian matrix G of the graph G is symmetric and positive semi-definite . It has an EVD G = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V and nonnegative eigenvalues. If the graph G is connected, the EVD has additional structure: the eigenvalue 0 has multiplicity one, with the all-ones vector as its eigenvector . Moreover, there is then a distinguished eigenvector, called the Fiedler vector: an eigenvector of the smallest nonzero eigenvalue, the algebraic connectivity of G . The Fiedler vector can be used for clustering the nodes of the graph, which is the idea of spectral clustering . Fig.~3 shows the Fiedler vector of a connected graph with six nodes: two clusters of three nodes and a single edge joining the two clusters.

terms.name: explainability
terms.abstract: Explainability is the property of a machine learning method whose explanations let a human user anticipate the predictions it delivers. The method delivers an explanation along with every prediction, and that explanation is effective if it lets the user anticipate the prediction made for a data point; comprehending the explanation is not required for this test. Explainability is always relative to a specific user or group of users: an explanation can be effective for one and useless for another. Explainability can be measured by comparing the predictions of a learned hypothesis to the anticipations of a user before and after they are provided with an explanation.
terms.description: A machine learning method is explainable for a human user if the explanations it provides let the user anticipate the predictions it delivers. Explainability thus includes the notion of an explanation: each prediction is delivered with an explanation for this specific prediction (see Fig.~1), such as the feature values that drove it or, for image data, the relevant pixels. The definition asks for the existence of an explanation, not for a particular one: explainability is certified by exhibiting one explanation that works, and one explanation the user cannot follow does not show that the method is unexplainable. Explainability is relative to a specific user or group of users: the same learned hypothesis can be explainable for one user and inscrutable for another. The usefulness of an explanation can be measured by how much it enables the user to anticipate the predictions on a curated test set: the user states an anticipation for each data point in the test set. If the user comprehends the explanations, these anticipations should be close to the predictions of the learned hypothesis . A measure of this form is referred to as predictability . As with interpretability, predictability is weaker than comprehension of the explanations: anticipating the predictions does not require comprehending the provided explanations. The conditional differential entropy is defined for RVs. If the data point is modeled as the realization of an random variable, the prediction and the anticipation of the user are RVs too, and their joint probability distribution yields a second measure of this predictability: the conditional differential entropy of the predictions given the anticipations . A related measure, the mutual information between a selected subset of the features and the prediction, is maximized by the explainer of . The conditional differential entropy quantifies the uncertainty that remains about the predictions once the anticipations are known, so a smaller value means that the anticipations determine the predictions more tightly. In practice, this conditional differential entropy is unknown and must be replaced by an estimator. One such estimator bins the predictions and the anticipations on a test set, and takes the fraction of test data points that fall into each pair of bins as the joint probability distribution. An explanation raises explainability when the user can reason with it. Fig.~2 illustrates this for a user who reasons in terms of linear maps and anticipates the predictions of an opaque hypothesis (Gaussian kernel ridge regression, a kernel method). Without explanations, the user anticipates by a single linear map fitted to a few predictions, and the anticipations deviate strongly from the predictions. The explanation for a test data point with feature value x0 is a local linear approximation of the hypothesis around it (cf.\ local interpretable model-agnostic explanations), a slope and an intercept that the user evaluates at x0. With this explanation, the anticipations match the predictions almost exactly. The example presupposes that the user knows how to apply a linear approximation: the anticipations improve only because the user can evaluate the explanation for a data point. A user who cannot is left where they started. An explanation can also mislead. A computed explanation can be unfaithful to the learned hypothesis, so that anticipations based on it are confidently wrong . Saliency maps, intensity maps over the pixels of an input image (see explainable artificial intelligence), barely change for some methods when the trained deep net is replaced by one with random weights . The predictability test detects such an explanation: anticipations drawn from it deviate from the predictions. The international terminology standard for artificial intelligence defines explainability as the property of an artificial intelligence system to express important factors influencing its results in a way that humans can understand. An explanation is intended to answer the question of why the artificial intelligence system produced a result, without arguing that the result was optimal . The AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) ties explainability to a representation of the mechanisms underlying the operation of an artificial intelligence system. NIST reserves interpretability for the meaning of the output in the context of the designed purpose . The two frameworks thus divide the terms differently. The expressed factors influencing a result, which the terminology standard places under explainability, are close to the NIST notion of interpretability; the NIST notion of explainability is instead close to interpretability as comprehension of the computation of the method. Regulation treats explainability as an ingredient of transparency. The EU AI Act requires that high-risk AI systems are sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately . For individual automated decisions, the right to explanation entitles an affected person to a clear and meaningful account of the role that an artificial intelligence system played in the decision . The Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act of 2026 requires that the deployer give the affected consumer a plain-language description of the decision and of the role the technology played in it, together with the means to request further information . What counts as an automated decision is drawn widely: the Court of Justice of the European Union held that a credit information agency computing a person's ability to meet future payments already makes one, when a third party draws strongly on that value .

terms.name: explanation
terms.abstract: An explanation accompanies a prediction delivered by a machine learning method and states which properties of the data point led to that prediction. Explanations can be text, a score per feature, a simple hypothesis that approximates the learned one near the data point, or a heat map drawn over an image. Two requirements can be contradictory. On the one hand, an explanation must be faithful: it must reflect the computation by which the learned hypothesis arrives at the prediction. On the other hand, it must be understandable: its user must be able to anticipate the predictions it accompanies. An explanation that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis again, so a simpler one may have to give up faithfulness somewhere.
terms.description: One approach to enhance the transparency of a machine learning method for its human user is to provide an explanation alongside each prediction delivered by the method. Explanations can take different forms. For instance, they may consist of human-readable text or quantitative indicators, such as feature importance scores for the individual features of a given data point~, obtained, e.g., via the weights of a local linear approximation . Fig. 1 illustrates two types of explanations for a learned hypothesis h(x) of a single feature x. The first is a local linear approximation g(x) of the nonlinear h(x) around a specific feature value x'. The second form of explanation depicted in the figure is a sparse set of predictions h(x(1)), h(x(2)), h(x(3)) at selected feature values, possibly chosen by the user. Another form of explanation is a heat map: an intensity map that scores each region of an image by how much it drove the prediction, drawn over the image itself . For a convolutional neural network, those scores are computed from the network's own activations, which is what a class activation map does. Explanations differ in scope. The local linear approximation of local interpretable model-agnostic explanations concerns a single prediction; a global explanation, such as a decision tree fitted to the predictions of the learned hypothesis, describes its behavior across the whole feature space . A counterfactual answers a different question: not which features drove the prediction, but what change of the feature vector would have changed it . Whatever form it takes, an explanation carries two requirements: it must be (i) understandable and (ii) faithful. Understandable means that the user can work with the explanation on their own. Faithful means that the explanation reflects the computation the learned hypothesis carries out, rather than one that is easier to present. An intensity map over the pixels of an image is faithful when manipulating a few of the pixels it highlights changes the prediction while changing dark ones does not (see explainable artificial intelligence). These two requirements can be contradictory. An unfaithful explanation can even be understandable and let the user anticipate well, whenever it tracks the prediction without carrying anything about the computation. For some saliency methods, the map computed from a network with random weights is nearly the same as the map computed from the trained network. Such a map traces the edges of the input image and carries nothing about the prediction, yet it looks like a plausible explanation . An explanation that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis again, so a simpler explanation may have to give up faithfulness somewhere. Fig.~2 shows both requirements at work on a prediction made from weather radar. The features are the hourly precipitation over a 120\,km box around Krems an der Donau, and the prediction answers whether it will rain at Krems two hours later. A convolutional neural network fitted to these images is explained by a class activation map, which scores each cell of the image by how much it contributed to the prediction . For the hour drawn, the network is certain of rain, and the CAM puts its weight on the bands of precipitation south and south-east of the town rather than on the rain already overhead. Setting the precipitation to zero in the 360 cells with the highest CAM scores lowers the predicted score by 1.57, against 0.26 for the 360 cells with the lowest scores, and the same holds on 63 of the 72 held-out hours. The same content can be delivered as text. The sentence under the panels is generated from the CAM by computing the radius that holds the cells it scores highest and the direction of their center of mass. It is therefore faithful by construction and can be checked against the radar image on the left.

terms.name: feature learning
terms.abstract: Feature learning is the task of learning, from a dataset, a feature transformation that turns the raw features of a data point into new features that make a subsequent learning task easier. A feature learning method is specified by the two feature spaces, by a hypothesis space of candidate feature transformations, and by a quantitative measure of how useful a feature transformation is, computed from a dataset that need not carry labels. principal component analysis learns a linear feature transformation to fewer features, judged by the linear reconstruction error, and an autoencoder obtains a nonlinear one by the same criterion. The hidden layers of a deep net form a chain of feature transformations learned jointly with the output layer, so that each layer builds its features from those of the previous one. pretraining an encoder on unlabeled data points learns features that are reused across learning tasks. In weather forecasting, forty measurements from the five days before are turned into two learned features from which linear regression predicts the maximum temperature of the next day.
terms.description: Consider the task of forecasting the weather of tomorrow at a weather station from the measurements of the previous five days. Each day is a data point, and its label is the maximum temperature of that day. Its raw features are eight daily measurements: the lowest, highest and mean air temperature, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, the humidity, the air pressure and the wind speed. Taken over each of the five previous days, that is a list of forty numbers. A point with forty coordinates cannot be drawn in a scatterplot. A feature transformation that delivers two new features from the forty raw ones places every day in a scatterplot (see Fig.~1), and a linear model of the two new features may already predict the label. Feature learning is the task of learning such a feature transformation from a dataset instead of designing it by hand. Feature learning is the task of learning a feature transformation \featuretrafovec: \featurespace \rightarrow \featurespace', \qquad \featurevec \mapsto \vz \defeq \featuretrafovec(\featurevec) \text{.} The transformation reads in the raw feature vector x ∈ X of a data point and delivers a new feature vector z from a new feature space X'. A feature learning method is specified by three design choices: the two feature spaces X and X', a hypothesis space H of candidate feature transformations, and a quantitative measure of how useful a specific Φ ∈ H is. The measure is computed from a dataset, which need not carry labels, and it need not be the dataset of the learning task at hand. A useful feature transformation is one that makes a subsequent learning task easier : the data points become separable by a linear model, fewer features suffice, or the features learned once serve several learning tasks. In the weather example, usefulness is measured by the validation error of linear regression on the learned features. Alternative constructions of a feature transformation do not learn Φ . A kernel method fixes Φ through the choice of a kernel, with X' the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk and z = x·, the kernel with its first argument fixed, never evaluated explicitly, and learns only a linear hypothesis on X'. A hand-designed Φ encodes domain knowledge instead of a dataset. A measure of usefulness can be built from a second map. The feature transformation is then read as an encoder, and a decoder Φ*: X' → X rebuilds the raw feature vector from the new one . What the encoder kept is then measured by how well the decoder rebuilds the data point from it, the reconstruction error \[ \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \loss\Big( \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)},\, \featuretrafovec^{*}\big( \featuretrafovec\big(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big) \big) \Big) \text{.} \] The loss function L penalizes a rebuilt feature vector for differing from the original. A common choice is the squared error loss . The dataset it is computed on needs no labels: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself. The decoder may be learned alongside the encoder. The measure is then the minimum of the reconstruction error over a second hypothesis space of decoders. It may instead be fixed, and the encoder alone must then supply what the decoder cannot. Restricting the decoder therefore decides what the new features have to carry. principal component analysis is this construction with X := Rd, X' := Rd' for some d' < d, and the hypothesis space of linear maps, \hypospace \defeq \big\{ \featuretrafovec: \reals^{\featuredim} \rightarrow \reals^{\featuredim'}: \featurevec \mapsto \mW \featurevec \text{ with some } \mW \in \reals^{\featuredim' \times \featuredim} \big\} \text{.} The decoder is linear too and is learned alongside the encoder W. The usefulness of a specific Φ(x) = W x is therefore the minimum of the reconstruction error over the reconstruction matrices R. On the dataset D = x(1), …, x(m), that minimum is \min_{\mR \in \reals^{\featuredim \times \featuredim'}} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \normgeneric{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} - \mR \mW \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}}{2}^{2} \text{.} The rows of the best W are the d' eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalues . An autoencoder keeps the same criterion and replaces both linear maps by ANNs, so that the new features come from a nonlinear feature transformation. With a linear decoder and the squared error loss, it spans the subspace principal component analysis finds . Applied to the weather example, principal component analysis delivers the two learned features of Fig.~1. The forty raw features of the 361 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau are turned into two learned features. Each raw feature is first scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, because temperatures, precipitation and pressure carry different units. Warm and cold days separate along the first learned feature: 89 percent of the warm days have a positive z1 and 92 percent of the cold days a nonpositive one. linear regression on the two learned features is trained on the days from January to August. It then predicts the maximum temperature of the days from September to December with a validation error of 13.5 squared degrees Celsius. linear regression on all forty raw features reaches 10.2, and predicting the sample mean of the training labels reaches 110.9.
