For high-stakes applications, such as the medical triage of Fig.~1, using an interpretable model can be preferable to explaining an opaque model, since post hoc explanations can be unfaithful to the hypothesis they explain . Restricting H to interpretable hypotheses is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. The penalty-term route reaches an interpretable learned hypothesis without restricting the hypothesis space beforehand. A penalty term added to the objective function of empirical risk minimization de-incentivizes the hypotheses a user cannot follow, so training picks a comprehensible one out of a hypothesis space that mostly holds the others. least absolute shrinkage and selection operator does this for linear models, which are no more comprehensible than a deep net once they weigh hundreds of features. least absolute shrinkage and selection operator uses the ℓ1-norm w1 of the weights w as the penalty term, which sets most weights to exactly zero . The learned hypothesis is then a weighted sum of a few features, so a user can name the features the prediction uses and how much each one moves it. explainable empirical risk minimization extends this idea to the training of an arbitrary model. Its penalty term is built from the predictions that one specific user supplies for the data points of the training set (see explainable empirical risk minimization). It therefore delivers explainability to that user rather than interpretability, and it leaves the hypothesis space as it is. The user predictions need not be elicited one data point at a time. They might be obtained as the predictions of a simpler proxy model that the user considers interpretable, so that the penalty term measures the deviation from that proxy. In Fig.~2, the user predictions are obtained from a simple linear model fitted to the training set.

terms.name: kernel method
terms.abstract: A kernel method applies a linear method, such as a linear model or a linear classifier, to transformed feature vectors. The transformation is constructed from a kernel: each feature vector is mapped to a function with domain equal to the original feature space, and inner products between transformed feature vectors reduce to evaluations of a kernel. Kernel methods offer great flexibility in the choice of the feature space, which can consist of text documents or discrete structures such as graphs.
terms.description: A kernel method is a machine learning method that applies a linear method, such as a linear model for regression or a linear classifier for classification, to transformed feature vectors that are constructed from a kernel. Kernel methods are used in computer vision to decide whether an image shows a specific object , and in natural language processing to classify text documents by topic . Linear methods learn a hypothesis that combines the features of a data point linearly, e.g., h(x) = wᵀ x for the feature space X = Rd. Such a hypothesis predicts well only if the relation between the feature vectors and the labels of data points is approximately linear. Moreover, a linear method requires numeric feature vectors and is not directly applicable to data points from an arbitrary feature space X, such as text documents or graphs. Both limitations can be mitigated by a feature transformation φ: X → H from the original feature space X to a transformed feature space H, chosen as a Hilbert space. Fig.~1 shows a binary classification problem with the first limitation: no straight line separates the two classes in the original feature space. A suitable feature transformation makes a dataset ``more linear'': the relation between the transformed feature vectors φ(x) and the labels is closer to linear in H than the relation between the original feature vectors x and the labels is in X. A useful feature transformation φ often delivers transformed feature vectors in a Hilbert space H of high (possibly infinite) dimension . Computing and storing the transformed feature vectors φ(x) explicitly can then be infeasible. However, linear methods access the feature vectors of data points only through inner products between pairs of feature vectors (see linear model). For example, the prediction delivered by a trained support vector machine is a weighted sum of inner products between the feature vector of a new data point and the feature vectors in the training set. To apply a linear method to the transformed feature vectors, it is therefore enough to know the inner products φ(x)φ(x') for every possible pair of feature vectors x, x' ∈ X . These inner products are captured by a single function of two arguments, the kernel defined by \[ \kernelmap{\featurevec}{\featurevec'} \defeq \innerprod{\featuretrafo(\featurevec)}{\featuretrafo(\featurevec')} \text{, for } \featurevec, \featurevec' \in \featurespace \text{.} \] The value xx' quantifies the similarity of the feature vectors x and x'. As an inner product of transformed feature vectors, the kernel is symmetric, and every matrix of pairwise kernel values is positive semi-definite; these two properties characterize kernels. A linear method that is applied to the transformed feature vectors thus requires only the kernel k; the feature transformation φ itself is never evaluated. Kernel methods reverse this construction: they start from a kernel k: X × X → R and construct the feature transformation from it. The feature transformation sends a feature vector x ∈ X to the function x·, i.e., the transformed feature vector z := φ(x) = x· is itself a function with domain X, for every x ∈ X. These functions belong to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk associated with the kernel k . Take two original feature vectors x, x' ∈ X. The inner product between their transformed feature vectors is a single kernel evaluation, \[ \innerprod{\kernelmap{\featurevec}{\cdot}}{\kernelmap{\featurevec'}{\cdot}} = \kernelmap{\featurevec}{\featurevec'} \text{.} \] More generally, the inner product between the transformed feature vector x· and any function h ∈ Hk is a point evaluation, \[ \innerprod{\hypothesis}{\kernelmap{\featurevec}{\cdot}} = \hypothesis(\featurevec) \text{,} \] which is referred to as the reproducing property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk . This reproducing property contains x·x'· = xx' as a special case that is obtained for the choice h = x'·. The (possibly infinite-dimensional) transformed feature vectors therefore never need to be computed explicitly. Fig.~2 depicts the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk for a training set with two data points: a hypothesis h is a single vector in Hk. The value hx· = h(x) is a linear function of the transformed feature vector x· ∈ Hk, but the function x ↦ h(x) induced on the original feature space X is nonlinear in general. Linearity in the original feature vector x may not even be defined, since the feature space X need not be a vector space, e.g., when it consists of text documents or graphs. Kernel methods can be formulated as regularized empirical risk minimization over the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk, \[ \min_{\hypothesis \in \hilbertspace_{\kernel}} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\big(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}, \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)}\big)}{\hypothesis} + \regparam \normgeneric{\hypothesis}{\hilbertspace_{\kernel}}^{2} \text{,} \] over a training set with feature vectors x(r) and labels y(r), for r = 1, …, m. The regularization parameter α > 0 weights the penalty term hHk2. The loss function (x(r), y(r))h depends on h only through the prediction h(x(r)), i.e., it is a function of the prediction h(x(r)) and the label y(r) only. Since h ∈ Hk, the reproducing property delivers this prediction as an inner product, h(x(r)) = hx(r)·. By the representer theorem, this optimization problem has a minimizer of the form h = Σr=1m βr x(r)· with expansion coefficients β1, …, βm ∈ R . Fig.~2 illustrates the underlying projection argument. Replacing a hypothesis h by its orthogonal projection h onto the subspace spanned by x(1)·, …, x(m)· leaves the predictions on the training set unchanged and never increases the penalty term. Some minimizer h therefore lies in this subspace and has the above form. training thus reduces to a convex optimization problem in these m coefficients, and the prediction h(x) = Σr=1m βr x(r)x requires only kernel evaluations. Examples of such kernel methods are the kernel support vector machine, obtained for the hinge loss , and kernel ridge regression, obtained for the squared error loss . For X = Rd, a widely used choice of the kernel k is the Gaussian kernel xx' = exp(- x - x'22 / (2 σ2) ) with bandwidth σ > 0. kernels are also available for data points without numeric features, such as strings and graphs . Fig.~3 shows the nonlinear decision boundary h(x) = 0 of a hypothesis h learned by a Gaussian-kernel method with squared error loss from a training set of two concentric rings that no linear classifier separates. Here, kernel ridge regression fits the labels y(r) ∈ -1, +1 and the prediction is the sign of the fitted value, a construction referred to as regularized least-squares classification . Kernel methods impose the smoothness assumption through the reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. That norm hHk quantifies the smoothness of a hypothesis h: it is large for a rapidly varying h and small for a smooth h. Moreover, different kernels impose different kinds of smoothness. The Gaussian kernel gives infinitely differentiable functions and penalizes high-frequency components. The Mat\'ern kernels are a family of kernels indexed by a smoothness parameter ν > 0: their reproducing kernel Hilbert space coincides, with equivalent norms, with the Sobolev space of order determined by ν, whose functions have derivatives up to that order in the weak sense. The penalty term α hHk2 in the above regularized empirical risk minimization is the squared reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. It therefore implements smoothness as quantified by hHk: among hypotheses with the same training error, the regularized empirical risk minimization objective function is smallest for the hypothesis with the smallest reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. The choice of kernel shapes not only training but also the predictions of the learned hypothesis: for localized kernels, such as the Gaussian kernel, the prediction h(x) is dominated by the data points in the training set whose feature vectors are close to x. In this sense, kernel methods implement the smoothness assumption: data points with nearby feature vectors obtain similar predictions. The locality of the predictions also makes kernel methods a soft-weighted analogue of k-nearest neighbors: instead of averaging the labels of a fixed number of nearest data points, the prediction weights all data points in the training set by the kernel value x(r)x .

terms.name: kernel ridge regression
terms.abstract: Kernel ridge regression is a kernel method for regression that applies ridge regression to transformed feature vectors constructed from a kernel, and thereby learns a nonlinear hypothesis in closed form. It performs regularized empirical risk minimization over the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the kernel, combining the squared error loss with a squared-norm penalty term. By the representer theorem, the learned hypothesis is a weighted sum of kernel evaluations at the feature vectors in the training set, and the coefficients are obtained in closed form by solving a single system of linear equations. Like ridge regression, the method equals empirical risk minimization on an augmented training set: the transformed feature vectors are perturbed by realizations of a zero-mean Gaussian process whose covariance function is the kernel scaled by the regularization parameter. For the kernel that is a modified inner product of the feature space, kernel ridge regression is ridge regression with a matching penalty term. The perturbed copies of a data point then fill an ellipse whose shape the kernel sets, the circle of ridge regression for the standard inner product.
terms.description: Consider a regression problem where the goal is to learn a hypothesis for predicting the numeric label of a data point based on its feature vector, but where the relation between features and label is nonlinear. An example is the prediction of the temperature over the course of a day from the time of the day, a relation that rises and falls over the day. Kernel ridge regression solves such regression problems by applying ridge regression to transformed feature vectors constructed from a kernel, and thereby learns a nonlinear hypothesis in closed form. Fig.~1 shows a training set with a periodic relation between feature and label. With the Gaussian kernel xx' = exp( - (x - x')2 / (2 σ2) ) of bandwidth σ = 0.7, the learned hypothesis follows the data points smoothly, with a training mean squared error of 0.013, while ridge regression on the raw feature can only fit a straight line, with a training mean squared error of 0.36. Formally, kernel ridge regression learns a hypothesis from the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk of a kernel k: X × X → R by minimizing the penalized average squared error loss on a training set D(train) = x(r)y(r) r=1m with numeric labels y(r) ∈ R, \begin{equation} \widehat{\hypothesis} = \argmin_{\hypothesis \in \hilbertspace_{\kernel}} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \big( \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} - \hypothesis\big(\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big) \big)^{2} + \regparam \normgeneric{\hypothesis}{\hilbertspace_{\kernel}}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} The penalty term is the scaled squared reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm α hHk2 with a regularization parameter α > 0. The resulting method is an instance of regularized empirical risk minimization, as is ridge regression, whose penalty term is the scaled squared Euclidean norm α w22 of the model parameters . The average squared error loss is a convex function of h, and the squared norm is strictly convex. The kernel ridge regression problem \eqref{eq:krr_rerm} therefore has a unique minimizer h for any training set, as does ridge regression. By the representer theorem (see kernel method), the minimizer of the kernel ridge regression problem \eqref{eq:krr_rerm} has the form h = Σr=1m βr x(r)· with a coefficient vector β = (β1, …, βm)ᵀ. Inserting this form into the kernel ridge regression problem \eqref{eq:krr_rerm} yields the finite-dimensional optimization problem \[ \min_{\boldsymbol{\expcoeff} \in \reals^{\samplesize}} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \normgeneric{\labelvec - \mK \boldsymbol{\expcoeff}}{2}^{2} + \regparam\, \boldsymbol{\expcoeff}^{\top} \mK \boldsymbol{\expcoeff} \text{,} \] with the label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ and the Gram matrix K with entries Kr,r' = x(r)x(r') (see kernel). By the zero-gradient condition, a coefficient vector solving this optimization problem satisfies the system of linear equations \[ \mK\big( \big(\mK + \regparam \samplesize \mI\big) \boldsymbol{\expcoeff} - \labelvec \big) = \mathbf{0} \text{.} \] Since K is positive semi-definite and α > 0, the matrix K + α m I is invertible, and a minimizer is obtained in closed form as \begin{equation} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\expcoeff}} = \big( \mK + \regparam \samplesize \mI \big)^{-1} \labelvec \text{.} \end{equation} The prediction for a data point with feature vector x is \[ \widehat{\hypothesis}(\featurevec) = \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \widehat{\expcoeff}_{\sampleidx} \kernelmap{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}}{\featurevec} \text{.} \] training is a one-shot computation: kernel ridge regression requires no iterative optimization method (and hence no fixed-point interpretation), only the unique solution of the m × m system of linear equations with the invertible matrix K + α m I, which is the closed form \eqref{eq:krr_closedform}. For the linear kernel xx' = xᵀ x' on X = Rd, kernel ridge regression produces the same predictions as ridge regression applied to the raw feature vectors . Kernel ridge regression is also closely related to Gaussian process regression: the prediction h(x) coincides with the posterior mean of a Gaussian process with covariance function k and noise variance α m . Like ridge regression, kernel ridge regression has an interpretation as a form of data augmentation. training with noise added to the feature vectors is equivalent to adding a penalty term . Replacing each data point by a probability distribution centered at it is the vicinal form of empirical risk minimization , and its effect on kernel methods is a regularization of the learned hypothesis . Consider data points with two features, the feature space X = R2, and the kernel \begin{equation} \kernelmap{\featurevec}{\featurevec'} \defeq \featurevec^{\top} \covmtxgeneric^{-1} \featurevec' \text{,} \end{equation} with a positive definite matrix C ∈ R2 × 2. This kernel is an inner product of R2 with a modified metric: the squared norm xx = xᵀ C-1 x scales the two features differently and couples them, and its unit ball is an ellipse instead of the circle of the Euclidean norm. The reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk of this kernel is R2 with this inner product. The transformed feature vector x· is the linear function x' ↦ xᵀ C-1 x', every hypothesis in Hk is a linear model h(w)(x) = wᵀ x with model parameters w ∈ R2, and its reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm is h(w)Hk2 = wᵀ C w. The kernel ridge regression problem \eqref{eq:krr_rerm} therefore reads \begin{equation} \widehat{\weights} = \argmin_{\weights \in \reals^{2}} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \big( \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} - \weights^{\top} \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} \big)^{2} + \regparam \, \weights^{\top} \covmtxgeneric \weights \text{,} \end{equation} which is ridge regression with the penalty term α w22 replaced by α wᵀ C w. Its unique minimizer is w = ( Xᵀ X + α m C )-1 Xᵀ y with the feature matrix X = (x(1), …, x(m))ᵀ, and it coincides with C-1 Xᵀ β for the coefficients \eqref{eq:krr_closedform} with the Gram matrix K = X C-1 Xᵀ. For C = I, the kernel \eqref{eq:krr_metric_kernel} is the linear kernel and the penalized problem \eqref{eq:krr_metric_ridge} is ridge regression itself. Adding the penalty term in the penalized problem \eqref{eq:krr_metric_ridge} is equivalent to empirical risk minimization on an augmented training set, i.e., to computing the average squared error loss of h(w) on it. This augmented training set is obtained from the original training set. For each data point x(r)y(r), r = 1, …, m, the feature vector x(r) is replaced by realizations of infinitely many independent and identically distributed RVs x(r) + r with Gaussian RVs r ~ 0α C. The label y(r) is left unchanged. The penalty term is exactly the amount by which the average squared error loss of h(w) over the perturbed copies exceeds its squared error loss on the original data point. Since E r = 0, the increase is \[ \E \big\{ \big( \weights^{\top} \perturbation{\sampleidx} \big)^{2} \big\} = \weights^{\top} \E \big\{ \perturbation{\sampleidx} \big(\perturbation{\sampleidx}\big)^{\top} \big\} \weights = \regparam \, \weights^{\top} \covmtxgeneric \weights \text{.} \] The equivalence is exact for the linear model h(w), while for a nonlinear hypothesis it holds up to terms of higher order in the noise amplitude . As in ridge regression, this increase of the average loss under data augmentation is an estimate for the generalization gap. Accordingly, linear regression on a large augmented training set recovers the predictions of kernel ridge regression. The kernel determines the shape of these perturbations (see Fig.~2). The covariance matrix α C of r is the scaled inverse of the matrix in the kernel \eqref{eq:krr_metric_kernel}. The one-standard-deviation contour of the perturbed copies is therefore \[ \big(\featurevec - \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big)^{\top} \covmtxgeneric^{-1} \big(\featurevec - \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big) = \regparam \text{.} \] This contour is the set of feature vectors x with x - x(r)x - x(r) = α, i.e., the ball of radius √(α) around x(r) in the norm induced by the kernel. For C = I, this ball is a circle of radius √(α): the perturbations in the data augmentation interpretation of ridge regression have covariance matrix α I and no preferred direction. For a general C it is an ellipse, so the ellipses drawn around the data points display the kernel. The size of a perturbation is measured by its kernel norm, and the penalty term α wᵀ C w is the average squared error loss that perturbations of kernel norm √(α) cause. The ellipses also display the matrix C itself. Its eigenvalue decomposition C = Σj=12 j u(j) (u(j))ᵀ, with eigenvalues 1 ≥ 2 > 0 and orthonormal eigenvectors u(1), u(2), turns the contour into \[ \sum_{\featureidx=1}^{2} \frac{\big( \big(\eigvecCov^{(\featureidx)}\big)^{\top} \big(\featurevec - \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}\big) \big)^{2}}{\regparam \eigval{\featureidx}} = 1 \text{.} \] The principal axes of every ellipse therefore point along the eigenvectors of C, and the semi-axes have lengths α 1 and α 2. The perturbations spread most along the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, and the penalty term charges a displacement along u(j) at the rate j. For the kernel \eqref{eq:krr_metric_kernel}, the perturbation acts linearly on the transformed feature vectors, x(r) + r· = x(r)· + r·. The random function r· is therefore a zero-mean Gaussian process whose covariance function is the kernel scaled by the regularization parameter, \begin{equation} \E \big\{ \kernelmap{\perturbation{\sampleidx}}{\featurevec} \, \kernelmap{\perturbation{\sampleidx}}{\featurevec'} \big\} = \featurevec^{\top} \covmtxgeneric^{-1} \E \big\{ \perturbation{\sampleidx} \big(\perturbation{\sampleidx}\big)^{\top} \big\} \covmtxgeneric^{-1} \featurevec' = \regparam \, \kernelmap{\featurevec}{\featurevec'} \text{.} \end{equation} For a general kernel, the raw feature vectors cannot be perturbed in this way, but the perturbation of the transformed feature vector x(r)· by a zero-mean Gaussian process with covariance function α k remains defined . Up to the scaling by α in the covariance function \eqref{eq:krr_perturb_cov}, this is the Gaussian process whose posterior mean kernel ridge regression computes .

terms.name: k-fold cross-validation (k-fold CV)
terms.abstract: k-fold cross-validation (k-fold CV) divides a dataset into k folds of equal size and uses each fold once as the validation set while the other k-1 folds form the training set of a given machine learning method. The k resulting validation errors are averaged into a single estimate for the risk of the learned hypothesis. The choice of k trades bias against computation: small k leaves each training set a small fraction of the dataset and, when the learning curve is still steep at that size, overestimates the risk, while large k requires learning k hypotheses on training sets that overlap in almost every data point. leave-one-out cross-validation is the extreme case with one data point per fold, and stratified k-fold cross-validation preserves class proportions of the full dataset in every fold.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows four data points, each one day at Krems an der Donau. A day is characterized by its morning minimum temperature as the feature x and its maximum daytime temperature as the label y. Three of the days form the training set of a polynomial regression of degree three, and the remaining day is the validation set. A cubic has four coefficients and the training set holds three days, so the empirical risk minimization problem is underdetermined and its solution passes exactly through those three days: the training error is zero whichever day is held back. That makes the held-back day the only evidence about the learned hypothesis, and a single split can make a bad one look good. Holding back the first day gives a validation error of 1.37, which reads as a reliable hypothesis. It is not: over the plotted range that same hypothesis runs from 5.5 to 33.9 degrees while the four labels lie between 15 and 23, and it departs by 13.0 degrees from a straight line through all four days. k-fold CV averages over the splits instead of trusting one. Each of the four days serves once as the validation set, so k = 4 here, and the four validation errors 1.37, 8.05, 7.02, and 72.42 average to 22.22. The split that looked best understates that estimate sixteenfold. k-fold CV estimates the expected loss (or risk) of an empirical risk minimization-based machine learning method. It divides a dataset D evenly into k subsets, the folds D(1), …, D(k) (Fig.~2). For each fold b = 1, …, k, the model is trained on the union of all folds except D(b) and the resulting hypothesis is evaluated on the held-out fold D(b). The k per-fold validation errors are then averaged to obtain the CV estimate of the expected loss. Compared to a single split into training set and validation set, k-fold CV uses each data point for both training and validation. In Fig.~2, for example, each data point has been used four times for training and once for validation after all five iterations. For a typical empirical risk minimization-based method, the k-fold CV estimate is more accurate than one from a single validation set holding a fraction 1/k of the entire dataset . The choice of k trades off bias against variance of the k-fold CV estimate . Small k (e.g., k=2) tends to result in an overestimate of the true expected loss, since each training set then holds only a fraction (k-1)/k of the full dataset and the learning curve may still be steep at that size. Choosing large k reduces this bias at the price of learning k hypotheses, each on a training set that differs from the others in only a few data points. Whether that overlap also inflates the variance of the estimate splits into two questions with different answers. The first asks how the variance of the k-fold CV estimate can be read off a single dataset. It cannot, in general. That variance splits into three parts: the variance of one validation error, the covariance of two validation errors from the same fold, and the covariance of two validation errors from different folds, the last of which is what the overlapping training sets contribute . No estimator of it is unbiased for every probability distribution , and treating the k validation errors as independent drops both covariances and underestimates it. The second asks how much the estimate actually moves when the dataset itself is drawn again. That question is settled by drawing many datasets, which the impossibility above does not forbid, and the answer here is that larger k moves it less: over 2000 datasets of fifteen days, the standard deviation of the estimate is 1.87, 1.25, 1.09, and 1.01 for k = 2, 3, 5, and 15, falling as the bias falls (\texttt{pythondemos/kfoldcv.py}). The overlap between training sets costs nothing in this experiment. Several variants of k-fold CV adapt it to specific dataset structures: \begin{itemize} \item \emph{stratified k-fold cross-validation} preserves the class proportions of the full dataset in every fold, important for classification with imbalanced data . \item \emph{leave-one-out cross-validation} is the extreme case k = m, with m the number of data points in the dataset, where each fold contains a single data point . \item \emph{Repeated k-fold CV} averages the results of several runs with different random fold assignments, which reduces the variance contributed by the partitioning . \end{itemize}

terms.name: k-means
terms.abstract: k-means is a hard clustering method for data points with numeric feature vectors. Each data point is assigned to exactly one of k clusters, each represented by a cluster centroid, namely the cluster whose cluster centroid is nearest in Euclidean distance. The cluster centroids are chosen to minimize the clustering error, the average squared Euclidean distance between a data point and its nearest cluster centroid. The resulting k-means optimization problem is an instance of empirical risk minimization using a specific choice for the loss function. This optimization problem is non-convex and NP-hard, and typically solved using Lloyd's algorithm. This algorithm consists of a fixed-point iteration that never increases the clustering error and reaches a fixed point after finitely many iterations. Replacing the squared Euclidean distance by the Euclidean distance itself gives k-medians, whose averaging step computes a geometric median and which is less sensitive to outliers.

terms.name: label
terms.abstract: A label is an attribute of a data point that represents a quantity of interest and that typically requires human expertise to determine. Predicting the label of a data point from its features is the goal of supervised learning. Determining the label of a data point is error-prone and often involves human annotation. The choice of label determines the learning task: whether the task is classification or regression depends on the label space together with the loss function. In self-supervised learning, the label is constructed from the features themselves, so that no manual annotation is required.
terms.description: A label of a data point z is one of its attributes that represents a higher-level fact, or quantity of interest, and that typically requires human expertise or domain knowledge to determine. Unlike a feature, which can be computed or measured easily, a label is usually harder to obtain. For a data point that represents a patient, a feature could be the body weight, while the label could be the presence of a disease. Whether a given attribute serves as a feature or a label is often a design choice that depends on the resources available in a given machine learning application. If an oncologist is readily available, a cancer prognosis can serve as a feature. On the other hand, if no oncologist is available, the cancer prognosis is a label that needs to be predicted from patient features. One way to make the notion of a label precise is by introducing a labeling function h: Z → Y. The domain of this function is the data point space Z, the set of all possible data points that can occur in a given machine learning application. Its values lie in the label space Y, the set of all possible values the label of a data point can take on. The function assigns each data point z its label y = h(z). Note that the labeling function h acts on the data point z itself, that is, on the whole patient. A trained model (or learned hypothesis) h instead acts on the feature vector x, a fixed list of recorded features such as the patient's body weight and age. The feature vector usually captures only part of a data point. For example, in a health-care application, the data point space Z contains patients, whereas the feature space X contains only their recorded feature vectors. Two patients with the same feature vector may therefore carry different labels, since they can differ in information that was never recorded as a feature. No hypothesis h that reads only x can then deliver perfect predictions. In practice, the true label h(z) of a data point is rarely known exactly. Even with full access to the data point, its label must be determined by human judgment or measurement, which is imperfect. The available label is then a noisy version of h(z), as in the additive error model of . For instance, an object category assigned by a human annotator or a diagnosis obtained from a clinician may be wrong, even though the annotator or clinician examines the data point directly. The discrepancy between such an observed label and the true label is called label noise and can degrade training and raise the risk of the learned hypothesis. This source of error differs from the incompleteness of the recorded features discussed above: here the data point is accessible, but its label is determined imperfectly. Label noise also matters for regulation. The EU AI Act requires the training set of a high-risk artificial intelligence system to be, to the best extent possible, free of errors and the system to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy ; erroneous labels are one such error. When labels are personal data, the general data protection regulation requires them to be accurate. One way to reduce the effect of label noise is label smoothing, which slightly perturbs the labels of data points used for model training. It is a form of data augmentation that acts as regularization. The choice of label (or labeling function h) determines a specific learning task. For the image of a cow herd in Fig.~1, the label could be a binary indicator of whether the image contains cows (binary classification). Other choices are the number of cows or the average green level (regression), and a masked center pixel predicted from the surrounding pixels (self-supervised learning). Whether a learning task is a classification problem or a regression problem depends not only on the label space Y but also on the loss function. For example, the label space Y = 0,1,2,3,… can be used for a classification method that uses the 0/1 loss as the loss function. The same label space can also be used for a regression method that uses the squared error loss as the loss function. In self-supervised learning, the label is constructed from the features themselves, so no manual annotation is required. A prominent example is large language model training: consider the sentence ``All human beings are born free and equal,'' tokenized as the sequence (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'', ``are'', ``born'', ``free'', ``and'', ``equal''). The label for the subsequence (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'') is the next token ``are,'' the label for (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'', ``are'') is ``born,'' and so on. By sliding through the sequence, a single sentence produces many labeled data points from plain text alone.

terms.name: learning rate
terms.abstract: A learning rate is a hyperparameter of an iterative machine learning method that controls the extent of a single update of the current hypothesis. A prime example for a learning rate is the step size of gradient descent. A learning rate that is too small makes little progress within the available number of iterations, and one that is too large can result in divergent iterations. For a fixed number of iterations, the learning rate bounds the effective hypothesis space of an machine learning method, which makes it a means of regularization. The learning rate can be chosen by the validation error of the learned hypothesis.

terms.name: linear classifier
terms.abstract: A linear classifier is a classifier whose decision regions are separated by hyperplanes. Each linear classifier is obtained by comparing the value of a linear hypothesis map against a threshold. For binary classification, the sign of the value can be used to determine the predicted label, and the absolute value measures the distance of the data point from the decision boundary. The model parameters of a linear classifier are the weight vector of the underlying hypothesis map and the threshold. They are learned by empirical risk minimization with different loss functions: logistic regression uses the logistic loss and the support vector machine the hinge loss. For multi-class classification, a linear classifier is characterized by several linear model hypothesis maps, one per label value, and the resulting decision regions are intersections of halfspaces.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows a scatterplot of data points that represent geographical areas. Each area is characterized by two features, which are obtained from an aerial photograph. The label of each area indicates whether the area belongs to a vineyard (y = 1) or not (y = -1). A linear classifier is a classifier whose decision regions are separated by hyperplanes in Rd. For binary classification, with label space Y = -1, +1, each linear classifier can be written as the thresholding rule y = sign(h(x)) with the hypothesis \[ \hypothesis(\featurevec) = \weights^{\top} \featurevec + \offset \text{.} \] The hypothesis map is parametrized by the weight vector w ∈ Rd 0 and the threshold b ∈ R. A data point with feature vector x is classified as y = 1 if h(x) ≥ 0 and as y = -1 otherwise. The resulting decision boundary is the hyperplane \[ \{ \featurevec \in \reals^{\featuredim} : \weights^{\top} \featurevec + \offset = 0 \} \text{,} \] with normal vector w. This boundary separates two halfspaces, which are the decision regions 1 = x : h(x) ≥ 0 and -1 = x : h(x) < 0. Consider a feature vector x and any vector x' on the decision boundary, h(x') = 0. Subtracting wᵀ x' + b = 0 from h(x) gives \[ \hypothesis(\featurevec) = \weights^{\top} \big( \featurevec - \featurevec' \big) \text{.} \] The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the right-hand side in magnitude by w2 x - x'2 . Every vector of the decision boundary is therefore at distance at least |h(x)| / w2 from x. That distance is attained by the orthogonal projection \[ \featurevec' = \featurevec - \frac{\hypothesis(\featurevec)} {\normgeneric{\weights}{2}^{2}} \, \weights \text{.} \] The distance of x from the decision boundary is thus |h(x)| / w2, and the hypothesis value h(x) is that distance multiplied by w2. Fig.~1 illustrates the distance to the decision boundary for one data point. The value |h(x)| is a measure of the noise tolerance at the feature vector x. Perturbing x by a vector δ changes the hypothesis value by wᵀ δ, which the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds in magnitude by w2 δ2. The sign of h(x), and with it the prediction, therefore survives every perturbation with δ2 < |h(x)| / w2. Multiplying h(x) by the label y gives the margin, which is positive exactly on the correctly classified data points. For a linearly separable training set and a sufficiently small regularization parameter α, the support vector machine learns the linear classifier whose smallest margin is largest . The model parameters (w, b) are learned from a training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r)) r = 1m by empirical risk minimization. Using the 0/1 loss results in an objective function that is piecewise constant, and minimizing it is computationally hard in general . Practical methods replace the 0/1 loss by a convex loss of the margin: logistic regression uses the logistic loss and the support vector machine uses the hinge loss. Both learn the model parameters of a linear classifier by minimizing a convex objective function: gradient descent minimizes the smooth objective function of logistic regression, and subgradient descent the non-smooth objective function of the support vector machine. For multi-class problems, with label space Y = 1, …, K and K > 2, a linear classifier uses one linear model hypothesis gc(x) = ( w(c) )ᵀ x + b(c) per label value c ∈ Y and predicts the value with the largest score, y = argmaxc ∈ Y gc(x). The decision region c is then an intersection of K - 1 halfspaces and is therefore a convex set. The border between two decision regions c and c' lies in the hyperplane on which the two scores agree . The resulting partition of the feature space is shown in Fig.~2 for a linear classifier with K = 3 classes. A linear classifier can be generalized to allow for non-linear decision boundaries by using a feature transformation. Applying a feature transformation φ: Rd → Rd' first and a linear classifier to φ(x) afterwards gives a decision boundary that is a hyperplane in Rd' but can be highly non-linear in the original feature space. A kernel method constructs such a feature transformation from a kernel, and a deep net uses its first layers as a trainable feature transformation.

terms.name: linear regression
terms.abstract: Linear regression is a regression method that learns a linear hypothesis map for predicting the numeric label of a data point from its features. Its least squares variant chooses a map that minimizes the average squared error loss on a training set. Linear regression is an instance of empirical risk minimization that is obtained by using the linear model and the squared error loss. The optimal model parameters are determined by the normal equations. This system can be solved in closed form or iteratively, for example, by gradient descent. Adding a penalty term to the average squared error loss yields regularized variants such as ridge regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.

terms.name: large language model (LLM)
terms.abstract: A large language model (LLM) is an artificial neural network, typically with billions of model parameters, that implements a hypothesis map from a prompt to a response. The training of an LLM often proceeds in stages: pretraining uses self-supervised learning, splitting raw text into overlapping fragments that yield data points without manual annotation, and fine-tuning uses a small dataset of manually curated prompt--response pairs. LLM agents extend LLMs beyond text: a program interprets the response, for example as code to run or as a tool to execute, and can append the result to the next prompt, so the LLM chooses actions that the surrounding program carries out.
terms.description: Consider a chat-based artificial intelligence system such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, or Mistral: a user types a question, the prompt, and receives a reply, the response. The system that produces the reply is an LLM: an artificial neural network, typically a transformer with billions of model parameters , trained to output text given input text. Each data point of this learning task is a pair of texts, and the trained LLM implements a hypothesis map from the prompt to the response (Fig.~1). A prompt and a response are sequences of tokens, so the feature space and the label space of this learning task are sets of token sequences. In contrast, a text classifier that maps a document to one of a fixed set of labels is not an LLM: it returns a label, not text. Most LLMs implement h autoregressively: the response is generated one token at a time, each drawn from a probability distribution over the vocabulary that the network computes from the prompt and all tokens generated so far. Alternative constructions exist: masked probabilistic models predict removed tokens and serve text analysis rather than generation , and diffusion language models generate many tokens in parallel . The training of an LLM consists of several stages. One stage typically uses self-supervised learning: a given text is split into overlapping fragments, and each fragment amounts to a data point whose label is one of its tokens and whose features are the remaining tokens. training sets built from text fragments require no manual annotation; a next-token fragment construction is used by and a masked-token one by . pretraining then minimizes the average loss over the fragments, i.e., it is empirical risk minimization, the aim being a small expected loss on text fragments outside the training set. Another stage is fine-tuning, which uses a small dataset of manually curated prompt--response pairs . An LLM whose model parameters are reused across many learning tasks is a foundation model . LLM inference, i.e., computing the response for a given prompt, is computationally much cheaper than its training. Still, the inference itself is computationally costly and is often implemented using cloud computing services. Local execution is catching up, however: open-weight LLMs, whose model parameters are published , can be compressed by quantization . Quantization stores each model parameter in a few bits instead of a 16-bit floating-point number. An LLM with billions of model parameters then runs on a laptop or phone (see edge computing). The output of an LLM by itself is nothing but a sequence of letters that constitute the response. An LLM (or coding) agent interprets the response of an LLM as instructions for computations to be executed . For example, the prompt can steer the LLM to produce a response that is valid source code in a programming language such as Python, as in the spelled-out data point of Fig.~1. The delivered source code can then be executed, and the result can be appended to the next prompt. The response can likewise be read as a call to an external tool, so that the LLM generates the text that specifies the actions the surrounding program carries out.

terms.name: logistic loss
terms.abstract: The logistic loss is a convex and smooth surrogate for the 0/1 loss in binary classification, defined for a label y ∈ -1, +1 and a real-valued hypothesis h as a decreasing function of the margin y · h(x). Like the hinge loss, it uses a data point only through that margin. Rescaled by its value at margin zero it is an upper bound on the 0/1 loss, with equality there, so a small logistic loss forces a small 0/1 loss. Unlike the hinge loss it is differentiable everywhere, which suits it to gradient-based optimization methods such as gradient descent. Running empirical risk minimization with a linear hypothesis and the logistic loss gives logistic regression.
terms.description: A spam filter either flags an email or does not, so its mistakes are counted rather than measured: the 0/1 loss charges 1 for every wrong answer. That count is flat almost everywhere as a function of the model parameters, so it gives gradient descent no direction to move in. The logistic loss replaces it by a convex and smooth surrogate that lies above it. Consider a binary classification problem with label y ∈ -1, +1 and a real-valued hypothesis h: X → R. On a data point (x, y) the logistic loss is \begin{equation} \lossfunc{(\featurevec, \truelabel)}{\hypothesis} \defeq \log\big(1 + \exp(-\truelabel \cdot \hypothesis(\featurevec))\big) \text{.} \end{equation} Like the hinge loss, the logistic loss \eqref{equ_log_loss_gls_dict} depends on the margin y · h(x) (see 0/1 loss). After division by log 2 it is a convex upper bound on the 0/1 loss, with equality at margin 0 (see Fig.~1). Unlike the hinge loss, the logistic loss is everywhere differentiable. It is therefore well suited for gradient-based optimization methods such as gradient descent. empirical risk minimization with a linear hypothesis and the logistic loss yields logistic regression. For example, in medical diagnosis, logistic regression trained with the logistic loss predicts whether a patient has a disease (y = +1) or not (y = -1) based on clinical features.

terms.name: logistic regression
terms.abstract: Logistic regression learns a linear hypothesis map for binary classification, that is, for data points whose label takes one of two values, y ∈ -1, 1. The predicted label is the sign of h(x), and the absolute value |h(x)| measures the confidence in the classification. The parameters are learned by empirical risk minimization with the average logistic loss on the training set. This is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under a simple probabilistic model, under which σ(h(x)) is the probability of the label 1. When a data point carries this probability as a soft label instead of a class, the logistic loss is replaced by the cross-entropy between soft label and prediction, equivalently their Kullback–Leibler divergence. The resulting objective function is convex and smooth, so variants of gradient descent can be used to minimize it.
terms.description: Consider predicting whether it freezes tomorrow from recent temperature measurements. Records from a weather station turn this question into data: each day is a data point with two numeric features, the maximum temperature of the day and that of the preceding day, collected in the feature vector x = (x1, x2)ᵀ ∈ R2. The label y ∈ -1, 1 is y = 1 if the minimum temperature of the following day stays at or above 0∘C and y = -1 otherwise. Fig.~1 shows such data points. Logistic regression learns, for such a binary classification task, a linear hypothesis map h(x) = wᵀ x + b with weight vector w and offset b. Despite its name, the method solves a classification problem: the regression refers to fitting the real-valued map h, not to a numeric label. The prediction, i.e., the classification, is obtained from the sign of h(x), which makes the learned h a linear classifier whose decision boundary is the hyperplane wᵀ x + b = 0. The absolute value |h(x)| is used as a measure of the confidence in the classification: it grows with the distance of x from the decision boundary, and a value close to zero indicates low confidence. The parameters w and b of logistic regression are learned via empirical risk minimization. The loss it minimizes is the logistic loss. On a data point (x, y), a hypothesis h incurs \[ \lossfunc{(\featurevec, \truelabel)}{\hypothesis} = \log\big(1 + \exp(-\truelabel \, \hypothesis(\featurevec))\big) \text{.} \] Fig.~2 shows this loss for a data point with y = 1 as a function of h(x). A correct classification with high confidence incurs a small loss. A wrong classification incurs a loss whose size grows with the confidence in the wrong classification. Averaging this loss over the training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r))r=1m of m data points, empirical risk minimization delivers \[ \begin{aligned} (\widehat{\weights}, \widehat{b}) &\in \argmin_{\weights \in \reals^{\featuredim},\, b \in \reals} f(\weights, b), \quad\text{with} f(\weights, b) &\defeq \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \log\Big(1 + \exp\big(-\truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} (\weights^{\top} \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} + b)\big)\Big) \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The logistic loss is the negative log-likelihood of the label under a simple probabilistic model for the classification task. In this probabilistic model, given the label y, the feature vector x is a Gaussian random variable whose mean y depends on the label while its covariance matrix does not; the two means -1, +1 ∈ Rd are the parameters of the model. The best linear classifier under this model assigns x to the label with the nearer mean: its weight vector is w = 12(+1 - -1) and its decision boundary is the hyperplane midway between the two means. Learning the parameters w and b of the linear classifier is thus the same as estimating the parameters of the probabilistic model, and maximum likelihood is the principled way to estimate them. Under the model, the posterior probability of y = 1 is the sigmoid function σ(wᵀ x + b) with σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e-z). Maximizing the likelihood coincides with minimizing the average logistic loss f . \textbf{The hypothesis value as a confidence.} The probabilistic model gives the number h(x) a second interpretation beyond its sign: σ(h(x)) is the probability that the label of a data point with feature vector x is y = 1, and σ(-h(x)) = 1 - σ(h(x)) the probability of y = -1. A forecast h(x) = 2 thus says that 88 percent of the days with these temperatures are followed by a frost-free day, and a forecast of 0 that half of them are. Whether these numbers can be trusted is the question of calibration . In most applications a data point carries only its label, the class that occurred. The logistic loss is the loss for this case. It is the cross-entropy between the probability mass function concentrated on the observed label and the predicted probability mass function (σ(h(x)), 1 - σ(h(x))) . Some data points carry more than a class: a soft label y ∈ [0, 1], the probability of y = 1 itself. It may be the frequency of frost among the recorded days with the same temperatures, the share of several annotators who chose the class, or the output of a larger classifier, as in knowledge distillation. For such a data point the logistic loss is replaced by the cross-entropy between the soft label and the prediction, \[ \lossfunc{(\featurevec, \labelprob)}{\hypothesis} = - \labelprob \log \sigma(\hypothesis(\featurevec)) - (1 - \labelprob) \log \big(1 - \sigma(\hypothesis(\featurevec))\big) \text{,} \] which for y ∈ 0, 1 is the logistic loss again. Learning then minimizes the average of this loss over the training set, as before. This cross-entropy equals the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the predicted probability mass function to the soft label probability mass function (y, 1 - y) plus the entropy of the soft label probability mass function, which does not depend on h . Minimizing either therefore learns the same h, and the loss on a data point is smallest exactly when σ(h(x)) = y, when the confidence of the prediction matches the probability of the class. A hard label can never be matched this way, since σ never reaches 0 or 1. This is why the logistic loss keeps decreasing as |h(x)| grows on a correctly classified data point. \textbf{Minimizing the average loss.} With hard or soft labels, the parameters are found by minimizing the average loss f. Unlike linear regression with the squared error loss, the minimization admits no closed-form solution. As in linear regression, however, the objective function f is convex and smooth, so gradient descent applies. The parameters are collected as the pair (w, b), and the gradient descent step reads \[ (\weights, b)^{(\iteridx+1)} = T\big((\weights, b)^{(\iteridx)}\big) \text{, with } T(\weights, b) \defeq (\weights, b) - \lrate \nabla f(\weights, b) \text{,} \] with learning rate η. The gradient ∇ f of the average logistic loss has the weight part \[ \nabla_{\weights} f = -\frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} \, \sigma\big(-\truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} (\weights^{\top} \featurevec^{(\sampleidx)} + b)\big) \text{,} \] and analogously for b. The pair (w, b) is a fixed point of the operator T precisely when ∇ f(w, b) = 0, which by convexity of f is exactly when (w, b) is a minimizer. It can be shown that ∇ f is Lipschitz continuity continuous with some constant L . For a constant learning rate η < 2/L, every gradient descent step decreases f and the values converge to the minimum, f((w, b)(t)) → min f; the choice η = 1/L is the standard one. The iterates (w, b)(t) themselves need not converge: on a linearly separable training set the minimum is not attained, and the norm of the iterates grows without bound while the training error tends to zero. Adding the penalty term α w, with a positive α, to f makes the objective function strictly convex, with a unique minimizer that the iterates then approach . In practice, plain gradient descent is seldom used to minimize f: the smooth convex objective function is minimized faster by Newton's method, equivalently iteratively reweighted least squares , by the quasi-Newton solver L-BFGS , and, for a large training set, by coordinate descent . What these solvers minimize is the average logistic loss, but that is not the only loss with which a linear classifier can be learned. In principle, the squared error loss serves too: with the label values encoded as the real numbers +1 and -1, the squared error (y - (wᵀx + b))2 is well defined. Minimizing the squared error loss, however, has a flaw: it penalizes a prediction wᵀx + b that is large, positive, and correct, while the logistic loss keeps decreasing as this margin grows (Fig.~3). The hinge loss of the support vector machine shares this behavior on a correctly classified data point but stays flat once the margin exceeds one. For more than two label values, logistic regression extends in two ways. A simple reduction trains one binary classification logistic regression per label, each separating that label from the rest, and predicts with the most confident of them; this is one-vs-rest classification. An alternative replaces the sigmoid function by the softmax function, which models the probabilities of all labels jointly, so that they sum to one and no label is left without one; fitting it by maximum likelihood yields multinomial logistic regression .

terms.name: loss
terms.abstract: The loss incurred by a hypothesis on a single data point is a scalar that quantifies the error of the hypothesis when evaluated on that data point. The ultimate goal of machine learning methods is to train a model such that the learned hypothesis delivers predictions with minimum loss. A key characteristic of machine learning applications and methods is the accessibility of loss values. In supervised learning, the loss can be evaluated for every hypothesis. In reinforcement learning, the loss is observed only for the action actually taken.
terms.description: In temperature forecasting, the quality of a predicted temperature is naturally measured by how far it deviates from the temperature actually measured the next day. The loss formalizes this idea. The loss incurred by a hypothesis h ∈ H on a single data point is a scalar that quantifies the error of h when evaluated on that data point . A smaller loss value indicates a smaller error. In supervised learning, this error is the discrepancy between the prediction h(x) delivered for the features x and the label y of that data point. Some losses (e.g., the squared error loss) take a continuum of values, while others (e.g., the 0/1 loss) are binary, indicating only whether the prediction matches the label. For the temperature forecast, the loss on a given day can be the squared difference between the predicted temperature (the prediction) and the measured one (the label); see Fig.~1. Loss values are typically nonnegative: many losses are built from a norm or metric and are therefore bounded below by zero. Nonnegativity is not required, however: the logarithmic loss (negative log-likelihood) underlying maximum-likelihood methods can take negative values, since a probability density can exceed one. The loss is also not specific to supervised learning. In unsupervised learning there is no label: a clustering loss measures how far a data point lies from its assigned cluster centroid, and the loss of an autoencoder is the reconstruction error between a data point and its reconstruction. machine learning methods use observed loss values to construct an objective function for model training. The average loss across a training set of data points is the empirical risk that empirical risk minimization minimizes. machine learning applications can be categorized by how the loss values are accessible. In supervised learning, the loss can, in principle, be evaluated for every hypothesis in the hypothesis space, since the true label of each training data point is observed. In reinforcement learning, the situation differs . At each time step, the machine learning method (implemented by an agent) selects an action via the currently used hypothesis. The agent then observes the loss incurred by the action actually taken. The loss that would have been incurred by the other actions is not revealed. This limited accessibility of loss values is known as bandit (or partial) feedback . For example, a route-planning system learns the actual travel time only for the route the driver took, not for any alternative route. Similarly, a self-driving car selects a steering direction, and the incurred loss can be measured from onboard sensors such as collision detectors and lane-departure warnings, but only for the trajectory actually driven.

terms.name: matrix
terms.abstract: A matrix is a two-dimensional array of numbers, arranged in rows and columns. The entry Ar,j of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d sits in row r and column j. A prominent example in machine learning is the feature matrix of a dataset, obtained by stacking the feature vectors of m data points row-wise. A matrix represents several distinct mathematical objects. One is a system of linear equations, such as the normal equations of linear regression. Another is a linear map between two vector spaces, after fixing a basis for each. A third is a tabular dataset with one row per data point and one column per feature.
terms.description:
Consider a spreadsheet of daily weather records at one station: each row holds a single day, each column one measurement such as temperature or humidity. Such a tabular dataset holds m data points, each described by d numerical features. The features of the r-th data point are collected in its feature vector x(r) = (x(r)1, …, x(r)d)ᵀ ∈ Rd, one entry per column of the spreadsheet. Stacking these m feature vectors row-wise, so that the r-th row is (x(r))ᵀ, produces an m × d rectangular array of numbers. Its entry in row r and column j is the j-th feature of the r-th data point. This two-dimensional numeric array is referred to as the feature matrix X of the dataset; Fig.~1 carries out the construction on three days of the weather example. More generally, a matrix of size m × d is a two-dimensional array of numbers denoted by \mA =  egin{pmatrix} A_{1,1} & A_{1,2} & \dots & A_{1,

Recording how green each pixel is turns a 16 × 16 image into a 16 × 16 matrix G whose two indices are pixel positions (Fig.~2). Matrices represent several distinct mathematical objects , including the following:  egin{itemize} \item Systems of linear equations: A matrix collects the coefficients of a system of linear equations,  egin{pmatrix} A_{1,1} & A_{1,2} A_{2,1} & A_{2,2} \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} x_1 x_2 \end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix} b_1 b_2 \end{pmatrix} 	ext{, written compactly as } \mA \vx = \vb 	ext{.} Here, x is the vector of unknowns and b the right-hand side. One important example is the normal equations XᵀX w = Xᵀy, whose solutions are the model parameters that minimize the training error in linear regression. \item linear maps: Consider two vector spaces U and V, of dimension d and m, respectively. Fixing a basis u(1), …, u(d) for U and a basis v(1), …, v(m) for V, each matrix A ∈ Rm × d defines a linear map f(A): U → V (see Fig.~3) via f^{(\mA)} ig(\vu^{( eatureidx)} ig) = \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} A_{\sampleidx, eatureidx} \vv^{(\sampleidx)}	ext{.} Taking U = Rd and V = Rm with the standard bases, the image of a vector x under f(A) is the matrix-vector product f(A)(x) = Ax. \item datasets: As in the opening example, a matrix can represent a dataset with each row holding a single data point and each column a specific feature or label. \end{itemize} Written with the feature matrix, the training error that empirical risk minimization-based linear regression minimizes becomes a succinct algebraic expression.
