The alternating direction method of multipliers solves \eqref{equ_rpca_pcp_dict} by alternating two proximal operators : the proximal operator of the nuclear norm, which computes an singular value decomposition and shrinks every singular value toward zero by a threshold, and the proximal operator of the ℓ1 norm, which shrinks every entry toward zero by a threshold, followed by an update of the multiplier of the constraint. Each iteration applies the same operator to the triple of L, S and the multiplier, so the method is a fixed-point iteration, whose fixed points are the saddle points of the augmented Lagrangian and therefore the solutions of \eqref{equ_rpca_pcp_dict}; the operator is averaged, which is what guarantees convergence for a convex problem . On the temperature matrix the recovered L has rank nine out of 24 and the pursuit takes a few thousand iterations, each an singular value decomposition of a 366 × 24 matrix. The sparse part is as useful as the low-rank part. In a video from a fixed camera, with one frame per column, the static background is the low-rank part and the moving people are the sparse part, so robust PCA separates the two without a model of either . In a matrix of sensor readings, the sparse part flags the faulty entries, which is anomaly detection with the low-rank structure as the model of normal behavior. If entries of X are missing rather than corrupted, the same nuclear-norm criterion with the constraint restricted to the observed entries recovers L, which is the matrix-completion problem .

terms.name: random variable (RV)
terms.abstract: A random variable (RV) is a measurable function that maps each outcome of a random experiment to an element of a measurable space. Important types of RVs include binary RVs, discrete RVs, real-valued RVs, random vectors, and random matrices. The analysis of machine learning methods often relies on probabilistic models that represent data sources as RVs. The most widely used probabilistic model assumes that data points are independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution, which is unknown in general.
terms.description: The weather on a given day in the Austrian city Krems an der Donau is the outcome of a random experiment . Each possible outcome ω is characterized by a maximum daytime temperature, the temperature at 13:00, and reading off this temperature assigns a real number x(ω) to the outcome. This assignment is an RV x. The temperatures recorded on consecutive days are realizations of this RV (see Fig.~1). More generally, an RV maps the outcomes of a random experiment to elements of a measurable space. Mathematically, an RV is a measurable function x: Ω → X whose domain is the sample space Ω of a probability space and whose co-domain is a measurable space X. Measurability refers to the σ-algebras of the two spaces: the preimage x-1(B) of every measurable set B ⊆ X must belong to the σ-algebra of the probability space, so that the probability of x taking a value in B is defined. The value x(ω) ∈ X that x assigns to an outcome ω ∈ Ω is the image of ω under x (see Fig.~2). The sample space and the RVs on it are a modeling choice, not fixed by the data. The daily Krems temperatures admit two standard constructions (Fig.~3). In the first, each day r has its own probability space with sample space Ω(r), and the temperature of that day is an RV x(r) : Ω(r) → R; the recorded value is one realization x(r)(ω(r)). In the second, one probability space with sample space Ω carries the whole reality: a single outcome ω ∈ Ω fixes the temperatures of all days simultaneously, and each day is an RV x(r) : Ω → R on this common space. The independent and identically distributed assumption is a statement about the second construction: the x(r) share one probability distribution and are independent. The common-space construction is the one used for learning from data, because a single probability distribution then governs an entire dataset. Different types of RVs include \begin{itemize} \item {binary RVs}, which map each outcome to an element of a binary set (e.g., -1,1 or cat, no cat); \item {discrete RVs}, which take on values in a countable set (which can be finite or countably infinite; e.g., the number of heads in ten coin flips, with values in 0,1,…,10); \item {real-valued RVs}, which take on values in the real numbers R (e.g., the maximum daytime temperature in Krems); \item {random vectors}, which map outcomes to the Euclidean space Rd (e.g., the red-green-blue (RGB) values of a pixel, which form a vector in R3); \item {random matrices}, which map outcomes to a space of matrices Rm × d (e.g., the data matrix of a dataset). \end{itemize} In machine learning, RVs represent data sources, so that the behavior of learning methods can be analyzed. For example, the generation of a training set or validation set is represented by independent and identically distributed RVs sharing one underlying probability distribution; this is the common-space construction, in which a single probability distribution governs the whole dataset. This probability distribution is either postulated or estimated from actual datasets, for example via maximum likelihood. Ideally, an machine learning method should work well on datasets that arise as realizations of high probability. This is the generalization goal that empirical risk minimization pursues, minimizing the average loss on the training set as a proxy for the expected loss of the learned hypothesis on a new data point drawn from the common probability distribution.

terms.name: sample size
terms.abstract: The sample size is the number m of data points in a sample. Many machine learning methods model the data points as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs and judge a hypothesis by its expected loss, the risk; since the probability distribution is unknown, the risk is estimated by the average loss on the sample, for training by empirical risk minimization and for validation. How close that average is to the risk depends on the sample size. A concentration inequality such as Hoeffding's inequality bounds the deviation of the average from the risk and turns a required accuracy ε and confidence 1 - δ into a sample size of order log(1/δ) / ε2 for validation; for training, the sample size must also be compared with the size of the model. For data points recorded in sequence, autocorrelation lowers the effective sample size. The same reasoning sizes the sample for a statistical test, such as whether two features are correlated: the sample size needed to detect a correlation grows as the inverse square of that correlation.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau predicts, from the minimum and the maximum temperature of a day, whether the next day brings frost. Whether a hypothesis h for this task is any good is judged by its expected loss, the risk h = E zh, where the expectation is over a data point z drawn from the probability distribution P(z) of the days. Many machine learning methods use the independent and identically distributed assumption: the data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P(z). In practice, P(z) is unknown, and a method observes only these m data points, a sample. Their number m is the sample size. With the probability distribution unknown, the risk is estimated by the average loss on the sample, \begin{equation} \emprisk{\hypothesis}{\dataset} \defeq \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\datapoint^{(\sampleidx)}}{\hypothesis} \text{,} \end{equation} which is the empirical risk. empirical risk minimization minimizes this average over the hypotheses of a model on a training set, and validation compares the learned hypotheses by the same average on a validation set. Both uses require the average to be close to the risk, and how close it is depends on the sample size: by the law of large numbers, the average \eqref{equ_samplesize_emprisk_dict} converges to h as m grows. Fig.~1 shows this for the frost warning: the sample average of the 0/1 loss of one fixed hypothesis, computed on samples of m = 10 to 1000 days, scatters around the risk 0.118 with a spread that falls like 1/√(m). How large should the sample be? One approach uses a concentration inequality, which bounds the probability that the average deviates from the risk by more than a given amount. For a loss function with values in [0, 1], such as the 0/1 loss, Hoeffding's inequality gives, for every ε > 0, \begin{equation} \prob{ \big| \emprisk{\hypothesis}{\dataset} - \risk{\hypothesis} \big| > \epsilon } \leq 2 \exp\big( -2 \samplesize \epsilon^{2} \big) \text{,} \end{equation} see and . The bound holds for a hypothesis chosen before the sample is drawn, which is the situation of validation: the hypothesis was learned on the training set, and the validation set is a fresh sample. Setting the right-hand side to a tolerated failure probability δ and solving for m turns a required accuracy ε and confidence 1 - δ into a sample size: \begin{equation} \samplesize \geq \frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2 \epsilon^{2}} \text{,} \end{equation} and this many data points make the validation error lie within ε of the risk with probability at least 1 - δ . For the frost warning, ε = 0.05 and δ = 0.05 give m ≥ 738 days; at that sample size all of 2000 drawn samples in Fig.~1 land within 0.05 of the risk. The bound is loose, since it holds for every probability distribution and every loss function in [0, 1]; the sample size \eqref{equ_samplesize_choice_dict} is therefore enough, but not always needed. Its shape is what carries over: halving ε quadruples the sample size, while a smaller δ costs only a logarithm. For training, the same question has a second answer. The hypothesis is then chosen by looking at the sample, so the bound \eqref{equ_samplesize_hoeffding_dict} for a fixed hypothesis no longer applies to the learned one. The sample size then has to be compared with the size of the model. For a model of Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension d, a sample size proportional to d / ε2 makes the training error of every hypothesis in the model lie within ε of its risk at once . A sample that is small against the effective dimension of the model is the typical cause of overfitting, and the learning curve shows the validation error of the learned hypothesis as a function of the sample size . The sample sizes above assume independent and identically distributed RVs. data points recorded in sequence, such as consecutive days, often show autocorrelation: a frost day is more likely after a frost day, and so is a wrong prediction. Dependent data points carry less information than independent ones. For a stationary sequence with autocorrelation ρℓ at lag ℓ, the variance of the average of m consecutive values is that of m independent values multiplied by \begin{equation} 1 + 2 \sum_{\lagidx=1}^{\samplesize-1} \Big( 1 - \frac{\lagidx}{\samplesize} \Big) \rho_{\lagidx} \text{,} \end{equation} see . The average is therefore as accurate as that of m divided by \eqref{equ_samplesize_acf_dict} independent values, the effective sample size. For the 0/1 loss of the frost warning, the sample autocorrelation of consecutive days is 0.24 at lag 1 and stays positive for a week, and the factor \eqref{equ_samplesize_acf_dict} is 4.2 for m = 30. The average over 30 consecutive days therefore scatters as much as that over 7 days drawn at random: a month of consecutive days is worth a week of random ones. A sample of consecutive data points must then be larger than \eqref{equ_samplesize_choice_dict} or \eqref{equ_samplesize_corr_dict} say, by the factor \eqref{equ_samplesize_acf_dict}, or be drawn at random from the whole record, as the days of Fig.~1 are. Sample size enters a third task, hypothesis testing: are two features of a data point correlated? For the days of 2024 at Krems, is the minimum temperature of a day correlated with its diurnal range, the maximum minus the minimum? Over the whole year, the Pearson correlation coefficient of the two features is ρ = 0.16. A test sees a sample of m days and computes the sample correlation r, a function of sample means. Under the hypothesis that the two features are uncorrelated, r scatters around 0 with a standard deviation close to 1/√(m), whatever their probability distribution. For features that are Gaussian RVs, Fisher's transformation artanh(r) is approximately a Gaussian random variable with mean artanh(ρ) and standard deviation 1/√(m - 3) . The test rejects ``uncorrelated'' when |artanh(r)| √(m - 3) exceeds the quantile z1-α/2 of the standard Gaussian random variable, which bounds the probability of a false rejection by the significance level α. A correlation ρ is then detected with probability at least 1 - β, the power of the test, once \begin{equation} \samplesize \geq 3 + \bigg( \frac{z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}} {\operatorname{artanh}(\rho)} \bigg)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} For ρ = 0.16, α = 0.05 (z0.975 = 1.96) and a power of 0.8 (z0.8 = 0.84), the sample size \eqref{equ_samplesize_corr_dict} is 304 days. Fig.~2 shows the power of the test against the sample size: 0.84 at m = 304, and 0.10 for a sample of 30 days. The shape is that of \eqref{equ_samplesize_choice_dict} again: halving the correlation to be detected quadruples the sample size, so a weak correlation needs a large sample before ``uncorrelated'' can be rejected.

terms.name: self-supervised learning
terms.abstract: Self-supervised learning constructs the labels of a training set from the data points themselves. Some features of a data point are withheld and used as its label while the rest remain features, so what results is an ordinary supervised learning problem, solved by empirical risk minimization on data that no annotator has touched. In natural language processing the withheld feature is the next token, which is how a large language model is trained. In computer vision it is a set of pixels, deleted from an image and predicted from the patches left visible.
terms.description: An open image database returns thousands of photographs for a keyword such as \emph{cat}, and a web crawl yields billions of sentences. Neither comes with a label saying what should be predicted. A prediction task can be made from any one of them: hide the last word of a sentence, and the words before it become a question whose answer is already known. Self-supervised learning constructs labels this way, from the data point itself. uses the term for a classifier whose label for one sensory modality is derived from a co-occurring input in another. In general, some of the features of a data point are withheld and used as the label; the remaining ones stay as the features. The result is an ordinary supervised learning problem, solved by empirical risk minimization, and its training set needs nothing beyond the raw data. A single unlabeled collection yields as many training sets as there are ways of hiding part of a data point (see Fig.~1). The withheld feature can be a token. In natural language processing a data point is a stretch of text, its features are the n tokens v(1), …, v(n) of a context window of length n, and its label is the token v(n+1) that follows. Every position in every document is one labeled data point, so a corpus of m tokens gives on the order of m of them. This is the training task of a large language model such as GPT-3, an autoregressive language model, i.e., one trained to predict the next token . Masking a token in the middle and predicting it from both sides withholds a different feature of the same data point . Similarly, in computer vision the withheld features are pixels: an image is split into patches, most of them are deleted, and the method predicts the missing pixel values from those that remain. delete 75% of the patches and still recover recognizable content. A deep net solving either task computes a composition h = s ∘ φ. The feature transformation φ X → Rd, with X the set of raw inputs (texts or images), sends a data point to a vector of activations, and the map s predicts the withheld feature from that vector. That feature can be predicted only from what φ has kept: a next token cannot be recovered from a vector that has discarded the context, nor a deleted patch from one that has dropped its surroundings. Fitting the composition is therefore what shapes φ, even though φ appears nowhere in the loss. name the two halves: their encoder is φ and sees only the patches left visible, while their decoder is s and rebuilds the pixels from its output. What restricts φ there is the deletion of most of the input, not a narrow layer. In both domains it is φ that is carried over. The map s is dropped, and a small replacement for it is fitted on the output of φ using the few labels the later task does have (see transfer learning, foundation model). Self-supervised learning is therefore one answer to the same shortage that motivates semi-supervised learning: there, unlabeled data points assist a label-scarce problem directly; here, they are turned into a labeled problem of their own first. unsupervised learning is the third answer, and it gives up the label entirely: it looks for structure among the feature vectors instead of predicting a withheld one.

terms.name: sigmoid function
terms.description: The sigmoid function maps the real line into the interval between 0 and 1, turning the unbounded score that a classifier assigns to a data point into a probability. It is the function σ: R → (0,1) given by \[ \sigma(z) \defeq \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \text{.} \] It rises from σ(z) → 0 as z → -∞ to σ(z) → 1 as z → +∞, and passes through σ(0) = 1/2 (see Fig.~1). It is also called the logistic function, and it is the softmax function for two classes. The sigmoid function is smooth and strictly increasing, and it satisfies the symmetry σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z) . Its derivative is available in closed form, and in terms of the function itself, \[ \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big) \text{.} \] Once σ(z) has been evaluated, its derivative therefore costs one multiplication. That is what makes the sigmoid cheap to differentiate inside an artificial neural network. The product σ(z)(1 - σ(z)) is at most 1/4, and it approaches 0 for large |z|. A neuron whose score is large in magnitude therefore passes almost no gradient back. That is why the rectified linear unit replaced the sigmoid in the hidden layers of deep nets . The sigmoid function turns a log-odds into a posterior probability. Let the binary label y be either 1 or -1. Write a for the log-odds of the two classes at the feature vector x, \[ a \defeq \log \frac{\prob{\featurevec \mid \truelabel = 1} \, \prob{\truelabel = 1}} {\prob{\featurevec \mid \truelabel = -1} \, \prob{\truelabel = -1}} \text{.} \] The posterior probability of the label 1 is then exactly y = 1 | x = σ(a). The inverse recovers the log-odds, a = log(σ/(1 - σ)) . Taking the log-odds to be a linear function of the feature vector, a = wᵀ x with model parameters w, makes σ(wᵀ x) the posterior probability. That holds exactly when the feature vectors of the two classes follow Gaussian RVs sharing one covariance matrix .

terms.name: Sobolev space
terms.abstract: A Sobolev space is a set of functions whose derivatives, taken in a generalized sense, have bounded size. machine learning methods whose hypothesis space is a ball in a Sobolev space with a bound on the gradient enforce a well-defined quantitative notion of robustness. Any hypothesis map in such a ball can be locally approximated by a linear map with bounded slope. A small change of the features of a data point therefore changes the prediction by at most a proportional amount. The generalized derivative is needed because hypothesis maps such as those of a deep net with rectified linear unit activation functions have kinks. A decision tree, whose hypothesis map jumps, belongs to no Sobolev space and admits no such guarantee. linear regression whose hypothesis space is a ball in a Sobolev space, rather than the linear maps, is nonparametric regression. Sobolev norms also serve as regularizers, and they describe the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a Mat\'ern kernel.
terms.description: A weather service forecasts the maximum temperature of a day from its minimum temperature. Fig.~1(a) shows the 366 days of 2024 at the station Krems an der Donau of GeoSphere Austria as the data points of a scatterplot, with the minimum temperature of a day as its feature and the maximum temperature as its label. The panel also shows three hypotheses learned from these data points: the non-linear map of a deep net with rectified linear unit activation functions, the step function of a depth-2 decision tree, and the curve of linear regression with a Sobolev penalty term. A trustworthy forecaster must not change its prediction, the forecast, abruptly: a thermometer error of half a degree in the minimum temperature must not move the forecast by several degrees. Sobolev spaces make this requirement precise. They consist of the functions whose derivatives have bounded size . A bound on the derivative is a bound on how fast the forecast can change. The derivative is understood in a generalized sense, since the deep net of Fig.~1(a) has kinks and no classical derivative exists there. The generalized derivative starts from integration instead of differentiation. On the real line, a function with f(x) = f(a) + ∫ax g(t) dt is the integral of its slope g, the flow accumulated from a to x, and g is called a weak derivative of f. On an open set Ω ⊆ Rd, consider an infinitely differentiable test function that vanishes outside a bounded subset of Ω. A function gj is a weak partial derivative of f if, for every such , \[ \int_{\Omega} f(\featurevec) \frac{\partial \varphi(\featurevec)}{\partial \feature_{\featureidx}} \, \mathrm{d}\featurevec = - \int_{\Omega} g_{\featureidx}(\featurevec) \varphi(\featurevec) \, \mathrm{d}\featurevec \text{.} \] This is integration by parts with all derivatives moved onto . It holds when f is the integral of gj along the jth coordinate, and it never asks for a derivative of f at a particular point. The slope of the deep net, the step function of Fig.~1(b), satisfies it for every test function tried (\texttt{pythondemos/sobolevspace.py}). For p ∈ [1,∞], the Sobolev space W1,p(Ω) consists of the functions whose weak derivatives exist and have finite Lp norm ·p. The case p = 2 gives the Hilbert space H1(Ω), and the spaces Wk,p(Ω) require weak derivatives up to order k . The case that matters most for machine learning is W1,∞, the functions with a bounded weak gradient. A function f belongs to it with supx ∈ Ω ∇ f(x)2 ≤ L precisely when it is Lipschitz continuity continuous with constant L . Perturbing a feature vector by δ then changes f by at most L δ2. The deep net of Fig.~1 has L = 2.44, so an error of 0.5 ∘C in the minimum temperature moves its forecast by at most 1.22 ∘C; the largest change among 20000 random perturbations of that size was 1.21 ∘C. The bound also says that near almost every feature vector the hypothesis agrees with a linear map whose slope is at most L (Rademacher's theorem, ). This linear map is the explanation that gradient-based explainable artificial intelligence delivers and that local interpretable model-agnostic explanations fits from perturbed data points. For the forecast, it reads: one additional degree in the minimum adds s(x) degrees to the forecast, with the slope s(x) of Fig.~1(b) between 0 and 2.44. Since the deep net is piecewise linear, the approximation is exact whenever no kink lies between x and x + δ, which was the case for 98.0% of 20000 random pairs with |δ| ≤ 0.1 ∘C. The guarantee comes from the bound, not from the space: W1,∞ contains functions with every value of L. An machine learning method whose hypothesis space is the ball of functions with slope at most L learns a robust hypothesis by construction, whatever the training set. The choice p = ∞ is what makes the bound hold at every feature vector; H1 bounds the slope only on average. For the deep net, the weak gradient is bounded by the product of the spectral norms of its weight matrices, i.e., of their largest singular values, here 46.0 against the true 2.44: valid but loose. For a classifier that takes the sign of such an f, the bound certifies that no perturbation of Euclidean norm below |f(x)|/L changes the prediction . The decision tree of Fig.~1(a) has no such bound: at its root threshold of 5.5 ∘C, a change of 2 · 10-9 ∘C in the minimum temperature moves the forecast by 7.81 ∘C. A jump has no weak derivative that is a function, so no Sobolev space contains the tree. The bound concerns perturbations of the features only; robustness against perturbations of the training set is a property of the training map (see stability). Sobolev spaces also serve as hypothesis spaces in their own right. Plain linear regression minimizes the average squared error loss over the linear maps. Replacing the linear maps by a ball in H1, or equivalently adding the squared H1 seminorm ∫Ω ∇ f(x)22 dx as a penalty term, a norm that ignores constant shifts of f (see regularization), gives nonparametric regression . The dotted curve of Fig.~1(a) minimizes the training error plus ten times that seminorm; it reaches a training error of 18.03, below the 18.66 of the deep net, with slope at most 3.05 (\texttt{pythondemos/sobolevspace.py}). A computer cannot search all of H1, and it need not. A minimizer of the training error plus the seminorm is piecewise linear with kinks at the m data points, since between two data points the straight line has the smallest seminorm for given end values (a consequence of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality). The search therefore runs over m numbers, the values at the kinks; this is kernel ridge regression with the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of H1 . For a piecewise linear function the seminorm is a sum of squared slopes, one per segment and weighted by its length, so the normal equations of the penalized problem form one linear system. The demo places the kinks on 200 equally spaced points instead of the data points, which changes nothing in the arithmetic. The seminorm expresses the smoothness assumption. Its counterpart for a function on the nodes of a graph replaces the gradient by differences across edges, the form used by generalized total variation and generalized total variation minimization ; penalizing the gradient in L1 instead gives total variation regularization, which allows jumps . The reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a Mat\'ern kernel is a Sobolev space Ws,2(Ω) whose order s is set by the smoothness parameter of the kernel . A kernel method with that kernel is therefore again nonparametric regression over a Sobolev ball, the setting of above. Finally, a bound L is also of regulatory interest. Article~15 of the EU AI Act requires a high-risk artificial intelligence system to be robust and to have its accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use . A Lipschitz continuity constant is such a metric: it states, as a single number, how much a perturbation of a feature vector can change the prediction.

terms.name: stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
terms.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a variant of gradient descent in which the gradient of the objective function is replaced by a computationally cheaper stochastic approximation. Its main application in machine learning is empirical risk minimization on a training set that is large or stored in a distributed database: the gradient of the empirical risk requires an average over the entire training set. SGD approximates this average by the average over a randomly drawn batch of data points. The batch size trades the computational cost of a single update against the accuracy of the gradient approximation.

terms.name: supervised learning
terms.abstract: Supervised learning refers to machine learning methods that measure the quality of a hypothesis by comparing its prediction against a known label value. A main design principle for supervised methods is empirical risk minimization. It learns a hypothesis by minimizing the average loss, the empirical risk, incurred on a training set of labeled data points. Supervised learning methods are divided according to the label space: a numeric label makes the learning task regression, a discrete one classification. Because labeled data points are often expensive to collect, unsupervised learning, self-supervised learning and semi-supervised learning each reduce what must be annotated.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau records, for every day of 2024, the minimum temperature in the morning and the maximum temperature during the day. To forecast the afternoon from the morning, each day is taken as a data point: its feature is the morning minimum, and the maximum of that day is the quantity to be predicted. For the days already recorded, that quantity is known, because it was measured. Supervised learning refers to methods that measure the quality of a hypothesis by comparing its prediction against a known label value. Formally, the training set consists of labeled data points D(train) = x(r)y(r) r=1m with feature vectors x(r) ∈ X and labels y(r) ∈ Y. The goal is to learn a hypothesis h: X → Y that incurs a small loss on any data point, also those outside D(train). That requirement can be made precise by the independent and identically distributed assumption: the data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution. The independent and identically distributed assumption allows the expected loss, or risk, to be used as a performance criterion for a hypothesis. Choosing the hypothesis that minimizes the risk is often not possible, as the underlying probability distribution is unknown. The risk of a candidate hypothesis can however be estimated by its average loss on a training set, the empirical risk. For the learned hypothesis, this average is the training error. This yields empirical risk minimization: among the hypotheses of a hypothesis space H, choose one that minimizes the average loss on the training set, \[ \learnthypothesis \in \argmin_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\pair{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}}{\truelabel^{(\sampleidx)}}}{\hypothesis} \text{.} \] Whether the learned hypothesis is any good is measured on data points kept out of training, the validation set. Fig.~1 shows both for the days at Krems, with a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization using a linear model. Supervised learning methods are divided according to the label space. A numeric label space Y = R makes the learning task regression, a discrete one makes it classification. The weather records deliver both from the same data points. With the maximum temperature of the day as label the task is regression. With the label \emph{frost in the morning} the task is classification, where empirical risk minimization with the 0/1 loss delivers a classifier. The hypothesis of Fig.~1 attains a training error of 18.0, measured as the mean squared error in squared degrees Celsius, and a validation error of 24.9 on the held-out days. These numbers can be compared against a simple baseline: a constant prediction given by the sample mean of the training labels. That baseline incurs a training error of 81.4, which is the sample variance of the labels, and a validation error of 102.0. Using a larger model, given by the polynomials of degree up to twelve, empirical risk minimization lowers the training error to 10.2 and raises the validation error to 349.4 (Fig.~2). That is worse than the constant prediction, which uses no feature at all. A label for every data point of the training set is therefore not sufficient: the hypothesis space must also be small enough for the training error to indicate the loss outside D(train), which is what a validation set reveals (see overfitting) . The source of labeled data points can vary widely across applications. A label can be measured, as the maximum temperature of a day is; it can be recorded, as the price at which a house sold is; or it must be annotated by a person, as the diagnosis shown by a medical image is. In the last case the labels are the scarce resource: annotating requires the expert whose judgment is to be reproduced, so a dataset of unlabeled data points is typically much cheaper to enlarge than a training set of labeled data points. ImageNet, a dataset of 3.2 million annotated images at the time of its first publication, was assembled by annotators working through a crowdsourcing platform . An annotated label is a verdict rather than a measurement, and two annotators need not return the same one. How much a singing voice resembles Freddie Mercury is defined by nothing but the agreement of a panel of listeners, and no instrument settles it. ImageNet was assembled against this: several annotators vote on each image, and an image is kept only on a convincing majority. The number of votes required is fixed per category from an initial sample of its images (about five for \emph{Burmese cat}, fewer for \emph{cat}) . labels of this kind include the noise of the annotation process, so a validation error measured against them is bounded below by the disagreement among annotators. What sets supervised learning apart from other machine learning methods is the need for labeled data points to construct an objective function for training. unsupervised learning uses the geometry of the feature vectors to construct a loss function without the need for labels. self-supervised learning constructs the labels from the data points themselves, by withholding some of their features. semi-supervised learning uses a few labeled data points together with many unlabeled ones. reinforcement learning uses a reward signal to measure the usefulness of a prediction instead of comparing it with a known label value .

terms.name: singular value decomposition (SVD)
terms.abstract: The singular value decomposition (SVD) is a factorization of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d of the form A = V Λ Uᵀ with orthogonal matrices V and U and a matrix Λ that is zero off its main diagonal, whose entries are nonnegative and referred to as singular values. In contrast to an eigenvalue decomposition, which only exists for a square diagonalizable matrix, an SVD exists for every matrix. Truncating the SVD after the k largest singular values yields the best approximation by a matrix of rank k, which underlies dimensionality reduction. The SVD delivers the pseudoinverse, the spectral norm, and the condition number of a matrix.
terms.description: The SVD of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d is a factorization of the form \[ \mA = \mV {\bm \Lambda} \mU^{\top} \text{,} \] with orthogonal matrices \[ \mV = \big(\vv^{(1)},\,\ldots,\,\vv^{(\samplesize)}\big) \in \reals^{\samplesize \times \samplesize}, \qquad \mU = \big( \vu^{(1)},\,\ldots,\,\vu^{(\featuredim)} \big) \in \reals^{\featuredim \times \featuredim} \text{.} \] The matrix Λ ∈ Rm × d is zero off the main diagonal, whose entries Λj,j = j ≥ 0 are referred to as singular values and ordered as 1 ≥ 2 ≥ … ≥ 0. Multiplying the factorization by u(j) gives A u(j) = j v(j): A maps the orthonormal vectors u(j) to the scaled orthogonal vectors j v(j) (see Fig. 1). In contrast to an eigenvalue decomposition, which only exists for square diagonalizable matrices, an SVD exists for every matrix . The existence of the SVD and its computation build on the spectral decomposition of the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix AᵀA. That matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors u(j) of Rd, with eigenvalues j2 ≥ 0, the squares of the singular values. Setting the left singular vectors v(j) := A u(j) / j (for j > 0) then recovers A = V Λ Uᵀ. If A is itself symmetric and positive semi-definite, its SVD coincides with its eigenvalue decomposition. The largest singular value 1 equals the spectral norm A2, and the ratio of the largest to the smallest nonzero singular value is the condition number A. Retaining only the k largest singular values yields the truncated SVD \[ \widehat{\mA} \defeq \sum_{\featureidx=1}^{k} \eigval{\featureidx} \vv^{(\featureidx)} \big(\vu^{(\featureidx)}\big)^{\top} \text{,} \] a matrix of rank at most k. Among all matrices B of rank at most k, the truncation A minimizes the approximation error A - BF . The SVD can be used to compress data. A grayscale image, stored as a matrix of m × d pixel intensities, is compressed by keeping only the k largest singular values: the truncation requires only k (m + d + 1) numbers (\texttt{pythondemos/svd.py}). The SVD can be used to implement principal component analysis. For a centered feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d, the right singular vectors u(j) are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix (1)/(m) Xᵀ X, whose eigenvalues are j2/m. principal component analysis projects each data point onto the leading u(1), …, u(k), the k directions of largest variance, giving a linear dimensionality reduction. The SVD can also be used to analyze and to implement linear regression methods. Consider a feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d, whose r-th row is the feature vector of the r-th data point, and a label vector y ∈ Rm. linear regression minimizes the squared error X w - y22 over the model parameters w. That is the empirical risk minimization objective for the squared loss, the least squares problem. This objective is a proxy: the goal is a small squared error on data points outside the training set (see generalization), and the training set is what is available. Let k be the number of nonzero singular values (the rank of X). A component of w along a right singular vector u(j) with j > k leaves X w unchanged, so expand w = Σj=1k w(j) u(j) in the leading right singular vectors. Use X u(j) = jv(j) and the orthonormality of the left singular vectors v(j). The squared error then reads \[ \begin{aligned} \normgeneric{\featuremtx \weights - \labelvec}{2}^{2} &= \normgeneric{\textstyle\sum_{\featureidx=1}^{k} \eigval{\featureidx}\widetilde{w}^{(\featureidx)} \vv^{(\featureidx)} - \labelvec}{2}^{2} &= \sum_{\featureidx=1}^{k} \big(\eigval{\featureidx}\widetilde{w}^{(\featureidx)} - (\vv^{(\featureidx)})^{\top}\labelvec\big)^{2} + \sum_{\featureidx=k+1}^{\samplesize} \big((\vv^{(\featureidx)})^{\top}\labelvec\big)^{2} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] Only the components (v(j))ᵀy of y along the left singular vectors enter. The second sum is the constant, irreducible error from the part of y outside the column space of X. The first sum is minimized termwise at w(j) = (v(j))ᵀy / j for j ≤ k, the minimum Euclidean norm (pseudoinverse) solution.

terms.name: support vector machine (SVM)
terms.abstract: The support vector machine (SVM) is a binary classification method that learns a linear classifier by regularized empirical risk minimization, combining the hinge loss with a squared-norm penalty term. For a linearly separable training set and sufficiently weak regularization, the solution is the maximum-margin separating hyperplane. This hyperplane is fully determined by the feature vectors closest to it, which are called support vectors. The kernel SVM is obtained by combining the basic SVM with a feature transformation derived from a kernel function.

terms.name: tabular data
terms.abstract: Tabular data consist of data points that share a common, fixed set of attributes. The attributes serve as the features or as the label of a data point. The data points constitute the rows, or records, of a table, and the attributes are its columns. Every row has one cell per column, and the cells within one column hold values of the same attribute. The fixed attribute set separates tabular data from other types of data such as text or networks.
terms.description: Tabular data consist of data points that share a common, fixed set of attributes . As the name suggests, tabular data can be stored as a table: the rows of the table are the data points, and the columns of the table are the attributes (Fig.~1). In database theory, the relational model formalizes such a table as a relation. A relation is a set of tuples of attribute values. The relational model also provides the operations, such as selecting rows or joining tables, that database systems use to manipulate tabular data . The weather measurements at a Finnish Meteorological Institute weather station are typically represented as a table: one row for each day, with columns for the morning minimum temperature, the precipitation, and the maximum daytime temperature . The attributes serve as the features or as the label of a data point. In Fig.~1, a machine learning method forecasts the maximum daytime temperature of a day from its morning minimum temperature: it reads the minimum-temperature column as the feature and the maximum-temperature column as the label, while the precipitation column is left unused. The distinct characteristic of tabular data is the rigid shape of a table. Every row contains the same number of cells, one per column, and the cells within one column hold values of the same attribute of the data points. The value range for each cell must be clearly defined. Often the value range includes a special value (such as ``N/A'') that indicates an empty cell . An empty cell is how missing data arises in tabular data: an attribute that was not recorded for a data point leaves its cell empty, while the table keeps its shape. The fixed attribute set is what separates tabular data from other data types. A text is a sequence of tokens whose length varies from data point to data point, and a graph varies in its node and edge sets. For such data points there is often no natural choice for a fixed list of attributes. Instead, feature learning methods are developed that map such data points to feature vectors (or embeddings).

terms.name: trusted execution environment (TEE)
terms.abstract: A trusted execution environment (TEE) is a part of a computing system that runs code and holds data in isolation from the rest of the system. Neither the operating system nor the operator of the hardware can read or alter them, and the TEE can prove to another party which code it runs. Processor features such as Arm TrustZone and Intel SGX provide a TEE on an ordinary chip; a sealed, shielded embedded device without network connection is the physical extreme. In machine learning, a TEE protects three assets: the feature vectors handed to a learned hypothesis, the model parameters of that hypothesis, and the integrity of the computed prediction. It hides nothing about what the prediction reveals, which is the part that differential privacy addresses, and it protects against physical side channels only with hardware countermeasures. Compared with fully homomorphic encryption, a TEE runs at near-native speed but rests on trust in the chip vendor rather than on a mathematical proof.
terms.description: Consider a Raspberry Pi in a clinic that reads the signal of an electrocardiograph and computes, from the feature vector x of each heartbeat, the prediction h(x) of a learned hypothesis that flags an arrhythmia. The board sits in a sealed metal box with no network cable and no radio. The only inputs are the sensor cable and the power cable, and the only output is a display. The model parameters w of h and the recorded heartbeats never leave the box. A TEE is the part of a computing system that provides this kind of protection: code and data inside it cannot be read or altered from outside, and a party outside can verify which code runs inside . The sealed box is the physical extreme of a TEE. Most TEEs are instead a mode of an ordinary processor: Arm TrustZone splits the processor of the Raspberry Pi into a normal world, which runs Linux and the display software, and a secure world, which runs the prediction code and holds w and the heartbeats; the normal world cannot read the memory of the secure world even with root privileges . Intel SGX provides the same isolation for an enclave inside a process on a server , and remote attestation lets a client verify a signed digest of the enclave's code before it sends any data. Fig.~1 shows the Raspberry Pi and what each part can see. A TEE protects three assets of a machine learning system. The first is the data: the heartbeats are personal data that the clinic must not disclose. The second is the learned hypothesis: the model parameters w are the outcome of training on a costly dataset, and an attack that reads them out obtains the hypothesis without the dataset. The third is the integrity of the prediction: nobody can alter the code so that it flags fewer arrhythmias. A TEE does not protect what the prediction reveals. A membership inference attack that only observes predictions is unaffected by it, and differential privacy is the tool for that part. A TEE also does not, by itself, protect against side channels. The current drawn by the processor and the electromagnetic field it emits depend on the data it processes, and a probe held near the chip recovers secret keys from these traces . The same probe recovers the model parameters and the layer structure of an artificial neural network running on an embedded processor, one multiplication at a time . A short electromagnetic pulse or a glitch on the supply voltage can also skip an instruction, e.g., the check that rejects unsigned code . The metal enclosure of the Raspberry Pi attenuates the emitted field and blocks the pulse, tamper sensors erase w when the box is opened, and constant-time code makes the power trace independent of the data. Server TEEs face a software side channel instead: the memory access pattern of an enclave is visible to the operating system, so machine learning code inside an enclave must be data-oblivious, with access patterns that do not depend on the data , and speculative execution has leaked enclave memory outright . Two uses of TEEs beyond the sealed box are prediction in the cloud and federated learning. A hospital that rents a server can require an SGX enclave, verify by attestation that it runs the agreed prediction code, and send its feature vectors encrypted to the enclave's key, so that the cloud provider never sees them . In federated learning, an enclave on the server implements secure aggregation: the clients encrypt their model parameters updates to the enclave, which decrypts and sums them, and the server operator sees only the sum; the TrustZone secure world of each phone protects the local update in turn . A TEE, fully homomorphic encryption and differential privacy protect against different parties by different means. fully homomorphic encryption hides the data from the computing party by mathematics, at a cost of orders of magnitude in time and memory, and needs no trust in the hardware. A TEE hides the data by hardware isolation at near-native speed, and rests on trust in the chip vendor and in the absence of side channels. differential privacy bounds what the prediction reveals about any single data point and is combined with either.

terms.name: test set
terms.abstract: A test set consists of data points used to evaluate the performance of a hypothesis delivered by a machine learning method. These data points are used neither for training nor for model selection, which is why a test set is also called a hold-out set. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the average loss on the test set is an unbiased estimator of the risk of the learned hypothesis, and a concentration inequality bounds its deviation from the risk in terms of the test-set size. This yields a guideline for splitting a dataset: make the test set and the validation set just large enough for the required precision and train on the rest. The estimate stays valid only as long as no design choice depends on the test set; repeated evaluation with selection turns it into a validation set, and overlap with the training set constitutes test set contamination.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method that reads in weather recordings from the station Krems an der Donau (Austria) and delivers a hypothesis h that predicts the next day's maximum temperature from the current day's. Assessing the quality of h requires applying it to data points that the method has not used: the method typically uses a training set for learning a hypothesis via empirical risk minimization and a validation set for comparing the hypotheses learned from different models. The data points of these two sets have tuned the learned hypothesis, which therefore typically incurs a smaller loss on them than on other data points. A test set D(test) is a dataset of data points used to evaluate the performance of a hypothesis delivered by an machine learning method. Its data points enter neither the training of a model, e.g., via empirical risk minimization on the training set D(train), nor the model selection based on a validation set D(val) (Fig.~1). Since its data points are held back from training and model selection, a test set is also referred to as a hold-out set; some texts use that name for the validation set instead . For a hypothesis h that was learned and selected without reference to D(test), the test error is the average loss \[ \frac{1}{|\testset|} \sum_{\datapoint \in \testset} \lossfunc{\datapoint}{\learnthypothesis} \text{.} \] Interpreting the data points of D(train), D(val), and D(test) as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution p(z) (the independent and identically distributed assumption), the test error is an unbiased estimator of the risk of h . The distinction from the validation set is the direction of information flow: the validation error flows back into the choice of h, so it is an optimistic estimate for the chosen candidate. The test error is computed once, after all choices are frozen, and flows back into nothing. The sizes of the three sets are design choices (Fig.~2). Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the test error is an average of |D(test)| independent and identically distributed loss values, so a concentration inequality bounds its deviation from the risk: for a loss taking values in [0,1], with probability at least 1-δ the deviation is at most log(2/δ)/(2 |D(test)|) . The test set is therefore made just large enough for the required precision; the size of the validation set is chosen by the same argument, and the training set receives every remaining data point. No general rule fixes the proportions; a typical split is 50 percent for training and 25 percent each for validation and testing . The estimate stays valid only as long as the test set is used this way. Evaluating many candidate models on D(test) and keeping the best turns the test set into a validation set, and its error into a validation error; data points of D(test) that enter the training set constitute test set contamination. In an ML competition, the labels of the test set are therefore withheld from the participants: no design choice of theirs can then depend on the test data, and the reported error keeps its meaning as a risk estimate.

terms.name: training error
terms.abstract: The training error Et of a hypothesis h is its average loss over the training set, the empirical risk of h on the data points used for training. For a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization it is the smallest empirical risk that any hypothesis of the hypothesis space attains. Because the same data points selected h, the training error is below the risk on average, by a gap that grows with the size of the hypothesis space, so a hypothesis with zero training error can have a large risk. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training error of every hypothesis is a noisy estimate of its risk, and empirical risk minimization compares all of them at once, so a generalization guarantee for the empirical risk minimization solution requires the deviation to be small uniformly over the hypothesis space. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting, and a large training error indicates underfitting.
terms.description: Five years of days at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria), 2020 to 2024, are drawn in Fig.~1 as a scatterplot. Each day is a data point: its feature x is the morning minimum temperature, its label y the maximum temperature of the day. Three of the days, drawn in black, form the training set. The hypothesis space consists of the lines h(w)(x) = 10 + w x with a single model parameter, the slope w. empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss picks the slope with the smallest average squared error on the three days. The dashed bars are the prediction errors on the three days, the differences between the recorded maximum and the value of the line. The average of the three squared bars is the training error of the line. Over the hypothesis space, the training error is a function of the slope w. Fig.~2 shows it with the risk, the expected loss over the probability distribution of a day, approximated by the average over the five years. The two functions have different minimizers: the training error is smallest at the slope that empirical risk minimization picked, the risk at a larger slope. At the slope empirical risk minimization picked, the training error is a third of the risk. The training error is an average over the three days that determined the line; it does not measure the loss on a day outside the training set. The training error Et of a hypothesis h is its average loss over the training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m, \[ \trainerror = \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\datapoint^{(\sampleidx)}}{\learnthypothesis} \text{,} \] i.e., the empirical risk of h on the data points used for training. For a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization, the training error is the smallest empirical risk that any hypothesis of the hypothesis space attains on D(train), since empirical risk minimization minimizes this average. With the 0/1 loss, the training error of a classifier is the fraction of training data points it misclassifies; with the logistic loss, it is the negative average log-likelihood of the training labels . The training error is computed on the same data points that selected h, which limits its use as a measure of quality. The goal of a machine learning method is a small loss on data points that did not belong to the training set, formalized as a small risk for data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. Because h was picked to make the average on D(train) small, the training error is below the risk on average over the draw of the training set. The gap grows with the effective number of parameters of the hypothesis space . A hypothesis with zero training error can therefore have a large risk. The validation error, computed on data points that did not enter the training, is not biased in this way and estimates the risk. The difference between the risk and the training error is the generalization gap. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training error is a noisy estimate of the risk. For one fixed hypothesis h ∈ H, the empirical risk hD(train) is an average of m losses that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. It is therefore the realization of an random variable with expectation h and a variance proportional to 1/m. empirical risk minimization does not evaluate this estimate at one fixed hypothesis: it compares the estimates of all hypotheses in H and picks the smallest. The estimates form the family hD(train) h ∈ H, a stochastic process indexed by the hypothesis space: one random variable for each hypothesis, all realized by the single draw of D(train). The minimizer h of this process is itself an random variable, and its training error Et = hD(train) is the minimum of many noisy estimates, so it is below h on average. A guarantee of generalization for the empirical risk minimization solution must therefore hold uniformly over the hypothesis space: if \begin{equation} \sup_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace} \big| \emprisk{\hypothesis}{\trainset} - \risk{\hypothesis} \big| \leq \epsilon \text{,} \end{equation} then h ≤ Et + ε, and the risk of h exceeds the smallest risk in H by at most 2ε . A hypothesis space for which the uniform deviation \eqref{eq_trainerr_uniform} falls below any ε with probability at least 1-δ once m is large enough has the uniform convergence property . For a finite hypothesis space and a loss with values in [0,1], a union bound over the hypotheses and Hoeffding's concentration inequality give ε = log(2 |H| / δ) / (2 m) . For an infinite hypothesis space, log |H| is replaced by a measure of its size such as the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension or the Rademacher complexity. The validation error estimates the risk of the single hypothesis that training delivered, and one Hoeffding bound without |H| suffices for it . Fig.~3 shows the three deviations for one year of the Krems record. The risk of a line is approximated by its average loss over the days of the year, and a training set is drawn at random from them. The hypothesis space is a grid of lines h(x) = w1 x + w0. Over repeated draws, the deviation of the training error of one fixed line from its risk has mean zero. The training error of the line that empirical risk minimization picks is below its risk on average, and the largest deviation over the grid is several times the standard deviation of the fixed line's deviation. The gap of the empirical risk minimization line never exceeds the largest deviation, as the uniform deviation \eqref{eq_trainerr_uniform} requires, and both decrease as the training set grows (\texttt{pythondemos/trainerr.py}). The size of the gap depends on the hypothesis space. Every ninth day of 2024 forms a training set of forty days, and the rest of the year is held back. A straight line learned from the forty days has a training error only slightly below its average squared error on the held-back days: a line has two model parameters and can adapt little to the particular forty days. Fig.~4 shows the two errors for polynomials of degree p = 0, …, 12. The hypothesis spaces are nested, a polynomial of degree p being one of degree p+1 with a zero leading coefficient, so the training error never increases with the degree. The error on the held-back days is smallest at a low degree and grows by orders of magnitude at degree twelve, where the polynomial oscillates between the forty days it was learned from. Compared with the validation error, the training error indicates two failures of an machine learning method. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting . A large training error indicates underfitting: a hypothesis space too small, or an optimizer that stopped before the minimum. Fig.~4 also shows the effect of regularization by model pruning on the two errors: restricting the hypothesis space from degree twelve to the line raises the training error a little and lowers the error on the held-back days by four orders of magnitude.

terms.name: training
terms.abstract: Training is the application of an optimization method to a model, so that its model parameters make a loss computed from data points small. Which method applies is settled by the machine learning setting rather than by the model alone. Offline empirical risk minimization over a fixed training set is solved by gradient descent, or by stochastic gradient descent when that training set is large. In online learning, where data points arrive one at a time, online gradient descent takes one step per arriving data point. Unsupervised settings use alternating optimization instead: the expectation–maximization algorithm trains a Gaussian mixture model by alternating between responsibilities and component parameters, and the k-means algorithm alternates between cluster assignments and cluster means. All of these iterate a map from the current model parameters to the next, and training stops at or near a fixed point of that map.
terms.description: Fitting a straight line to a year of electricity records, adapting an hourly forecaster to each new reading as it arrives, and splitting customer profiles into groups are all called training. Each one adjusts the model parameters of a model H until a loss computed from data points is small. Training is therefore the application of an optimization method, and which method applies is settled by the machine learning setting rather than by the model alone. For a parametric model, each hypothesis h(w) is fixed by a choice of model parameters w, so training searches over w. Nearly every method used for that search is an iteration, \[ \weights^{(\iteridx+1)} = T(\weights^{(\iteridx)}) \text{,} \] whose operator T is what changes from one setting to the next. Training stops at, or near, a fixed point of T, where a further iteration leaves the model parameters unchanged. The learned hypothesis h is the one that these final model parameters define. Four settings and their operators are collected in Fig.~1. Offline empirical risk minimization minimizes the average loss f(w) over a fixed training set, and its operator is a step of gradient descent, T(w) = w - η ∇ f(w) with step size η . When the training set is too large to pass through at every step, stochastic gradient descent replaces ∇ f(w) by the gradient of the average loss over a few data points . In online learning there is no fixed training set: the data points arrive one at a time, and online gradient descent takes one gradient step per arriving data point, on the loss of that data point alone . Unsupervised settings replace the single gradient step by alternating optimization, which splits the model parameters into groups and minimizes over one group while holding the others fixed. Training a Gaussian mixture model alternates between the responsibilities of the mixture components for each data point and the parameters of those components, which is the expectation–maximization algorithm . The k-means algorithm alternates between assigning each data point to the nearest cluster and recomputing the cluster means . Both reach a fixed point of their operator, and neither is guaranteed to reach the smallest loss available in H. The setting therefore decides the method even when the model does not change. A shop forecasts daily bread demand from the weather with a linear model. It trains that linear model by gradient descent on a year of past records. To let the forecaster follow a changing clientele instead, it trains the same linear model by online gradient descent on each new day's sales. One of the main challenges in machine learning is to control the discrepancy between the loss on the training set and the loss on data points outside it, and no choice of optimization method removes that challenge .

terms.name: training set
terms.abstract: A training set is a dataset used to train a model: it consists of data points for which the loss incurred by each candidate hypothesis can be evaluated, so that training methods can pick the hypothesis that performs best on it. empirical risk minimization, for example, learns the hypothesis minimizing the average loss on the training set, the empirical risk, whose minimum value is the training error. Because the learned hypothesis is picked to perform well on the training set, a small training error can be misleading and result in overfitting. The validation error on a held-back validation set probes whether the learned hypothesis also predicts well outside the training set.
terms.description: The ultimate goal of a machine learning method is to learn a hypothesis (or to train a model) that incurs a small prediction error not only on the data points used for training but on any data point that is typical for the application. The prediction error is measured by some loss function: the loss is a number, typically nonnegative, that quantifies the error of a hypothesis on a single data point, such as the squared difference between the predicted and the true label. The goal is formalized probabilistically as a small risk: the expected loss under the probability distribution from which the data points are drawn (independent and identically distributed assumption). The method must therefore compare the candidate hypotheses from its hypothesis space on data points for which the loss can be evaluated. For example, in regression or classification, the loss can only be computed for data points with a known label. These data points form a dataset referred to as the training set, D(train) = z(r)r=1m. A training method is a map A whose input is the training set and whose output is a learned hypothesis, h = A(D(train)). training evaluates this map on the given training set. For example, empirical risk minimization minimizes the average loss on the training set, the empirical risk, to learn a hypothesis \[ \learnthypothesis \in \argmin_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\datapoint^{(\sampleidx)}}{\hypothesis} \text{.} \] The empirical risk of the learned hypothesis is the training error. Consider three days of weather recordings: for each day, the morning minimum temperature is the feature and the maximum daytime temperature is the label. Fig.~1 shows a training set of these three days along with two hypotheses learned from it: the straight line h(1) delivered by empirical risk minimization on the linear model, and a degree-two polynomial h(2) that passes through all three data points and therefore attains a training error of zero. Which data points are contained in D(train) decides what is learned. The choice of the training set is therefore crucial for trustworthy artificial intelligence: a training set that underrepresents a group of data points can yield a learned hypothesis that incurs a larger loss on that group, a source of unfairness (see fairness). Since h is chosen to make the empirical risk small, the training error is typically smaller than the loss that the same hypothesis incurs on data points outside D(train) . A small training error therefore does not guarantee a small loss outside the training set. Fig.~1 illustrates this: the polynomial h(2) has a smaller training error than the straight line h(1), so the training error prefers the polynomial. The figure shows no data points outside D(train), but it shows that the two curves predict different labels for feature values between and beyond the three training data points. At most one of the two curves can therefore incur a small loss on a new data point with such a feature value, and the training error cannot tell which one (see overfitting). A second subset of data points, the validation set D(val), is therefore held back from model training (Fig.~2): the average loss on D(val), the validation error, probes the learned hypothesis on data points it was not trained on. Comparing the two errors diagnoses the machine learning method: if both are small, the learned hypothesis is likely to predict well outside D(train) as well. A small training error paired with a validation error far above it indicates overfitting; one typical cause is a hypothesis space that is too large for the number of data points in D(train).

terms.name: transfer learning
terms.abstract: Transfer learning is the reuse of what was learned on one learning task to solve another learning task. A learning task can be characterized by a probability distribution of data points, and the effectiveness of transfer learning depends on the similarity of the corresponding probability distributions. Task similarity can be encoded as a similarity graph whose edge weights couple the learning tasks at its nodes; transfer learning methods can then be obtained by optimization over this graph.

terms.name: transformer
terms.abstract: A transformer is an artificial neural network built by composing layers, each of which transforms the features of a data point made up of smaller units, so-called tokens, such as the words of a text or the patches of an image. The feature vectors of the tokens are stacked into a matrix; each layer maps this matrix to one of the same shape, so that layers can be composed freely into a deep artificial neural network. The layers alternate between token mixing, which combines information across tokens, and a position-wise multilayer perceptron, which transforms each token separately.
terms.description: Many machine learning applications involve data points that consist of smaller units, so-called tokens: a text consists of words, and an image consists of patches of pixels (see Fig.~1). A transformer is an artificial neural network that is built by composing layers, each of which transforms the features of such a token-based data point . The feature vectors (or embeddings) x(1), …, x(n) ∈ Rd of the n tokens are stacked into a matrix X = (x(1), …, x(n))ᵀ ∈ Rn × d. Each layer of the original transformer maps such a matrix to a transformed matrix of the same shape, so that layers can be composed freely into a deep artificial neural network . For example, a transformer that translates a sentence transforms the stacked word embeddings, layer by layer, into feature vectors from which the translated words are predicted ; transformers also process images by taking patches as tokens . Contemporary LLMs, such as GPT-3, are transformers trained to predict the next token of a text . Some transformer variants reduce the number of tokens in deeper layers . The layers of a transformer alternate between two types of transformations of X (see Fig.~2). A token-mixing layer maps X to a new matrix X, each row of which is a weighted sum of the rows of X, with weights that can depend on X itself; the tokens thereby interact. In the original transformer, token mixing is implemented by multi-head attention ; attention distinguishes transformers from RNNs, which process the tokens of a data point sequentially instead of in parallel . A position-wise multilayer perceptron then transforms each row of X separately . For each of the two transformations, a residual connection adds the input of the transformation to its output, and a subsequent layer normalization standardizes each row of the resulting matrix . The matrices produced by successive layers represent the tokens at increasingly abstract levels. This progression is measured by probing: a simple classifier is trained to predict a chosen property from the output of a single layer, and the depth at which the property becomes predictable locates it in the network. In a language transformer, word-level properties are predictable from the output of early layers. One example is a part-of-speech tag, which marks whether a word is a noun, a verb, or an adjective. Relations between tokens far apart in the text become predictable only in deeper layers . Deep CNNs show the same progression, from edges and textures in early layers to object parts in deeper ones . Vision transformers develop it too: their early layers split attention between nearby and distant patches, while the deeper layers attend across the whole image . In language and vision transformers alike, the most informative representations often arise in the middle layers, whose outputs can outperform those of the final layer as features for other tasks . The token mixing that produces the matrix of each layer is computationally expensive. attention compares every pair of tokens, so its cost grows as n2 with the number n of tokens . This quadratic growth motivates alternative techniques for token mixing. Any transformation that combines the rows of X can replace attention: an multilayer perceptron applied across tokens , a fixed Fourier transform , or a state-space layer whose cost is linear in n .

terms.name: transparency
terms.abstract: Transparency is a key requirement for trustworthy artificial intelligence: it names the duties to close the information gaps between the provider of an artificial intelligence system, its deployer, and the persons affected by its predictions. For machine learning methods, transparency is often used interchangeably with explainability: explanations, delivered along with the predictions of a learned hypothesis, let a human user anticipate those predictions. The EU AI Act makes transparency a binding design requirement. Under the Act, the provider must design a high-risk artificial intelligence system so that its deployer can interpret the delivered predictions. Persons interacting with an artificial intelligence system must be informed of that fact. Affected persons may obtain an explanation of decisions based on the predictions delivered by a high-risk artificial intelligence system. The Act also requires documentation of the algorithm design, the training datasets, and the intended use of an artificial intelligence system, as well as a machine-readable marking of synthetic content as artificially generated.
terms.description: Consider a bank that uses an artificial intelligence system to score loan applications. The loan officer sees only the score, and the applicant might not even know that an artificial intelligence system was involved. Transparency names the duties to close such information gaps; it is a fundamental requirement for trustworthy artificial intelligence . In the context of machine learning methods, transparency is often used interchangeably with explainability : explanations, delivered along with the predictions of a learned hypothesis, let a human user anticipate those predictions . Some machine learning methods inherently offer this form of transparency. classification methods quantify the confidence in an individual prediction via the distance of the feature vector from the decision boundary. A shallow decision tree does not require a separately constructed explanation: presenting the tree as a flow chart of explicit, human-readable decision rules is an explanation of every prediction it delivers (see interpretable machine learning) . In the broader scope of AI systems, transparency extends beyond explainability: it includes informing persons that an artificial intelligence system is in use and providing information about the limitations, the overall reliability, and the intended use of the system as a whole. The binding transparency obligations discussed below are those of the EU AI Act; other jurisdictions impose related but distinct duties, e.g., the Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act and the court proceedings State v. Loomis on the use of a proprietary recidivism-risk score in sentencing . The Act distributes its obligations among three roles: the provider that develops an artificial intelligence system, the deployer that uses it, and the persons who interact with the artificial intelligence system or are affected by its output (see deployer). The Act's term \emph{output} denotes the predictions delivered by a learned hypothesis; the machine learning term \emph{prediction} is used below. Like interpretability and explainability, which are relative to a specific user or group of users, transparency is relative to its addressee: what must be disclosed depends on the role. Concretely, Fig.~1 locates these obligations in a scatterplot of training set data points together with a learned hypothesis, for the credit-scoring example. The solid curve depicts the learned hypothesis h that the artificial intelligence system applies: it maps the income x of an applicant to a predicted credit score h(x), and a loan is approved when the predicted score exceeds an approval threshold (dotted line). Art.~13 concerns the use of this map: the deployer must be able to interpret the delivered predictions — here, to read off the prediction h(x') for an applicant with income x' (open square) and its distance from the threshold. The filled circles depict the training set D(train) of completed loans, with income as the feature x and credit score as the label y, from which h was learned, e.g., via empirical risk minimization — by minimizing the average loss of the hypothesis over D(train). Art.~11 requires the provider to document both ingredients of this training: the dataset D(train) and the design of the algorithm, including the model and the loss used. Income levels outside the range covered by D(train) (shaded region) are a limitation that the documentation must state, since no estimate of the risk computed from D(train) covers them. The right to explanation of Art.~86 concerns a single prediction: the applicant with income x', whose predicted score falls below the threshold, may ask why. One answer is a counterfactual: the smallest change of the feature that flips the decision — the income x'' (open diamond, arrow) at which h reaches the threshold. Specifically, toward the deployer, the provider must design and develop a high-risk artificial intelligence system so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable the deployers to interpret its predictions and use them appropriately . In medical diagnosis, the provider is, e.g., a company that develops an X-ray analysis tool, and a clinic that uses the tool acts as the deployer. The provider can meet the duty of Art.~13 by designing the tool to disclose to the clinician the confidence level for the predictions delivered by a learned hypothesis. This duty targets the meaning of the predictions in the context of their use; the AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology reserves the term \emph{interpretability} for this contextual meaning . This usage differs from interpretability as the comprehension of the computational process of the method; Art.~13 does not require that comprehension. Toward persons who interact directly with an artificial intelligence system, such as an artificial intelligence-powered chatbot, the provider must design the artificial intelligence system so that these persons are informed of that fact . providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must mark such content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated . This marking duty applies whether or not the artificial intelligence system is a high-risk artificial intelligence system; it is waived, e.g., where the artificial intelligence system only performs an assistive function for standard editing . For a deep fake, the deployer must, in addition, disclose visibly that the content is artificially generated or manipulated . A person can be affected by an artificial intelligence system without directly interacting with it. A patient whose diagnosis is supported by an artificial intelligence-based system deals only with the clinician. Nevertheless, the deployer must inform the patient that a high-risk artificial intelligence system is used concerning them . The EU AI Act also grants the affected person a right to explanation: the deployer must, on request, provide a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the artificial intelligence system in a decision based on its predictions . In credit scoring, for example, a loan applicant faced with an adverse automated decision may obtain from the deployer, under this right, an explanation of the contributing factors, such as income level or credit history, and use it to contest the decision (see Fig.~1). Transparency also encompasses documentation detailing the purpose and design choices underlying the artificial intelligence system.
