For a high-risk artificial intelligence system, the provider must provide documentation that covers the algorithm design and the datasets used for training . The provider of a general-purpose AI model must additionally publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training . Datasheets for datasets and model cards help practitioners understand the intended use cases and limitations of an artificial intelligence system. Fig.~2 summarizes these transparency obligations as information flows between the provider of an artificial intelligence system, its deployer, and the persons exposed to its predictions.

terms.name: unsupervised learning
terms.abstract: Unsupervised learning is the machine learning setting in which the data points of a dataset carry features but no label, so nothing says what a correct answer for a data point would be. What is sought instead is structure: clustering collects similar data points into clusters, dimensionality reduction (the unsupervised case of feature learning) replaces many features by few, and density estimation trains a probabilistic model on the feature vectors. The quality of a hypothesis is measured by how well it conforms to the geometry of the data points in the feature space, not by a comparison with a known label value. empirical risk minimization remains the design principle, with a loss built from that geometry. The price of the missing labels is the missing criterion. A validation error tells a supervised learning method when a hypothesis is worse, while the clustering error keeps falling as clusters are added and so cannot say how many there should be. Judging an unsupervised result needs something outside it, such as a downstream learning task or a person inspecting the clusters. self-supervised learning and semi-supervised learning are the other two answers to the cost of labels, differing in what they do with the same unlabeled data points.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau records eight measurements for each day of 2024: three temperatures, precipitation, sunshine duration, humidity, air pressure and wind speed. Nothing in the record says which of them is to be predicted from the others, and no quantity outside the record is attached to a day. What can still be asked of these days is how they arrange themselves: which of them resemble each other, how many of the eight numbers are needed to tell them apart, and which combinations of values are common. Unsupervised learning is the machine learning setting in which the data points of a dataset carry features but no label, and what is sought is structure among them. Formally, the input is a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of feature vectors x(r) ∈ X, with no label space. In supervised learning the label of a data point says what the correct answer would have been, and here nothing does, which is why the two settings are called learning with and without a teacher . The goal is unchanged: a small loss on any data point, also those outside D, made precise by the independent and identically distributed assumption and the risk it allows. What changes is the loss. It is a function of the feature vector alone, xh, built from the geometry of X instead of from a comparison with a label. Learning then follows the principle of supervised learning: among the hypotheses of a hypothesis space H, choose one that minimizes the average loss on the dataset, \[ \learnthypothesis \in \argmin_{\hypothesis \in \hypospace} \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \lossfunc{\featurevec^{(\sampleidx)}}{\hypothesis} \text{.} \] One choice of loss gives k-means. A hypothesis is then a list of k cluster centroids, and the loss of a data point is the squared distance from its feature vector to the nearest of them. Three learning tasks make up most of the setting, and the days at Krems carry all three. clustering partitions the data points into clusters of similar ones. The k-means algorithm with k = 2 clusters, applied to the eight measurements after each is scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, reaches a fixed point after ten iterations. Its two clusters agree with the cold and the warm half of the year on 90% of the days (see Fig.~1), although no month, season or other label entered the computation. dimensionality reduction replaces the eight features by fewer. It is the unsupervised case of feature learning, the task of learning a feature transformation from a dataset instead of designing it by hand, and what makes it unsupervised is that the feature transformation is learned from the feature vectors alone. principal component analysis delivers two features, which carry 64% of the total variance and leave a reconstruction error equal to the number of data points times the sum of the dropped eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix. Density estimation trains a probabilistic model on the feature vectors: a normal distribution learned from the temperatures of the first 244 days assigns the remaining days an average log-density of -6.45, against -7.19 for one that keeps the same means but a diagonal covariance matrix. What the missing labels cost is a criterion. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman state it plainly: supervised learning has a clear measure of success, the loss on data points held out of training, and unsupervised learning has no such direct measure . The loss minimized by an unsupervised method is intrinsic to the method, so it compares its own outputs and not its fitness for a purpose. The clustering error of k-means on the days at Krems shows what follows: it falls from 2928 for one cluster to 1156 for six, with every added cluster (Fig.~2), and it would reach zero if every day were its own cluster. The criterion therefore cannot say how many clusters the days have, whereas a validation error does grow once a hypothesis becomes worse. Judging an unsupervised result needs something from outside it: a downstream learning task it should help, or a person inspecting the clusters. Where no label exists at all, the structure is itself the deliverable. The k-means algorithm is the basis of vector quantization in image compression: an image is cut into 2 × 2 blocks of pixels, each block is a feature vector in R4, and the cluster centroids learned from the blocks form a codebook. Every block is then stored as the index of the nearest cluster centroid. With 200 cluster centroids the compressed image needs 0.239 of the original storage, and with four it needs 0.063, at a visible loss of quality . No label is involved anywhere: what the method exploits is that many blocks of a photograph look alike. Unsupervised learning is one of three answers to the cost of labels, and the three differ in what they do with the unlabeled data points. It uses them on their own and gives up the label entirely. What an annotated label would have contributed, a judgment and the disagreement that comes with it, is then contributed by the choice of loss instead. self-supervised learning constructs labels from the data points themselves by withholding some of their features, which turns the same raw collection into an ordinary supervised learning problem. semi-supervised learning keeps a few labeled data points and uses the unlabeled ones to support them. The boundary is a matter of where the label comes from, not of the data: one unlabeled dataset serves all three.

terms.name: validation error
terms.abstract: The validation error Ev of a hypothesis h is its average loss over a validation set D(val), with h fixed. For data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, Ev is the realization of an random variable whose expectation is the risk of h: the validation error is an unbiased estimator of the risk, with a standard deviation that decreases as the validation set grows. The learned hypothesis is itself random, and the validation error is unbiased conditioned on it: given the hypothesis that training delivered, the conditional expectation of the validation error is the risk of that hypothesis, provided the validation set is independent of the training set. Comparing the validation errors of hypotheses learned from different models is model selection. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting.
terms.description: Five years of days at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria), 2020 to 2024, are drawn in Fig.~1 as a scatterplot. Each day is a data point: its feature x is the morning minimum temperature, its label y the maximum temperature of the day. Three of the days, drawn in black, form the training set. A decision tree with three leaves is learned from them: it splits the range of the morning minimum at the midpoints between the three training days and predicts, on each piece, the maximum of the training day there. The resulting step function passes through all three days, so its training error is zero. Five further days, drawn as red triangles, form a validation set. The dashed bars are the prediction errors of the tree on them, the differences between the recorded maximum and the value of the step function. The average of the five squared bars is the validation error of the tree. The validation error is the average loss of the tree on days that did not belong to the training set. The training error carries no information about such days: the tree passes through the three training days by construction. The validation error is of the same order as the average squared error of the tree over all days of the five years. The validation error Ev of a hypothesis h is its average loss over a validation set D(val), \[ \valerror = \frac{1}{|\valset|} \sum_{\datapoint \in \valset} \lossfunc{\datapoint}{\learnthypothesis} \text{,} \] with h fixed. Because no data point of D(val) entered the training, Ev estimates the risk of h. The training error, computed over the training set whose average loss empirical risk minimization minimized, is below it on average: the same data points both selected h and assessed it . The validation error is an average of |D(val)| losses. For data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, Ev is the realization of an random variable whose expectation is the risk of h, since each summand has that expectation. The validation error is therefore an unbiased estimator of that risk. Its variance is the variance of a single loss divided by |D(val)|, so its standard deviation decreases as |D(val)| grows. That argument treats h as fixed. In practice h is the output of training on a training set D(train), so it is itself the realization of an random variable: a different draw of D(train) would have delivered a different hypothesis. The validation error is then unbiased conditioned on the learned hypothesis. If the data points of D(val) are independent of those of D(train), and hence of h, the conditional expectation of Ev given h is the risk of that hypothesis, \[ \expect \big\{ \valerror \mid \learnthypothesis \big\} = \risk{\learnthypothesis} \text{,} \] whichever h the training set produced . The training error has no such property: conditioned on h, the data points of D(train) are no longer independent and identically distributed realizations of the probability distribution of a data point, because h was chosen to make their average loss small. A guarantee for the validation error concerns one hypothesis only: for a loss with values in [0,1], Hoeffding's concentration inequality gives |Ev - h| ≤ log(2/δ) / (2 |D(val)|) with probability at least 1-δ, with no term for the hypothesis space H . A guarantee for the training error of the empirical risk minimization solution must hold uniformly over H, since empirical risk minimization compares all its hypotheses, and it loosens with the size of H. In a repeated experiment on one year of the Krems record, forty days are drawn at random as the training set, empirical risk minimization learns a quadratic from them, and the risk of the quadratic is approximated by its average loss over the whole year. On twenty further days drawn from the rest of the year, the deviation of the validation error from the risk of that draw's quadratic has mean zero over the draws, although the quadratic changes with every draw. The average loss over a validation set of twenty days of which ten are training days is below the risk on average, and the training error is further below (\texttt{pythondemos/valerr.py}): data points that entered the training bias the average downward. A second split of the same year: every ninth day is the training set, forty days; twenty of the remaining days are the validation set; the other days are held back from both. The hypothesis is the straight line that empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss over the linear model h(x) = w1 x + w0 delivers from the forty days, \[ \learnthypothesis(\feature) = 10.47 + 1.05 \, \feature \text{,} \] with x and h(x) in degrees Celsius, and it is fixed from here on. The risk h = E zh is an expectation over the probability distribution of a day and cannot be computed from a record of one year. The average loss of the line over the held-back days is used as its estimate, below and as the dashed line of Fig.~2. A validation set of twenty days estimates the risk with a standard deviation larger by the square root of the ratio of the two sizes. The held-back days are not a test set: nothing is selected on them. For this line the training error is slightly below the risk and the validation error is close to it. The difference between the risk and the training error, the generalization gap, is smaller for a line than the standard deviation of a twenty-day average, so one validation set of that size cannot resolve it. For a polynomial of degree nine learned from the same forty days, the training error is a small fraction of the risk. Fig.~2 shows the validation error of the line over repeated draws of a validation set of each size from the held-back days: its mean is the risk at every size, and its standard deviation decreases in proportion to 1/|D(val)|. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting . Comparing the validation errors of several candidate models is model selection . A validation set reused many times for this purpose is itself overfitted, so a test set is kept apart for the final assessment.

terms.name: validation set
terms.abstract: A validation set consists of data points that have not been used for model training. For a learned hypothesis, the average loss on the validation set, the validation error, indicates how well the hypothesis predicts the labels of data points outside the training set. The validation error is used for model selection: the hypotheses learned by different machine learning methods are compared, and the one with the smallest validation error is selected. The selected hypothesis depends on the validation set, so assessing it requires a test set whose data points entered neither training nor selection. The size of the validation set determines how reliable the validation error is. When data points are scarce, k-fold cross-validation uses each fold of the dataset in turn as validation set and averages the k validation errors.
terms.description: Consider three days of weather recordings: for each day, the morning minimum temperature is the feature and the maximum daytime temperature is the label. Fig.~1 shows a training set D(train) of three such days along with two hypotheses learned from it: the straight line h(1) delivered by empirical risk minimization on the linear model, and a degree-two polynomial h(2) that passes through all three data points and therefore attains a training error of zero. Three further days, marked by open triangles, were held back from model training: they form a validation set D(val). The validation error of a hypothesis h learned from the training set is its average loss on the validation set , \[ \frac{1}{|\valset|} \sum_{\datapoint \in \valset} \lossfunc{\datapoint}{\learnthypothesis} \text{.} \] Here, zh is the loss of h on the data point z. In Fig.~1, the polynomial h(2) attains a training error of zero but a validation error of 17.3, while the linear hypothesis h(1) has a training error of 2.9 and a validation error of 3.0. The comparison of the two validation errors is an instance of model selection: the hypotheses learned by different machine learning methods are compared, and the one with the smallest validation error is selected . In Fig.~1, the hypothesis h(1) is selected, since 3.0 < 17.3. The selected hypothesis depends on D(val): its validation error is the smallest of the compared validation errors, so the validation error of the selected hypothesis is biased downward. A bound that covers the selected hypothesis must hold for all compared hypotheses at once, which requires a validation set larger than the size that Hoeffding's inequality suggests for one hypothesis . Assessing the hypothesis learned from the model that was chosen on the basis of the validation errors requires a third dataset whose data points entered neither training nor selection: the test set D(test) . In Fig.~2, the three days of the test set, marked by open squares, yield a test error E(test) = 1.3 for the selected hypothesis h(1). The test error is the only one of the three numbers that was not used to choose anything, so it is not biased by selection. With only three test days, however, it is itself a noisy estimate of the risk of h(1). The size |D(val)| determines how well the validation error reflects the overall performance of a learned hypothesis: the validation error is an average of |D(val)| losses, one per validation data point, and a validation set that is too small results in an unreliable validation error . For a loss with values in [0,1] and a fixed hypothesis h, Hoeffding's inequality guarantees that, with probability at least 1 - δ for a confidence parameter δ ∈ (0, 1) chosen by the user, the risk of h lies within an uncertainty band of half-width ε around the measured validation error. The guarantee requires that \[ |\valset| \geq \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 \epsilon^{2}} \text{.} \] Fig.~3 shows this lower bound as a function of the half-width ε for three values of δ; it holds for any validation error, not only those of the weather example. Narrowing the band is costly: halving ε quadruples the required size. To have the validation error within ε = 0.1 of the risk with δ = 0.1, it suffices to hold back |D(val)| ≥ 150 data points, the point of the dashed curve at ε = 0.1 in Fig.~3, regardless of the hypothesis space and of the size of D(train). The bound can be checked by simulation. Fig.~4 reports how often the validation error of a fixed hypothesis deviates from the risk by more than ε, when the validation set holds exactly the number of data points that the bound requires. The loss used there takes the values 0 and 1 with equal probability, so its variance is the largest a loss with values in [0,1] can have. Each share is measured over 200,000 validation sets. Every measured share stays below its δ, and below δ / 4, so the size the bound requires is larger than the size the measured deviations call for. A validation set eight times smaller does fail the guarantee: at ε = 0.1 and δ = 0.1, where the bound asks for 150 data points, 19 of them leave 36 of every 100 validation errors farther than ε from the risk. When data points are scarce, holding back a large validation set leaves few data points for the training set. As a remedy, k-fold cross-validation divides the dataset into k folds and, for each fold in turn, uses that fold as validation set and the other k - 1 folds as training set, so each of the k validation errors is computed on different data points and for a different learned hypothesis. Every fold yields a noisy validation error, an average of the losses over the few data points of the fold, and averaging the k per-fold validation errors produces a more reliable estimate of the risk. Taken together, a typical machine learning workflow splits the available dataset three ways: a training set to learn hypotheses, a validation set to select among them (or the folds of k-fold cross-validation in its place), and a test set, used only once, to assess the selected hypothesis.

terms.name: variance
terms.abstract: The variance of a real-valued random variable is the expectation of the squared difference between the random variable and its mean. It quantifies the spread of the probability distribution of the random variable around the mean: a small variance means that realizations concentrate near the mean. The term also refers to the sample variance of a dataset; the two usages are consistent, since the sample variance is the variance of the random variable obtained by drawing a data point uniformly from the dataset. Under the squared error loss, the variance is the smallest risk that a constant prediction of a numeric label can achieve. For a random vector, the variance is the expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of the deviation from the mean. This quantity equals the trace of the covariance matrix of the random vector, i.e., the sum of the variances of its entries.
terms.description: The Helsinki Kaisaniemi weather station recorded daily maximum temperatures of 20.1, 19.9, 22.2, 21.7, 20.3, 19.6 and 19.7 ∘C on 24--30 August 2026 , and every reading lies within two degrees of their average of 20.5 ∘C. How far readings scatter around their average is what the variance measures. The variance of a real-valued random variable y is the expectation E ( y - Ey )2 of the squared difference between y and its expectation Ey, also called its mean. The term is also used to refer to the sample variance of a finite dataset D = y(1), …, y(m) ∈ R. These two usages are consistent. A dataset defines a discrete random variable y(D) = y(I) on the sample space 1, …, m. Here, the index I is chosen uniformly at random, i.e., I=r=1/m for all r=1,…,m, so the probability distribution of y(D) is the empirical distribution of the dataset. The variance of y(D) is precisely the sample variance \[ \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx=1}^{\samplesize} \Big( \truelabel^{(\sampleidx)} - \frac{1}{\samplesize} \sum_{\sampleidx'=1}^{\samplesize} \truelabel^{(\sampleidx')} \Big)^{2} \text{,} \] i.e., the average squared deviation of the data points from their sample mean. Fig.~1 depicts the seven Helsinki readings of 24--30 August 2026 as realizations of such an random variable, together with their sample mean and the deviation of each measurement from it. For the seven temperatures of Fig.~1, the sample variance is the number 6.34/7 ≈ 0.91, computed from the readings alone. It estimates the variance of the random variable that generated them, which is a property of its probability distribution and is never observed exactly. The sample variance also serves as a threshold for detecting outliers: a common rule declares a data point an outlier when its squared deviation from the sample mean exceeds nine times the sample variance, i.e., three standard deviations . The reading of 22.2 ∘C deviates by 1.7 ∘C, whose square 2.89 is about three times the sample variance, so the rule keeps every reading. For an random variable with a finite second moment, i.e., E y2 < ∞, the mean is the constant b that minimizes the risk E ( y - b )2. The variance is the smallest value this risk attains, i.e., its minimum at b = Ey : \[ \expect\big\{ \big( \truelabel - \expect\{\truelabel\} \big)^{2} \big\} = \min_{\offset \in \reals} \expect\big\{ ( \truelabel - \offset )^{2} \big\} \text{.} \] This minimum-risk characterization applies directly to the simplest machine learning problem, predicting a numeric label y without using any features. The hypothesis space for this problem consists of the constant maps h(·) = b with b ∈ R. Each such hypothesis amounts to a single bias term: it delivers the same prediction b for every data point. Given a training set D(train) = y(1), …, y(m) that consists of labels y(r) ∈ R only, empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss amounts to finding the constant that best predicts the label of a data point. The solution b is the sample mean of the labels (see mean), and the training error of the learned hypothesis is the sample variance of the labels . For the temperatures of Fig.~1, the learned hypothesis is the dashed line: b = 20.5 ∘C, with training error 6.34/7 ≈ 0.91. The variance of the label is the smallest risk that a constant prediction can achieve under the squared error loss. It therefore serves as a baseline: an machine learning method that uses features is useful only if its risk falls below the variance of the label. Variance extends from a real-valued random variable to a random vector x as the expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of the deviation from the mean, E x - Ex 22 = trx. This is the sum of the variances of the entries of x, written compactly as the trace of the covariance matrix x, whose diagonal carries those variances .

terms.name: explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)
terms.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is the subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with making the predictions of machine learning methods understandable to humans. Much of it can be posed as a function approximation problem: a learned hypothesis is explained by a simpler function that a human can comprehend. explanations differ in what they are made of. One kind reports a score for each feature, the weights of a linear map fitted near the data point (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) or additive contributions to the prediction (SHapley Additive exPlanations). A counterfactual instead names another feature vector, the closest one whose prediction differs. A concept activation vector states the explanation in a concept the user names, located in the activations inside the trained method. All three are post hoc and treat the learned hypothesis as fixed. The alternative is a hypothesis that needs no separate explanation, reached by restricting the hypothesis space to hypotheses a human comprehends or by regularization that favors such hypotheses. explainable empirical risk minimization instead keeps the hypothesis space and penalizes deviations from the predictions of one specific user.
terms.description: XAI is the subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with making the predictions of machine learning methods understandable to humans. It aims to complement each prediction by an explanation of how it has been obtained. If the machine learning method uses a sufficiently simple hypothesis space, the learned hypothesis may be inherently interpretable and no separate explanation is needed ; see interpretable machine learning, discussed further below. The term XAI was popularized by a program of the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency ; in the context of machine learning, the synonymous term explainable machine learning is also used. The underlying property is explainability, which the international terminology standard for artificial intelligence defines for AI systems in general . XAI can be posed as a function approximation problem. A trained hypothesis h: X → Y, e.g., delivered by an opaque deep net, is typically a composition of many nonlinear layers, a function on a high-dimensional feature space X . Explaining h at a data point with feature vector x ∈ X means answering one question about that function in a form a human can comprehend. The examples of explanations below are of three kinds, distinguished by what the explanation is made of. The first is a score for each feature of the data point. The scores are the coefficients of a simpler hypothesis that agrees with h near x and comes from a user-parsable hypothesis space. local interpretable model-agnostic explanations fits a linear map as that simpler hypothesis, and its weights are the scores. Fig.~1 draws that construction. The second is another feature vector, one whose prediction differs. The third is a concept the user names, located inside the trained method rather than among the features of the data point. All three are post hoc: they treat the learned hypothesis as fixed and construct the explanation after training. The first kind of explanation reports one score per feature, saying how much that feature contributed to the prediction. local interpretable model-agnostic explanations obtains the scores as the weights of a linear map fitted to h near x . SHapley Additive exPlanations obtains them by decomposing the prediction into a base value and one contribution per feature, the contributions being Shapley values. The two deliver the same kind of explanation and differ in how its scores are computed. When features are properties of image pixels, the feature scores are a second image of the same size: one relevance score per pixel (see Fig.~2). The class activation map is one construction of such a per-pixel score. The second kind of explanation is a counterfactual. It reports no scores and approximates nothing. It asks instead where h takes a different value, pointing out how the features must be modified for the prediction h(x) to come out differently. A counterfactual identifies the smallest such modification, with closeness measured by a chosen metric (see Fig.~3). In a loan-approval setting, for example, local interpretable model-agnostic explanations reports which of the applicant features, such as income and credit history, its local linear approximation assigns the largest weight to in a rejection. A counterfactual instead states the smallest modification of those features that would turn the prediction into an approval. The third kind of explanation refers not to the features of the data point but to a concept the user specifies. Such a concept is defined by a dataset of examples the user supplies. A concept activation vector locates such a concept as a direction in the space of the activations of one hidden layer of an artificial neural network: the normal vector of a decision boundary that separates the supplied examples carrying the concept from those that do not . In contrast to local interpretable model-agnostic explanations and counterfactual explanations, a concept activation vector needs access to the internal computations of a machine learning system. One such internal computation is the activation z = f(x) of a hidden layer in a deep net. A deep net computes h by feeding the activations z to the final layers, which deliver a score s(z) for each label; the prediction h(x) follows from those scores (see concept activation vector). In an image classifier, for example, a user who suspects that photographs are labeled zebra through the concept \emph{stripes} supplies photographs that show stripes and photographs that do not. Each of these photographs results in an activation z in the layer of interest. These activations are then used to fit a linear classifier that separates the two sets, and its normal vector is the concept activation vector for \emph{stripes}. How much the concept contributed to the prediction of a zebra photograph is then measured by the directional derivative of the score s along that concept activation vector. The above XAI methods construct an explanation after training, for a learned hypothesis that is already fixed. The alternative is to arrive at one that needs no separate explanation. interpretable machine learning does so by admitting only hypotheses a human comprehends directly. This can be achieved by manually choosing a hypothesis space that is simple enough, or by regularization that favors hypotheses with specific properties, such as sparsity or predictability. explainable empirical risk minimization uses regularization but not to that end: it leaves the hypothesis space as it is and delivers explainability to one specific user. That user supplies their own predictions for the data points of a training set, and the penalty term measures the deviation of the predictions of the learned hypothesis from the user predictions . Three aspects of an explanation are studied: whom it serves, how much of the learned hypothesis it covers, and whether it is faithful. How much an explanation achieves depends on who receives it: explainability is measured relative to a specific user. explanations can be local, concerning a single prediction, or global, characterizing the learned hypothesis as a whole . An explanation must be faithful, i.e., reflect the computation that the learned hypothesis carries out. When the explanation scores the features, this can be tested rather than asserted. A class activation map is faithful for a prediction if flipping the pixels it scores highest changes that prediction more often than flipping as many of the pixels it scores lowest. Perturbing the highest-scoring regions first and recording how quickly the predicted class score falls is the standard form of the test . For the image of Fig.~2 and a linear classifier fitted to images of that kind, flipping the three highest-scoring pixels changes the prediction, while flipping the pixels in the opposite order leaves it unchanged through all 36 of them. The map-guided order also changes the prediction sooner on each of 200 noisy variants of the image. Faithfulness also limits what a post hoc explanation can achieve: one that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis itself, so a simpler explanation deviates from it somewhere . Two legal instruments explicitly state requirements on XAI. Under the general data protection regulation, a person subjected to a decision taken by automated means is entitled to ``meaningful information about the logic involved'' in that decision . Communicating the algorithm itself is not a sufficiently concise and intelligible explanation . counterfactual information can be appropriate: the extent to which a variation in the personal data would have led to a different result. The second instrument is the EU AI Act, which requires for a high-risk artificial intelligence system that affected persons obtain ``clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure'' (see right to explanation).
